John too was baptizing at Aenon, near Salim, because there was abundant water there, and people came and were baptized. For the Lord would come to the city for the feasts,
so that he might perform signs in the midst of all the people, and after the feasts he would go back to the Jordan, for many gathered there as well.
Wherever there was a large crowd, the Lord would always go there to teach and to do good. Yet it was not he himself who baptized, but his disciples, as the evangelist says further on:
"Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did." So why did he not baptize himself?
The reason is this: John had said earlier, "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire," but the Lord had not yet given the Holy Spirit,
and therefore he rightly did not baptize himself; instead his disciples baptized, so that they might bring many to Christ.
Why then, when the Lord's disciples began to baptize, did John not stop baptizing, but went on baptizing at Aenon as well?
And why did he not stop, so that the baptism of the Lord's disciples might become more acceptable? He did not stop baptizing for this reason:

so that he would not throw his own disciples into still greater jealousy toward them. For if with so much teaching and preaching about Christ he could not bring them to accept him, then had he done this, would they not have fallen into great jealousy?
For this reason too Christ began to preach more fully at the time when John had died.
And I think that John's early death was permitted for this reason: so that all that multitude might follow Christ, and their minds might no longer be divided between the two of them.
And apart from this, he also went on baptizing while always preaching Christ and showing him to be superior;
and since he acted in this way, his baptizing was all the better and was no opposition to Christ's disciples, for he was helping them and sending to Christ all who had been baptized by him,
not drawing glory to himself but to Christ; and the people accepted his testimony more readily than that of the apostles,
for all held him to be great, as Matthew says:
"Jerusalem and Judea beyond the Jordan went out to him." And both baptisms, that of John and that of Christ's disciples, were one and the same, for neither he nor they could yet give the Holy Spirit.
Rather, this was the reason for both their baptism and his: that they might receive Christ. And so that you may know that both those baptisms were one, listen to the words that follow:
Gospel: There arose a dispute between John's disciples and the Jews about purification.

Interpretation: John's disciples were always envious of Christ's disciples and of Christ himself. When they saw his disciples baptizing, they began to talk to those who had been baptized. They praised the baptism of their own teacher and spoke of it as the higher one.
So they began to talk to one of the people baptized by Christ's disciples and tried to persuade him, but they could not persuade him.

This is why the evangelist says: "A dispute arose between John's disciples and the Jews about purification." Look at the evangelist's [?]: he did not say this to accuse them. Instead, as far as he could, he softened their error and said only that a dispute took place, when in fact they did all of it out of envy. The words that follow show this, for they came to John and said to him:
Gospel: "Rabbi, the one who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, behold,
he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him."

Interpretation: That is, "The one you baptized, whom you made known and taught everyone about through your testimony, has now become your equal. He was with you beyond the Jordan. He was at the level of your disciples, but now he has separated from you and is baptizing, and everyone is going to him, while we are held in contempt." From this it is clear that they had not beaten that Jew in argument, the one they were disputing with.

They said this because their minds were weak and they had not been cleansed of human feelings. But John did not rebuke them harshly, because he was afraid that they too might break away from him and fall into some other evil. Instead he said to them:
Gospel: A man cannot receive anything of himself unless it has been given to him from heaven.
You yourselves bear me witness that I said: "I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him."
Interpretation: That is, if you believe my testimony, since you say "to whom you bore witness," then accept it from this and understand

that he is far superior to me. For I bore witness to this very thing: "I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals." And again, that testimony was not mine but God's, for what good could a man have of himself, except from God?

So that testimony too was from God. For if you consider it trustworthy, I also bore witness to this, that "I have been sent before him," and I am a servant, one who carries out the word of the one who sent me.
It is not by any human act that I bestow this on him; rather, by the sending of his Father I say everything that has been commanded to me.
And do not suppose that because I bore witness to him I am therefore greater than he, for he is Lord of all. For this reason he went on to add:
Gospel: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom,
but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice."
Interpretation: How is it that he who said, "I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandals," now calls himself his friend? It is not that he now exalts himself. Far from it!
Rather, by this name of friendship he shows that he is not grieved at this matter, but is very glad and eager. He had striven hard for this matter to come about in this way.
And he showed all this by that name of friendship, for the servants of the bridegroom do not rejoice the way his friends rejoice.

And again, he did not say this to cause his disciples to stumble, nor was he making himself equal to him. He said it, first, for the sake of his disciples, and second, so that no one would think he was grieved over this matter. That is why he called himself a friend: to show that not only is he not grieved, but he even rejoices greatly. It is as if he were saying: "I came for this, that it should be done this way, and I would have been very grieved if it had not been done so. If the bride had not been joined to the bridegroom, then I would mourn. But now I rejoice, for what I wanted has been accomplished, since through his advancement we are saved. And now I am glad that my work has been completed and the bride has come to know the bridegroom. And are you grieved at this, you who say, 'All are going to him'?

For this is what I strove for, and now that it has come about, I rejoice and exult." But what is meant by the saying "stands and hears"? Simply that he took this saying from the figure of speech and applied it to this matter. Since he mentioned the bridegroom and the bride, he shows that the union of spouses is brought about in this way, by voice and word. In the same way the Church was joined to God. That is why Paul said: "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing from words," and "I rejoice at the voice." Nor did he say the word "stands" idly. He said it to show that his own part has entirely come to rest. From then on he has handed over the bride, which is the assembly of believing people, to the bridegroom, and he himself needs only to stand and hear. Therefore he says:
Gospel: "This joy of mine has been fulfilled."

Commentary: That is to say: "I have accomplished the work that it was mine to do, and I am no longer able to do anything more." And he showed them beforehand that great glory of his, which was to come even after the passion, and said to them:
Gospel: "He must increase, but I must decrease."

Commentary: That is to say: "What you are afraid of is not only as it is now, but after a little while it will be far greater; yet over all this I rejoice, for his glory is my joy." Do you see how, little by little and with wisdom, he dissolved the passion of their envy and showed them that they were attempting impossible things? For this reason it was arranged by providence that this should happen in his own lifetime, so that he himself might tell them of the glory of the Lord, and so that, if they did not believe, they would no longer have any argument, for they themselves asked him and heard all of this from him.
And if they had not believed, they would no longer have had any argument, like the Jews, who sent to him and afterward did not believe his word and so shut themselves out from every argument.

Instruction 29, on vainglory. But what do we learn from all this? Only this: that vainglory is the cause of every evil. It led them to envy, and it also persuaded them, and they came to Jesus and said to him, "Why do your disciples not fast?" Let us flee, then, beloved, from this passion, and if we flee from it, we shall escape Gehenna. For this is what kindles the fire of Gehenna; it spreads its branches everywhere and has taken hold of every age and every nation.
It has turned churches upside down, and cities and nations,
until it went out into the deserts, and there too it showed its evil power. For those who had withdrawn far from the glory of the world, from every luxury and from those mighty desires,
these it often put to shame. This passion of vainglory overcame them, and through this passion they lost all of that,
and [he] was shown to be worse than the tax collector who had committed many sins.
Yet it is not hard to censure this passion, and everyone is able to do that; the real task is to overcome it.
And we shall overcome it in this way: if we set glory against glory.
For just as we despise wealth when we look toward another wealth, and we despise this life when we consider the eternal life,

so too let us trample down vainglory, if we have a desire for that future glory. For human glory is empty and vain; it has only the name and not the reality. But that heavenly glory is true, and not men but angels and archangels and the King of angels will be the praisers of such a person. If you keep in mind that eternity and that Judge, nothing of the affairs of the world will lead you astray. For even in this world, who among those standing before the king, one whom the king himself and all his soldiers praise, would choose the praise of flies and gnats? And such is human glory in comparison with God: like the sound of flies and gnats compared with that praise of the king and the rulers. But we who know this worthlessness of human affairs, let us seek by every means that eternal and incomprehensible glory, which may we all be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 30
This saying: "He who comes from above is above all, and he who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth."
Interpretation: Evil is that disease of vainglory, full of many thorns, a wild and many-headed beast, for it devours those who love it.
For just as a worm devours that from which it is born, and rust consumes the iron from which it comes, so pride destroys the soul that nurtures it.
So we must make great efforts to root it out of ourselves. For see here too how much John taught his disciples, who were gripped by this disease, and how he calmed them only with difficulty.
For in addition to what he said before, he also says the words that have now been read:
that "He who comes from above is above all, and he who is from the earth is of the earth and speaks of the earth."
Now this saying is as if you were to say: "By your testimony he has become great."
But know this: it is impossible that he who has come from heaven should be glorified by this one who is from the earth. And this saying, namely:
"He is above all," indicates this: that he has no need of another's testimony, but he is sufficient as a witness to himself, for he is higher than all.
And he calls himself "of the earth and speaking of what is earthly," not because he was saying anything of his own accord, but just as Christ said:
"If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe," and he called baptism earthly, not because it is earthly, but because compared with his incomprehensible birth it is earthly;
so too here John, compared with the teaching of Christ, called himself one who speaks of what is earthly,

That is, he is saying: "My words are lowly and worthless compared with his, for all the treasures of wisdom are hidden in him. But I am one who lives on the earth and am unworthy of him, for he has come from heaven."
So in this way he loosened their passion, and only then began to speak loftier words about Christ with boldness. For first he pulled up the thorns, and then he sowed the good seed, and said:
Gospel: "He who comes from heaven is above all, and what he has seen and heard, to this he testifies, and no one receives his testimony."
Commentary: He spoke a great and lofty word about him, and now he has again brought it down to lowliness, saying: "What he has seen and heard," and these words are human.
Yet he did not know what he knew through hearing and seeing, but he possessed all of it by nature,
for he has come forth perfect from the bosom of the Father, for he says: "As the Father knows me, I also know the Father."
What then does this saying mean, when he says:

"What he has seen and heard, to that he testifies"? It means this: we confirm every matter through these two senses, sight and hearing. What we have seen or heard, we hold to be trustworthy. In the same way John was confirming this.

For this reason he said: "What he has seen and heard," that is to say, that nothing of what he has said is false, but all is true, for he is not one who speaks of unknown matters, so as to say something he did not know, but all that he has seen and knows in truth, this he teaches. For even when the Lord himself says: "As I hear, I judge," and: "What I have heard from the Father, this I speak," and whenever he says anything of the kind, he does not say it so that we should understand that he needs teaching,

for that would be the ultimate impiety, but he said all this so that the impious Jews could not say that "he does not speak the truth." For since they did not hold the opinion of him that was fitting, for this reason he continually brought forward the Father as a witness, and many times the Scriptures as well, and he did all this because of their weakness.
Now this saying of John's amounts to this: It is fitting for me to listen to the things spoken by him,
for he has come from heaven and tells us what he alone knows,

and no one else. And this is what is indicated by the saying he spoke: "What he has seen and heard, to that he testifies," meaning that he teaches us the mysteries that he alone knows. But the saying he spoke, "No one accepts his testimony," does not indicate that no one at all was found obedient to him. For the Lord had disciples, and others also believed; but here he shows how few the believers were. Otherwise, if he were saying that absolutely no one believed, how could he have said immediately that:
Whoever has accepted his testimony has set his seal to this: that God is true.
For here he also reproves his own disciples for not having believed,
who did not believe even after this.

And this too is evident from the fact that, when he was in prison, he sent them to him so that they might believe, those to whom Christ said: "Blessed is he who is not offended because of me." And for this reason he said here that:
"No one receives his testimony." It is as if he were telling them: "Do not think that his word is in any way false and that this is why many do not believe it. For he has seen everything,
and he speaks what is true."
Now this "he says" he was also saying as a reproof to the Jews, just as the Evangelist too said at the beginning of his discourse: "He came to his own, and his own did not receive him."
Gospel: "He who has accepted his testimony has set his seal that God is true."
Commentary: He frightens them and makes them understand that whoever does not believe him angers not only him but the Father as well.
Gospel: He whom God has sent speaks the words of God.
Commentary: Since he speaks the words of God, it is evident that whoever believes him believes what is God's; and whoever is unbelieving is unbelieving toward God.
And as for "has set his seal," this means that he has shown that God is true. By this saying he increases their fear, for he says that:
It is impossible to disbelieve him, unless someone accuses God who sent him of falsehood, for he speaks everything that is his.
Do you see how he frightened them? For they as yet counted disobedience to Christ as nothing, but he has shown that disobedience to him is contempt of God.
And then he spoke yet another saying, according to the measure of their weakness:
Gospel: "For God does not give the Spirit by measure."

Interpretation: Again he brought his speech back down to lowliness, for he varies it in different ways so that his hearers might find it acceptable. If he had said something great and lofty about Christ, they would not have accepted it. For this reason he brings in the Father, speaks of everything in relation to him, and teaches about Christ as about a man. But what does this saying mean, when he says:

"God does not give the Spirit by measure"? He means this: "All of us have received the grace of the Spirit by measure." For here by "Spirit" he means the grace of the Holy Spirit. That grace is distributed among the saints, and we have it by measure, each according to his own measure. But Christ has it undivided, not by measure but completely. He has the whole Holy Spirit within himself, whose grace is beyond counting and whose essence is still more incomprehensible. For if his grace is incomprehensible, how could anyone comprehend his essence? He has all the grace of the Holy Spirit completely within himself and knows all that belongs to God. "So how can you doubt him and refuse to believe him?" he says. For he says nothing that was not of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. He has not yet said anything about the Word of God. Instead, he made his teaching credible by appealing to the Father and the Holy Spirit. They knew that there is God and that there is the Holy Spirit, though not in the way they should have, but they did not know the Son at all.

For this reason he brought his words back to the Father and the Holy Spirit, and in this way confirmed what had been said. For if those words had not been spoken because of their weakness, it would have been quite unfitting to say such things about Christ. Christ was not trustworthy because he had the grace of the Holy Spirit; he does not need help at all, but is himself sufficient for himself. Rather, John spoke this way because of their weakness. I say all this so that we do not pass over the words of Scripture without examining them. We should also look carefully into the speaker's intention, the hearers' understanding, and everything else of this kind. Teachers do not say everything as they would wish. They say many things in a way that suits the understanding of the weak. That is why Paul says: "I could not speak to you as to spiritual people. As to people of the flesh, I gave you milk to drink, and not solid food." It was not that he was unable to speak to them as spiritual people; they were unable to bear it. In the same way, John wanted to teach his disciples great things, but they were unable to bear them.
That is why he keeps to humble words.

Homily 30. That we should use the Scriptures as is proper, and on right living. It is necessary, then, that we understand and use the Scriptures well and properly, for the Scriptures are the weapons of the Spirit, but if we do not arm ourselves with them as is proper, they will be of no benefit to us. Understand this from bodily things: if someone has a well-made coat of mail, a helmet, a shield and a spear, and does not put on that armor as is proper and according to the rule, but puts the coat of mail on his feet, and does not place the helmet on his head but sets it backward on his face, and does not hold the shield against his chest but ties it to his feet, would he gain anything from this? Would he not rather be harmed, not through any weakness of the armor, but because of his own inexperience, since he did not use it as was the rule? So also with the Scriptures: if we do not use each word in its own place and according to its own rule,

they have their own force, but they profit us nothing. I am always telling you such words as these and I see no benefit; instead you have turned to earthly affairs and have despised spiritual ones. For this reason the teachers of the truth have no great power, but we are reproached by Jews and pagans.
And if we were negligent in everything, even then we would have nothing to say in our defense, though there would be some small excuse.

But as it is, in worldly affairs each one is sharper than a sword, while in spiritual matters I see great negligence, for outward things are reckoned as inward, and these inward matters as outward, and even more contemptible than outward things.
Or do you not know that all these writings were written not only for the people of that time,
but were written also for the instruction of us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, as the apostle Paul says about this?

"I speak at all times and no one listens, yet I will not cease speaking, and so may God give me the reward." For the one who teaches the obedient has consolation: the obedience of his hearers. But the one who speaks continually, and no one listens to him, and he still does not cease speaking, is worthy of a greater reward, because by the will of God, even though no one listened, he has fulfilled his own part. But I long for you also to be saved, and this I hold as a great reward; and I am grieved if you do not bear fruit. But may we all be worthy to bear spiritual fruits and to attain the eternal good things, by the grace and lovingkindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father belongs glory, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 31
The passage: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hands. Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life,
but whoever does not believe the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.
Commentary: It is good for a person not to strive to do everything all at once, but to accomplish his work little by little.
For this is how the arts are learned, this is how cities and temples are built, this is how all human life is sustained.

And not only bodily but also spiritual work is brought to completion in this way, for it was thus, by teaching little by little, that the Jews were delivered from idolatry, and likewise again the apostles, by drawing them little by little, converted the pagans;
likewise Christ acted toward many.
John too did this with his disciples, for he began to speak about Christ as about some marvelous man, and he wove lofty words together with lowly ones; for when he made his beginning, he spoke thus:
"A man cannot receive anything at all of himself."
Then he added a lofty statement and said: "He who comes from above is above all." Then he brought his words down again to a humble level, and said many other things, including:
"God does not give the Spirit by measure." And then he added and said: "The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hands."
And then he said, in effect: "The proclamation of good things does not bend a person as much as the proclamation of torment does." For this reason he concluded his speech here, for he said:
"Whoever believes in the Son shall have eternal life, but whoever is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God abides upon him."
Here again he has carried his word up to the Father, for he did not say, "the wrath of the Son,"
though the Son is the judge, but he named the Father, because they still feared the Father greatly, whereas they did not yet know the Son well.
What then? If someone only believes in the Son of God, is this enough for his salvation? Far from it! For he says:
"Not everyone who says to me,

'Lord, Lord,' shall enter the kingdom of heaven," for even blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is enough to be handed over to Gehenna. And why do I speak only of heresy? For even if someone is orthodox, if he does not have good works, he goes to hell. John, however, does not speak in this way, that:

"Whoever believes, he shall be saved," but he says, "This thing is what procures life." That is, if he has good works; but if he has evil works, he does not enter into life. But whoever does not have faith, even if he acquires every virtue, the wrath of God abides upon him. So that you may not suppose that he says "shall not see life" concerning this visible death, he speaks rather of the eternal judgment. For this reason he said this word, to show that the wrath is already upon him. John said all these words in order thus to bring them to accept Christ, when he showed them that upon everyone who does not believe in the Son the wrath of God remains forever and ever, and thus he ended his discourse.
Gospel: "When Jesus perceived that the Pharisees had learned that Jesus had more disciples and was baptizing
than John, although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples, he left Judea and went to Galilee."
Commentary: Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his accusers were telling the Jews that he was.

But why did the Lord go away from there? Not out of fear of them, but so that the cause of their envy might subside, for he had the power, if they had come upon him, to stop them. But he did not wish to do this repeatedly, so that the nature of his flesh might not appear unbelievable to some.
For this reason he does many human things, so that his incarnation might not come to be doubted,
for just as he wished it to be believed that he is God, so too he wished his humanity also to be believed.
For this reason after the resurrection he said to his disciples: "Examine and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bone, as you see that I have."
For this reason he also rebuked Peter, when he said: "Forgiveness be to you, Lord; let this not be so."
He was eager to make this matter believable, for his incarnation became the beginning of our good things.
Through it death was undone and sin was abolished, the curse vanished, and myriads of good things came into our life.
And for this reason he wished the nature of his flesh to be believable to all; yet he did not hide his divinity either, but revealed it as well. And when he went away from there,
he did not go toward the region of Galilee to no purpose, but accomplished great things in Samaria by that wisdom of his,
And so that the Jews might have nothing to say, which the evangelist also indicates when he says:
Gospel: But he had to pass through Samaria.

Commentary: The evangelist shows that this came about incidentally, along the way. For just as the apostles, whenever the Jews persecuted them, would then go to the gentiles, so also the Lord did: whenever they persecuted him, he would then go to the gentiles. So too the miracle was performed for the Phoenician woman.

And he did this so that every argument of the Jews might be brought to an end, and they could not say: "He abandoned us and went to the uncircumcised." For this reason the apostles said: "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you,
but since you show yourselves unworthy, therefore we turn to the gentiles."
And Christ said: "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel." Since, then, they did not listen, he therefore opened the door to the gentiles.
And thus he came there not by design but incidentally: as he was passing through, he came to the city of the Samaritans, as the evangelist says:
Gospel: He came to a city of the Samaritans called Sychar, near the village that Jacob gave to Joseph his son, and Jacob's spring was there.

Commentary: Why does the evangelist tell us the distinguishing marks of that place in such detail? Only so that when you hear the woman say, "Jacob our father gave us the well," it will not seem strange to you. You will know that this is the place where Levi and Simeon caused the uproar and carried out that wicked slaughter. It is good to say first how the Samaritans came to be, since that whole region was called Samaria. Where did they get that name?

Originally the mountain was called Somor (Shemer), after its owner, as the prophet Isaiah says: "And the head of Somor is Ephraim." But the inhabitants of that mountain were called Israelites, not Samaritans. After some time had passed, they sinned against God. When Pekah became king in Assyria, Tiglath-pileser came up and took many cities of the Jews. He fought against Elah and killed him, and gave the kingdom to Hoshea in his place. Later Shalmaneser came against him again, took other cities and made them pay tribute, and was ruler there. In the end he fell away from that rule and went over to the Indians. The Assyrian learned that Shalmaneser had been cast off. He came up against them and destroyed many of them. Because he suspected them of rebellion, he no longer allowed them to live there. Instead he took them away to Babylon and Media. From there he brought up peoples of many nations and settled them on Mount Somor, so that there would no longer be any fear of rebellion. When this happened, God wished to show that he had not handed the Jews over to the Assyrians out of weakness, as if he were unable to save them. He handed them over because of their sins.

For this reason he sent lions against those gentiles who had settled there, and the lions kept destroying their whole race. The king heard of this and sent them a priest of the Jews, so that he might teach them the law of God. Even so, they were not entirely freed from their own disobedience. But after many days had passed, they turned away from idols and believed in God. When the Jews came back from there, they felt envy and hostility toward them as toward foreigners. They named them Samaritans after that mountain. These people accepted only the writings of Moses and not those of the prophets. They called Abraham their father, because he was a Chaldean, and likewise Jacob, because he was his grandson. But to the Jews they seemed utterly loathsome. That is why they reproached Christ, saying, "You are a Samaritan." The evangelist mentioned the name and the marks of the place for this reason too, so that you might recognize the wretched state of the Jews: because of their sins, foreigners took possession of the lands of their forefathers.

What had not belonged to their fathers, these people acquired; what had been their own, the Jews lost. Those foreigners came to know God through the wounds inflicted by the lions, but the Jews, after so many torments, did not give up their own disobedience.
So Christ came to Samaria, not by chariot but by the toil of walking on foot. He always sought out this kind of life, so that he might teach us to struggle and labor and not to seek comfort.
This is why he said:
"Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have resting places, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head."
For this reason he was in the mountains most of the time. David too foreshadowed this, saying, "He will drink from the brook on the way." For see how his prophecy was fulfilled in this place:
"When Jesus, tired from walking the road, was sitting by the spring, and it was about the sixth hour, a woman came from Samaria to draw water.
Jesus said to her, 'Give me water to drink,' for his disciples had gone into the city to buy food." From this we understand
that the Lord lived humbly in the world and treated the matter of food as secondary.
For he shows this when they were rubbing the heads of grain, and when he went to the fig tree to find food. And here too they had nothing, and they had not taken thought for it before the time,
but only then were they buying, and not as we do, who, as soon as it dawns, summon only the cooks and the table servants.
And that is our business, while care for the soul we treat as secondary.
For this reason all our affairs have been turned upside down, for we treat what matters as secondary and what is secondary as what matters. But see how the Creator of heaven and earth was.
For not only was he tired, but he had also been left alone.
And none of his disciples was with him.
Gospel: "But Jesus, tired from walking the road, was sitting by the spring. It was about the sixth hour. A Samaritan woman came to draw water."
Interpretation:
See how the evangelist shows that the woman too had come for another purpose.

In this way he shut the mouths of the Jews on every side, so that they would have nothing to say about Jesus contradicting his own word. He had said, "Do not enter the city of the Samaritans," and yet here he was talking with a Samaritan woman. For this reason the evangelist also says, "His disciples had not yet come."

And in this way he brings in many reasons for his talking with her. But listen to what the woman said when the Lord said to her, "Give me water." She said to him, "You are a Jew, and you ask water of me, a Samaritan woman? For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans." When she saw his appearance, she knew that he was a Jew. Otherwise, how else would she have known that he was a Jew?

But see how careful that woman was. When she saw that he kept himself from sin, she in turn guarded against another sin, the sin of breaking the law. Otherwise, why would she have needed to say this? For it was not that the Samaritans had no dealings with the Jews, but that the Jews had none with the Samaritans. And if someone should say, "Why then did the Lord ask her for water, since the law did not command it?", let us understand it this way: the Lord was abolishing such unprofitable practices. He came for this very purpose, to do away with those shadows and to reveal the truth. For it is not that:

"what goes in defiles a person, but what comes out." This incident is also no small condemnation of the Jews, since even so much teaching could not bend them. But this woman was converted by a single word. She had not come for this purpose but was going about her own business, and the Lord, for his part, had not sought a conversation with her,
but since she came, he did not withhold his teaching from her. And he spoke to the disciples like this:
"Do not enter the city of the Samaritans." He did not say this: "Even if they come, turn them away," for that would have been utterly unworthy of his goodness. For this reason he said to that woman:
Gospel: "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, 'Give me water to drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
Interpretation: The Lord knew from the beginning that woman's sincere mind, and that she did not deserve to be neglected. That is why he began to speak to her,

for he knew that as soon as she learned of the gift of God, she would immediately seek it. The Jews never did this: they always heard of the gift of God and never asked for it. But hear how this woman immediately said to him:
Gospel: "Lord, you have no vessel to draw with, and this well is deep. From where do you have living water?"

Commentary: She understood at once that he was not like one of the many, but was someone great. For this reason she did not scorn that marvelous word, but calls him Lord and marvels at that marvelous word. And if in that moment she did not grasp the full force of that word,
do not be surprised at this, for Nicodemus too, after those many words, still did not understand the force of the Lord's words.
And she too said to him with respect: "Lord, you have no vessel to draw with, and this well is deep. From where do you have living water?"
For the Lord was speaking of one thing and she was understanding another. And if she had had a mind like that of the Jews, she would have said shamelessly:
"If you had living water, why would you ask me for water? No, you are lying."
Yet she spoke to him with all reverence, both now and before, for at that time she said:
"You are a Jew, and you ask me for water?"
And she did not say to him in anger, "Far be it from me to give water to the enemy of my people." And now again she answered with reverence:
Gospel: "Are you perhaps greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well?
And he himself drank from it, and his sons and his flocks."

Commentary: From these words it appears that from his first statement she received a lofty understanding and came to suspect that he had some other water, and yet she could not discover it. For this reason she said: "How can this be?
For Jacob and his sons had no other water better than this, but they drank from this; and you, lord, have no vessel for drawing.
Even if I were to say that you have drawn up from here that water of which you speak, then again, from where did you find other, better water, which Jacob and his sons could not find?

Unless you are greater than Jacob? Otherwise, from nowhere could you have that water which you say you will give." But the Jews never showed such a disposition. He spoke to them too about living water, and they did not want it. And when he mentioned Abraham, they even threw stones at him. But this woman endured standing in the heat and listening to his words, and she did not conceive a single Jewish-like thought, so as to regard him as a blasphemer or to say anything else evil.

Moral teaching 31 [?], on virtue. Now if the Samaritan woman showed so much eagerness to learn something good, and stayed with Christ, whom she even recognized [?], what answer will we give, we who know him? We are not under the heat, but in the church, and still we do not listen to his words patiently. Let us not imitate the Jews. Instead, let us become like that Samaritan woman and hear his words with joy, for even now he stands among us and speaks to us through the prophets and the apostles. So let us hear his words while we are in vanity, and even more in evil, for not doing the will of God is evil.

For if someone who receives money to trade with and wastes it uselessly is punished, what will become of us, who waste in evil this time of life that was given to us for good? God did not create us, bring us into this world and breathe a soul into us so that we would live only for this passing life. He did it so that we would trade everything for that eternal life. The beasts exist only for this passing life. But we have an immortal soul so that we may care for the eternal life, shine there, live with the angels, and stand before the King of all through the endless ages. This is why we were given an immortal soul, and why we will then be given immortal bodies: so that we may delight in the eternal good things. If we despise heavenly things and care about earthly things, see how we insult the Giver. When he holds out heavenly things to us and we do not value them, is that not an insult to him? This is why he also prepared Gehenna for those who insult him, so that we may know what good things we are shutting ourselves out from.

But may we never taste those bitter torments. Instead, may we become pleasing to him and inherit the eternal good things by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 32
This passage: Jesus answered and said to her: "Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst forever.
And the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water flowing to eternal life.

Interpretation: Scripture sometimes names the grace of the Holy Spirit fire and sometimes water, in order to show that these names do not belong to his essence but to his operations; for it is not possible that the Holy Spirit should be composed of various essences,
he who is invisible and simple. For John speaks thus: "He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire."
And the Lord cries out: "Rivers of living water will flow from his belly."

And this he said about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive. In the same way, then, he said to the woman: "Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give will no longer thirst forever."
And this he said about the Holy Spirit. For by the name of fire he signifies the sharpness and heat of his grace and its destruction of sins,
while by water he makes known the purification that comes from him and the great consolation given to the minds of those who receive him. For like a paradise of delight,
adorned with many fruit-bearing trees, so he makes the soul that receives him,
and he quenches all the burning arrows of the enemy.
But you, observe the wisdom of God, how little by little he leads the woman to understanding,
for first he asked for water and gave an occasion for conversation. Then he said to her: "If you knew who it is that says to you:
'Give me water.'" And when she mentioned the patriarch Jacob and said to him:
"Are you perhaps greater than our father Jacob?" the Lord did not say,

"Yes, I am greater," so as not to make her mind stumble, but from his deeds he showed her his superiority and how great a difference there was between him and Jacob. For he said to her: "If you wonder how I could give you water better than this, and you say:
'Are you perhaps greater than Jacob?'
if I give you that water of which I speak, will you not then all the more acknowledge my superiority?

See the woman's impartial judgment: she was judging who was superior on the basis of deeds. But the Jews did not regard him in this way when he cast out demons. Not only did they not say, "He is greater than the patriarch," but they even called him demon-possessed. For this reason the Lord says: "If I do not do the work of my Father, do not believe me.

If I do it, even though you do not believe me, believe the works." And in this way the woman believed the works. For this reason too, since the Lord knew that she judged according to works, he left off speaking about Jacob and speaks about the water, saying: "Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again, but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will not thirst forever." For the woman had first heard of "living water" and did not understand; she supposed that by living water he meant a visible spring, flowing unceasingly. For this reason Christ said to her:
"Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst. Instead, it will become in him a spring of water flowing to eternal life."

By these words she understood that he was not speaking to her of anything visible. For what visible water has ever done this: that once received, it would no longer let one thirst, but would become a spring within him? And when she heard this, the woman believed at once. She showed herself far more understanding than Nicodemus, and not only more understanding but also more courageous. He heard many such things, yet preached to no one and did not grow bold. She, however, did the work of an apostle: she converted a whole city to the Lord and preached to everyone. Moreover, the matter seemed impossible to Nicodemus, and even when the Lord offered him the image of the wind, he still could not accept the word. The woman at first marveled. But when the Lord told her, not with an image or with much contrivance but by simple declaration, that "whoever receives the water from me will never thirst," she believed at once and said to him:
Gospel: "Lord, give me that water, so that I may not thirst and may no longer come here to draw water." When she first heard:

"living water," she supposed it was visible water, but when she learned that that water is spiritual, she believed that it has the power to stop thirst, though she did not know what it is. This she understood,
that it is superior to these visible things, though she did not know what it truly is; but this she recognized,
[?] that he is greater than Jacob, and she began to ask for that water. This is a good soul and mind,
for she neither received the word idly but examined it well, nor did she, on the other hand, become contentious and unbelieving,
but when she recognized the truth of those words, she asked him for the water. She did not act as the Jews did, for when they heard the word of the Lord which he spoke, "Whoever eats my flesh,"
will not hunger," they took offense. But that woman asked all the more.
But if the Lord had said to her: "I will give you living water
when you believe in me, for faith in me is living water," she would not have accepted that word, for she did not know who he is.

For to the Jews he first showed many signs, and only then said to them: "Whoever believes in me will not thirst." But this woman had seen no sign, and how would she have believed if he had said: "Faith in me is living water"?
For this reason he first showed her his power through prophecy, and he did not reprove her immediately, but first said to her:
Gospel: "'Go, call your husband and come here!' The woman answered and said to him: 'I have no husband.'
Jesus said to her: 'You have spoken well, for you have no husband. But you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband. What you have said is true.'
The woman said to him: 'Lord, I see that you are a prophet.'

Commentary: Oh, how great is the wisdom of this woman, and how meekly she accepted the reproof, and not as the Jews did! For he also reproved them many times for the thoughts of their minds, and to know a thought is a greater thing than to know a deed that has been done.
For this is the work of God alone.
But the Jews not only did not marvel, they even grew angry, when he said to them: "Why do you seek to kill me?"
They had also seen many other signs of his, and in the face of all of that they said: "You have a demon. Who is seeking to kill you?" But the woman had seen only this one wonder,
and yet she was not outraged, but marveled and confessed him to be a prophet.

And if anyone should say: "Why did he say to her: 'Call your husband'?", understand that it was for this reason: the woman was asking for that gift of living water, and the Lord wished to show her the power of his signs, so that the woman might believe in him. For if she had not believed, how could she have received that living water? And again, was he to reprove her thus without questioning her? Therefore he said to her: "Call your husband." But the woman wished to conceal that foul deed, for she looked on him as a mere man, and she said to him: "I have no husband."
When Christ heard this, he then again, at the proper time, spoke that word of reproof to her unerringly,
for he enumerated the former husbands and exposed the present one, who was not a true and lawful husband.

When she heard this she did not take offense, but confessed him to be a prophet. And having confessed him to be a prophet, she did not ask him about bodily health, or wealth, or anything else, but immediately asked about faith and said to him:
Gospel: "Our fathers worshiped on this mountain."

Commentary: She is speaking of Abraham, for they say: "There he brought up Isaac to be slaughtered." "And how is it that you say," she says, "that in Jerusalem is the place where it is right to worship?" Do you see how lofty she became in her mind? For this reason Christ led her up to a greater height by his word, since he had brought her to faith in himself.

Homily 32, on the reading of the divine Scriptures. Let us then also be ashamed. For if the Samaritan woman, who had had five husbands, showed such eagerness to learn the divine words, and neither the heat nor that pressing hour held her back, what shall we say,
we who never show even a little zeal to learn divine matters or words?
For which of you, when he goes home, takes the divine books in his hands and searches the Scriptures? Most have no care for them at all; they are as though they did not own them,
for they keep them sealed up and never read them, and they acquired them not for the benefit of the soul but for the sake of wealth.
So great is the evil of vainglory: for no one boasts of this, "I know everything that is written in them," but they boast of this, "They are written in letters of gold."
There is no profit in this, for the Scriptures were not given to us so that we might write them down in books, but so that we might write them down in our hearts,
and merely possessing books belongs to the law of the Jews, for it was given to us to be written not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of the heart.
Yet I say this also: I do not forbid you from acquiring books; rather, I rejoice at this. But I beg you
that along with this we also inscribe in our minds the powers and the words of the books. For if the devil cannot enter a house where the Gospel lies,
will he not much more fear to enter a soul in which the power of these words dwells? And not only the devil, but every nature of sin.
Sanctify, therefore, your soul, and sanctify your body also, by making these divine words dwell in your heart and in your mouth.
For if speaking evil words defiles a person, will not training in and reading of spiritual words sanctify both soul and mouth and establish in them the grace of the Holy Spirit?
For the divine Scriptures are medicines of the soul; let us therefore heal our souls by them.
I say these words to you always, and I will not stop saying them.

For how is it not wicked that lovers of the world know the whole nature of their possessions and of each of their horses, their grandsires and breeds, while you who gather in the church do not know the words spoken here, nor even the number of the books that we constantly use?

For these things are far more worthless and less desirable than those. Tell me [?], which is more wonderful to behold: the combat [?] of man against man, or the combat [?] of man against the devil, the fight of the bodily against the bodiless, and the victory? And if you behold such a thing, you too will likewise learn victory over the devil. I tell you such things always and will not stop saying them. But do not let my words seem burdensome to you. If anyone had the right to feel burdened, it would be I, who always teach you while you always disobey me. You have no right to feel burdened, you who always listen and never act on it. But may the Lord make you worthy, so that this accusation may not always be upon you, but that you may turn away from every evil deed and become worthy of understanding divine things in word and deed. Then you may bring forth good fruit and become worthy to inherit the eternal good things of the kingdom, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 33
This saying: "Jesus said to her: 'Believe me, woman. Neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but you shall worship the Father.
You worship what you do not know, but we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.'"
Commentary: In every place faith is necessary for us, beloved, for faith is the mother of all good things and a life-giving medicine, for without it we shall understand nothing of those lofty words,

but you will become like men who, without [?], undertake to cross the sea, who are able to traverse a small distance with their hands and feet, but if they go further in, they are quickly swallowed up by the waves.

So also those who by their own reasoning strive to find something of Scripture before finding [?] are drowned, as Paul says: "those who have made shipwreck of the faith." But so that we may not fall into the same thing, let us take up that good rampart by which Christ now drew the Samaritan woman to himself, for when she herself said:

"As you say, in Jerusalem is the place where one must worship," Christ said to her: "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but you shall worship the Father." He revealed to her a very lofty word, one that he said neither to Nicodemus nor to Nathanael, for that woman was striving to show the affairs of the Samaritans to be superior to those of the Jews, and she brought in the fathers as witnesses. But Christ did not answer according to her question, for it was not then needful to show why the fathers worshiped on that mountain and the Jews in Jerusalem. Therefore he kept silent about this, and told her what was higher than both, and showed that neither the Jews nor they have anything of great account compared with what was to come, which was about to be given. And when he had made her understand this, only then did he show her the difference between the two, and he showed the Jews to be more honorable,
not that he gave honor to the place, but he showed their superiority from their understanding, as though he were saying to her:
There is no need to dispute about places, but in understanding the Jews have the advantage over the Samaritans, "for you worship what you do not know, but we worship what we know."
But how did the Samaritans not know whom they worshiped? Because they knew God as confined to that place, and in this way they served him;
and so they sent word about him to the Persians, saying: "The god of this place is angry with us." And therefore this thinking was contemptible and evil,
for they served both God and the devil, and joined together these things that cannot be joined.
But the Jews were pure of this practice and knew him as the God of the whole world, although not all of them did. For this reason he said to her:
"You worship what you do not know, but we worship what we know." Do not be surprised that he counts himself among the Jews,
because he was speaking to her according to the woman's own idea, since she took him for a Jewish prophet.
For this reason too he said, "We worship": he who is to be worshiped by all, for to him every knee shall bow,
but now he was speaking to her as a Jew,
But he confirmed the statement, so that she would not suppose that he was speaking those words out of love for his own people.

For this reason he said to her: "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when you will worship neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem." And then he further showed the superiority of the Jews, and that salvation is from the Jews, he says. And by "salvation" he means either this,
that the knowledge of God and the contempt of idols began first from them, and you too, he says, even though you do not know God rightly,
yet what you do know comes from them; or else he was calling his own appearing "salvation." Both of these are from the Jews, as Paul says:
"From whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all."
Do you see the kinship of the Old with the New?
And when he had told her these words, he says to her again:
Gospel: "But the hour is coming, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth."

Commentary: When he mentioned the "true" worshipers, he set aside both the Jews and the Samaritans. For although the Jews are better than the Samaritans, yet they are as far inferior to those who were to come as a shadow is to the truth. And he is speaking of the Church, saying that this is the true and fitting worship, for the Father also seeks such worshipers of him. And since he desires such as these, it was certainly not willingly that he allowed those others to act in this way, but because of their great weakness, and so that in this way, little by little, they too might be converted. For true worshipers are those who serve God not in particular places but in the spirit, as the Apostle says: "whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son."

And when he says, "God is spirit," he signifies nothing other than this, that he is incorporeal, and it is fitting that the service of the incorporeal One be performed by us with what is likewise incorporeal, that is, the soul and purity of mind. For this reason he says: "Those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth." For since both the Samaritans and the Jews took no pains over the soul and showed great zeal for the purification of the body, for this reason he says: God is served not by washing of the body but by purity of mind. Do not offer sheep and calves, but offer yourself wholly to God.

And this is true worship, for were not all the former things shadows, circumcision and those sacrifices? But now everything is truth, and what must be done is not the purification and cutting of the body but of evil thoughts, and the crucifying of oneself and the slaying of evil thoughts. And the woman trembled and marveled at these words, and for this reason she said to him:
Gospel: "'I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will tell us everything.' Jesus said to her: 'I am he, who am speaking to you.'"

Commentary: And from where did the Samaritans have the expectation of Christ, if not from the books of Moses? For he clearly reveals the Son: "Let us make man in our image" was said to him; and "The Son conversed with Abraham in the tent"; and Jacob said concerning him: "A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it is laid up, and he is the expectation of the Gentiles." And Moses himself said:
"The Lord will raise up for you a prophet like me; listen to him!"

And the bronze serpent, and the rod of Moses, and the slaughter of Isaac, and many other such things were types of his coming. But if someone should say: Why did he not bring her a type from the Scriptures, as he did with Nicodemus and Nathanael?

Understand that they were learned in the Scriptures, but this woman was poor and uneducated, and therefore he drew her by the mention of that living water. And so, little by little, she came to remember what she had indeed heard of Scripture, and only then did he reveal himself to her; for at the beginning she could not have borne to believe the words of Scripture.
And the Jews said: "How long will you take away our souls?
If you are the Christ, tell us." And he said nothing to them, but to this woman he revealed himself without any inquiry,
for he knew that her mind was more sincere than that of the Jews,
for they asked in order to scorn him; otherwise, if they had wanted to know, the signs and the teachings and the words of Scripture were enough to show him to them.
But she spoke with a sincere mind, and therefore she believed quickly once she heard, and she drew others to him as well.
And in every respect great is the faith of that woman.
Gospel: And at this very word his disciples came, and they marveled that he was speaking with a woman; yet no one said to him: "What do you seek?" or "Why are you speaking with her?"
Commentary: They came at a very fitting time, when the teaching of that woman had been completed.

And they marveled at that incomprehensible humility of his, that one so glorious took it upon himself to converse so humbly with a poor Samaritan woman. But although they marveled, they did not ask him the reason, it says.
So well were they instructed in the rule of discipleship, so much did they fear and revere him; for although they did not yet have a fitting understanding of him,

they nevertheless looked upon him as upon someone wondrous and revered him so, even though at times they became bold, as John did when he leaned on his breast, and as when they said to him: "Who is the greatest?"
and many other such things. But they did this when there was something necessary for themselves to ask; here, however, the matter concerned someone else, and therefore they did not ask.
And when John leaned on his breast, that was at the end, when greater boldness had been given to him, he who was the disciple whom the Lord loved.

Homily 33. On wealth and meekness: that the evangelist John possessed these, and for this reason the Lord loved him. For what could be greater than this blessedness? But let us not merely call that apostle blessed, beloved brothers,

But let us hasten to draw near to that blessed one and to become like that evangelist by every means, and let us see for what deed the Lord loved him more than all; for he left his father and followed the Lord.
But his brother also shared in this deed, as did Peter and Andrew.
Why, then, was this one loved more than all?

He himself, out of humility, did not state the cause of that love, but I understand it to be this: that he possessed great gentleness and humility and simplicity. For this reason the Gospel nowhere shows

that he had grown bold enough to ask about anything, as Peter and Philip and Judas and Thomas did, except only at the time when Peter compelled him to ask, for those two had great love for one another. Otherwise he was never bold, but showed great gentleness and humility.

Such virtue is known from Moses as well, for it was this that brought him to that great measure, and nothing is equal to gentleness and humility. For this reason Christ began the Beatitudes with it, for he mentioned it first, as the foundation of the virtues, saying: "Blessed are the poor in spirit." Without it, life is impossible; whether someone fasts or prays or does anything else, if it is done with pride, it is abominable before God, but if it is done with humility, then every deed of his is honorable. Let us therefore acquire humility, beloved, for if we are willing, this virtue is very easy. What is it, man, that makes you proud? Do you not see the worthlessness of your nature and the errancy of your mind?

Remember your sins. And if you do have virtues and are proud because of them, by this you destroy everything. For if you give to the poor, you give not what is yours but what is God's, and you ought all the more to be humble when, by looking at the poor, you come to understand the worthlessness of your nature; for though we are rich today, we are to depart naked [?]. What is wealth? A worthless shadow, vanishing smoke, a flower of the grass [?], and weaker than a flower. Why then are you proud over grass? Do not harlots and robbers also acquire wealth? But if you love honor and glory, seek that which comes from God, which never fades away. Acquire humility and the other virtues, that you may be made worthy of that glory by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 34
This saying:
The woman left her water jar and went to the city and said to the people:
'Come and see a man who told me everything that I have done. Could this be the Christ?'"
Commentary: Great zeal is required of us, beloved, in every spiritual undertaking; otherwise, it is impossible to accomplish anything good through negligence.
Christ indicated this when he said: "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me." And again he says: "I came to cast fire upon the earth."
And by all these sayings he indicates zealous striving.
Such was this woman,
for her heart was so inflamed by the Lord's words that she even left her water jar and ran and proclaimed him; for she had come to draw water and,
When she had found that living spring, she no longer took up the visible water but left it behind, so that we too may learn, when we find the spiritual, to count the bodily as nothing any longer.

For according to her ability she did what the apostles did. The Lord called them and they followed, but she, without being told, left her water jar and took up the work of the evangelists, made winged by joy,
and she called not one or two, but that whole city.
And see how wisely she acted: she did not say, "Come and see the Christ," but:
"Come and see a man who told me everything I have done." She did not try to hide her own shame,
for when the soul is set on fire with divine zeal,
it no longer looks at earthly things.
"Can this perhaps be the Christ?" She did not wish to prove by herself that he is the Christ, but hastened to bring them to him,
and she knew of that living spring that, if they experienced its taste, they would believe for themselves, just as she had believed.
Do you see the wisdom of that woman? For she even made public the exposure of her own sins, only so that she might draw them to the Lord.

Gospel: And meanwhile his disciples were saying to him, "Rabbi, eat." But he himself said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know." The disciples said to one another, "Has someone brought him food?"

Commentary: They saw him weary from walking the road and from the heat, and they wanted to comfort him, and they said to him, "Rabbi, eat." But when they heard about food, they understood visible food. What wonder is it, then, if that woman, when she heard "water," thought it was visible water, since even the disciples thought it was visible food? But according to the custom of disciples they shrank from asking and inquired among one another. For this reason alone the Lord, who knows hearts, said to them:
Gospel: "My food is this, that I do the will of him who sent me and accomplish his work."

Commentary: Here he gave the name of food to the salvation of people, in order to show how much eagerness he has for our salvation; for just as eating is desirable to us, so is our salvation to him. And see how he always first speaks his word in a hidden manner, and when the hearer begins to inquire, only then does he reveal it. For why did he not say at the outset, "My food is this, that I do the will of my Father," but first said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know"? When they began to inquire what this saying was, only then did he tell them, so that they might listen better, and after that he also explained what the will of the Father is, and said to them:
Gospel: "Do you not say, 'There are yet four months, and the harvest comes'?
Behold, I say to you: 'Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are white for harvest.'"

Interpretation: See, he is again speaking in a parable. When he spoke of food, he meant the salvation of the people who were about to come to him. The field means the same thing again: the great number of believing souls. He speaks of the eyes of both the mind and the body, because they could see how the Samaritans were coming. By "fields that have turned white" he meant their minds, which were ready to receive him. Just as a field that has turned white is ready for harvest, so these people are ready for salvation. But why did he not speak about the matter openly, instead of speaking in parables both here and throughout the Gospel? The prophets, too, always spoke in parables.
What is the reason for parables? The Holy Spirit did not establish them for nothing. First, they make the words clearer and easier to understand,
for when the mind also hears an image of the matter and sees it, it understands more fully the matter about which it is being taught; and again for this reason,
so that it may be more sweetly remembered by a person,
for plain speech does not attract hearers as much as when it also has an image of something known from experience. And there are many other reasons for which parables have been spoken.
Gospel: "And the reaper receives wages and gathers fruit for eternal life."

Interpretation: The store gathered from this visible field is not for eternal life but for this passing world. But the store from the field I am speaking of is life for ever and ever. Just as when he said,
"Whoever drinks of this water will never thirst again," he showed that he was not speaking about visible water, so he did the same here when he said:
"They gather fruit for eternal life."
Gospel: "So that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together."
Commentary: Who is the sower, and who is the reaper? The prophets are the sowers, but they did not reap; rather, the apostles reaped.
But it is not that they had no joy because of this, for they share in the joy together with you, for "I have reserved you for the harvest," he says,
where this labor is small and the joy is greater.
By these words he shows that this was also the will of the prophets, that people should come to him, and that it was for this that they sowed.
And he shows that it was he who sent them too, and that the old has great kinship with the new.
And he also recalled a proverbial saying which many people used to say:
Gospel: "For in this the saying is true: 'One is the sower and another is the reaper.'"
Commentary: People used to say this saying when one person sowed and another carried off the fruit. And the Lord says: "This saying has here above all been fulfilled well:
for the prophets labored, and you reap what they sowed."
He did not say "their grace," for it is not that they were left without grace; rather, "you have received the fruit," he says.

For this reason he said earlier: "so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together," so that no one could say that he was excluding the prophets from grace. And he said something unusual. In this world, if one person sows and another reaps, they cannot both rejoice.
Instead, the sower is sad and only the reaper rejoices. But here both rejoice, because the prophets too became heirs of that grace.
Gospel: "I send you to reap that for which you have not labored; others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."

Interpretation: Since he was sending them out to preach to the world, and the task seemed difficult, he therefore says to them: "The harder work was that of the prophets, the sowing of the seed and preaching among the utterly ignorant, but for you it is easier, for the reaper does not need as much labor as the sower: long stretches of time, and plowing, and waiting for rain, and many such things." And the events themselves were showing the truth of his word, for as he was saying this, the Samaritans were coming and believing in him, and that spiritual fruit was being gathered, and many of that city believed in him through the word of that woman, for she testified: "He told me everything that I have done."

Homily 34: That the penitent must not only withdraw from sin in deed, but must also loathe it in the mind. Let us then also imitate that woman, and let us not be ashamed to reveal our sins, but let us be afraid of God, for he sees everything and there will punish the unrepentant. For we are not afraid of him who is going to judge, yet we dread revealing our sins before a human being, and we do not know that whoever does not repent of his evil deeds will have them revealed on that day, not before one or two people, but before all creatures, for there the spectacle of each person's deeds will be set up, just as they were, whether good or evil. Understand this: if you have done some evil, or have devised it, and you hide it from people, you still cannot hide it from God. And you are afraid of people, yet the fear of God does not come to your mind?
And understand that you will not be able to hide it even from people on that day, for all our evil deeds, as if written out,

will stand before us, so that we ourselves may be condemned, just as the rich man saw Lazarus before his eyes, and the one who had seemed loathsome to him, he longed for his finger, that he might comfort him.
Therefore I beseech you: let each of us enter into his own mind and set up the tribunal, and let us bring our sins forward into the midst, and let the mind be the judge.

And if we do not wish to be exposed on that day, let us heal our wounds here and now, and let us pour upon them the medicine of repentance, for it is possible for our wounds to be healed, as the Lord says:
"If you forgive, your sins will be forgiven you,"

We will do the same if we are willing, through repentance. Repentance happens like this: we turn away from doing evil, wipe our evil deeds completely out of our minds, and then begin to put medicine on our wounds.
And if you have been seizing what belongs to others, withdraw from it and apply to yourself the medicine of almsgiving; and if you have committed fornication,
withdraw from it and apply to yourself the medicine of chastity; and if you have slandered your brother, show him love in return. And let us act in this way in each matter,
and let us not pass over our sins, for the time of judgment has drawn near, as the apostle says: The Lord is near.
Do not be anxious, you who are in struggles and afflictions; but you who are in sins,
to you I say this: The Lord is near; be anxious, for the end has drawn near.

And if three hundred years ago, when Paul lived, he said, "The Lord is near," is he not much nearer now? If at that time the apostle called it the end of the ages, is the end not much more upon us now?

So let us guard ourselves with the fear of God, for when we do not know and are careless, then the end will come suddenly, as the Lord says: "As in the days of Noah and of Lot, so it will be." For it comes suddenly, just as the pain of childbirth often overtakes a woman unexpectedly and suddenly, when she is not expecting it. Therefore let us always be ready, for the time of repentance is not always given to us, as it is written: "In hell who will confess you?" Instead, let us repent here, so that the Lord may be merciful to us on that day and we may find forgiveness by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 35
The text: The Samaritans came to him and asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days, and a greater multitude believed his words, and they said to the woman:

"We no longer believe because of your word, for we ourselves have heard from him and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world." And after two days he went out from there and went away to Galilee.
Commentary: Nothing is weaker than envy and pride. These are the doers of countless evils.
Through these events the Jews, who had more understanding than the Samaritans and had been brought up with the prophets, turned out to be worse than the Samaritans.

For the woman believed from these words alone, without seeing any signs, and they went out to him and begged Christ to stay with them. But the Jews, after seeing so many signs, were driving him out of their land. That is why the Lord did not think it right to turn away those who begged him and fell down before him. Instead he stayed with them, as suited his love for humankind, because they wanted him to be with them and begged him to stay. But the Lord agreed to stay only two days, and many believed in him during those two days,
and it was difficult for them to believe, for they had not seen a sign,

and because they were hostile to the Jews. But since he stayed unharmed, they listened to his words with zeal; nothing became a hindrance to their faith, and they said to the woman: "It is no longer because of your word that we believe; we ourselves have heard and we know that this is the Savior of the world, the Christ."
The disciples outstripped their teachers and proved far superior to the Jews. For such is the truth: when it finds a sincere soul, it becomes established in it, and,
if it does not become established in it, the fault is that soul's and not the truth's,
for the sun too gives light to healthy eyes but cannot give light to weak ones, not because of any weakness of its own, but because of those eyes.
Hear, then, what those Samaritans say: "We know that he is the Savior of the world, the Christ."

Do you see what understanding they immediately came to? They recognized that he intended to convert the whole world to himself, and that he would not leave his saving dispensation among the Jews alone,
but would enlighten the whole world,
But the Jews did not act this way; instead they sought to establish their own righteousness, and they could not attain to the righteousness of God.
But these confess: "All have sinned, but they are justified freely by the grace of God."
And this is truly the Savior of the world, Christ, the redeemer of that lost nature and the giver of true life.
This is the work of fervent faith, for it is amazing about them that, without seeing signs, by teaching alone they believed so fervently.
But as for what teaching he gave there, the Evangelist says nothing further, so that you may know that the Evangelists pass over many of his words and signs.
Gospel: And after two days he went out from there and went to Galilee, for Jesus himself testified: "A prophet has no honor in his own country."
Commentary: Why is this written in this place, "He has no honor in his own homeland," except for this reason: that in this place he calls Capernaum his homeland, and so that no one may say:

"Why did he stay among the Samaritans and pass by Capernaum?" You say this, and the answer is so that you may learn that he did this for no other reason than that they were unbelieving and would not listen to him. That is why he did not go there, so that their judgment would not be heavier.
Gospel: "And when he came to Galilee, the Galileans received him, for they had seen all that Jesus had done at the feast in Jerusalem.
And they too had come to that feast."

Commentary: Do you see that those whom the Pharisees and scribes held in contempt were the ones who turned to him all the more? For they said about Galilee, "No prophet has arisen from Galilee," and the Samaritans in turn they held to be abominable, so much so that when they reviled him they said to him, "You are a Samaritan!" And behold, both the Samaritans and the Galileans believed in the Lord, to the shame and reproach of the Jews.
Gospel: "Jesus came again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made the water wine, and there was a certain royal official whose son was sick at Capernaum.
This man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee. He came to him and begged him to come and heal his son."

Commentary: He came to Cana of Galilee in order to remind them of the sign he had done and to make them believe in him all the more. As for this royal man, either he was of royal family, or he was called royal because of his office. Some say that this was the man of whom Matthew speaks, but it is not he, for it is evident not only from his rank that it was not that man, but also from his faith. For that man said, "I am not worthy that you should come under my roof," whereas this one begged him to come.
And there he had come from the mountain to Capernaum, and here from Samaria to Cana.
Gospel: Jesus said to him: "Unless you see signs and wonders, will you never believe?"
The royal official said to him: "Lord, come before my son dies." Jesus said to him: "Go, your son lives."
Commentary: In this place he either praises the Samaritans, in that they believed without signs, or he reproaches that city, Capernaum,
Whence that man was [?], for although he believed, yet not fully; for this reason he also questioned his servants as he was going.
When they told him of his son's recovery, only then did he understand, and he believed, together with all his household. And the Lord, who sees minds, knew this.
For this reason he said to him: "Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe."
For he saw how weak his words were, since he said, "Come down before my child dies," as though he could not heal from a distance or raise from the dead.
