But why did he go there of his own accord, while here he does not go even when invited? Because there the centurion had perfect faith.

He went there so that we may know that the man was pleasing to him. This man, however, did not have such faith and did not know that he could heal even from a distance, so he was pressing him to come.
For this reason he did not go, so that when he found him healed, he would believe that the Lord is able to heal even from afar.
And when you hear that saying, "Unless you see signs and wonders, you will not believe," understand that he is saying this: you do not have faith as you ought.

Moral Teaching 35: That one ought to give thanks to God in all things. Let us learn from all this not to seek the sight of miracles from God, nor to need to see any form of evidence of God's power, for I see even now
For many people are amazed at the power of God at a time when either their children,
or a brother,

or someone else is freed from sickness. But whether or not we see such a miracle, we ought to thank the Lord and glorify him in everything. This is the work of faithful servants, and this is the form of the love of God: that whether he afflicts us or gives us joy, we love him, for the Lord disciplines the one he loves. When we love him only in times of rest, that is not love. And why do I speak of sicknesses or bodily trials? Even if you hear of Gehenna and hell, not even then should you stop thanking God.

For this is the form of perfect goodness. Whoever lives this way will pass this life in rest, will attain the eternal good things, and will find boldness before God. May we all be worthy to attain this by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 36
The text: "This again is the second sign that Jesus performed when he came from Judea to Galilee."
"After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem."

Commentary: Just as in veins of gold mines no one among those searching for it despises even a small vein, so too in the Scriptures it is improper to pass over even a single hair's breadth, but everything must be examined,
for all those words were spoken by the Holy Spirit.
So listen here too to what the Evangelist says: "This again is the second sign that Jesus performed when he came from Judea to Galilee."
For it was not in vain that he said this phrase, "a second sign," but so that you may know that he performed a sign among them twice, and still they did not become equal to the Samaritans,
who had not seen any.
Gospel: "After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem."

Commentary: I think that he means the "martvria" [?]. Jesus would come to the city repeatedly at the feasts: first, to show that he was keeping the feast with them; and second, to draw to himself the guileless multitude, for it was especially at such feasts that unlearned and simple people would gather.
Gospel: And there is in Jerusalem, at the Sheep's bathing place, a pool which is called in Hebrew Bethel,
and it had five porticoes, and in these lay a multitude of the sick, the blind and the lame and the withered, who were waiting for the stirring of the water.
Commentary: What was this figure of healing, and what mystery does it teach us?
For it was not without purpose, but it foreshadowed what was to come, for God was going to give us baptism,
which has great gift and power, cleansing sins and giving life to the soul,
and it was prefigured, as if in an image, by this bathing place and by many other figures; and first it was prefigured by that water

which was given for washing away defilements, and many other things were performed by means of water, all of which were figures of baptism. And this too was a figure of baptism; for this reason also it healed diseases.

And an angel would come down and stir that water, and whoever went in first would be healed, so that the Jews might know that if the healing of diseases was brought about by an angel, how much more will the King of angels cleanse all the diseases of the baptized?

There, if the water had worked by itself, people would have been healed at all times, but the thing happened through the coming of the angel. In the same way, for us the water does nothing merely by itself, but when it receives the grace of the Holy Spirit, it looses all sins.
But back then, weakness was a hindrance to healing for the one who wished
to be healed. Now, however, each person has the power to do this, for it is not an angel who stirs the water but the King of the angels.

Now no one can say any longer, "I have no one, and while I am coming, someone else goes down before me." For even if the whole world should come, that grace is not used up, but remains as it is. Just as the light of the sun always shines and is never used up, so even more is it with this grace of the Holy Spirit: it is never diminished by the multitude of those who receive it. That event also took place so that people would understand that if water cleanses bodily sicknesses, God is surely able to cleanse spiritual ones through water as well.

But why did the Lord pass over everyone else and go to the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years? It was so that everyone would know the greatness of his patience, which was wonderful, for he had been ill for thirty-eight years,

And he was not healed, yet he still stayed there patiently and did not leave. Nor did he think to himself: "Since I have not been able to get down into the pool in all these years, I will not be able to from now on either, because there are so many sick people."

Homily 36. That we should not grow weary in the godly virtues. Let us then be ashamed, beloved, of this sloth of ours, for he had spent thirty-eight years and did not despair of asking of God and of hope.

But if we ask God for something for ten days and he does not give it to us, we grow weary and give up our prayer. Yet if we are seeking human glory, we never stop pleading, serving and trying every means for all the days of our life, and often we are disappointed in that hope of ours.
But with God, the King of all, we are fully confident that every prayer and every virtue will surely be rewarded. Even so, you do not persist in hope in him even for a short time.
Does this not deserve much punishment? Even if our request were not granted at all, is it not better than countless good things simply to pray to God and to speak with him? But if you say:
"Constant prayer is hard," then tell me, which of the virtues is easy? But those lovers of idleness say:
"And why is it that sin is so desirable, while hardship is joined to virtue?"
And many inquire into this matter; so what is the reason for it?
"For at first God gave us a life free from cares and hardships,

but we did not use that grace and gift of God properly. Instead we turned away from the good and were cast out of Paradise. Because of this our life was bound up with toil, as though he were saying to the human race:
"I gave you from the beginning delight and rest, but you used that rest wickedly and were harmed all the more by it. Therefore I have commanded labor and sweat for you."

And since not even that life of labor was able to keep us from sin, for this reason the written law was also given to us, and many teachings, so that by some means we might depart from sin. And for this reason a life of hardship has been given to us, for God saw that freedom from hardship was harmful to us, since our nature could not bear to stand idle,
but inclines toward evil. Or if we had been at rest, how would we have used that rest, except that we would have inclined toward evil? But those speakers of vanity say:
"And why is it that great sweetness goes with sin, but great hardship with virtue?" But I say to the one who says this:
"What credit would be yours, or why would you receive a reward, if virtue were entirely free of hardship?
For I could show you many to whom union with a woman by nature appears loathsome and who hate it; would they then receive the crown of virginity?

"God forbid!" For virginity exists when a person struggles against desire and overcomes that passion. A soldier, too, is crowned when he enters fierce battle, and there is no one fighting [?]. For this reason the Lord also spoke of three kinds of eunuchs, and of two of them he says:
they receive no crown. Only the one kind does he bring into the Kingdom. But the objector speaks again: "And why was there any need at all for sin and wickedness to be created?"

And I too ask this: why was there any need for sin to be created? But tell me, who is the creator of sin and wickedness? Who else creates it except the slackness of our own will? But if you say this: "Then why are we not simply good? Why do we lean toward evil?"

Then I ask you in turn: what is the nature of goodness? Is it vigilance and effort, or sleep and lying down? And if you say, "Why did God not make virtue easier, so that it could be practised without hardship?" then you are speaking like the brute beasts, whose god is their belly. Or tell me this: suppose a king and a general were together. Then the king got drunk and fell asleep, the enemy attacked, and the general rose up and defeated them. Would the credit not belong to the general, who toiled and won? Do you see how sweet the deed you toiled for becomes to the soul afterward? That is why he joined toil to virtue: so that the soul would love what it had won through toil. For this reason we love and admire virtue even when we do not practise it ourselves, and everyone finds sin loathsome, even though the devil makes it seem sweet at the moment it is done. And if you say:

"Why do those who are good by nature not seem as wonderful to us as those who have become good through struggle?" Understand that it is because it is right that one who has toiled should be more honoured than one who has not toiled. Toil was given to us because we did not make good use of freedom from toil, and idleness itself is evil and abominable. And if you say, "If work, which keeps us from being idle, is one thing and hardship is another, why were we not given work without hardship for the sake of virtue?", then hear me. God did give it to us in that way. He willed that we should have work without toil and without hardship, but you did not will it. For he placed you in paradise to work it. He appointed work, but he did not join hardship to it, because work without toil is possible, as with the angels, of whom it is said: "Mighty in strength, who do his will."

And he made you likewise too, but by your own will you acquired that hardship-filled work, and now life is impossible without hardship. Therefore I beg you that we cast away all negligence and acquire virtue. For the taste of sin is brief, but the sorrow is everlasting; and the labor of virtue is brief, and the joy eternal;

And sin, even before hell, torments the one who commits it through that reproof of the mind, while virtue, even before the kingdom, comforts the one who practices it. Apart from this, what is the pleasure of sin worth, since as soon as it appears it vanishes, whether you speak of the pleasure of the flesh or of luxury? And on top of all that, eternal torment awaits those who commit it. But let us, who know all this, show all zeal for virtue, so that in this way we may find the true glory by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 37
This saying: Jesus said to him: "Do you wish to be healed?"
The sick man said to him: "Lord, I have no one to throw me into the pool when this water is stirred."
Commentary: Great is the benefit from the holy Scriptures,
and the divine words are a treasury of medicines of every kind, whether you seek a medicine for pride,
or for lust, or for love of money, or for grief; all of it is found in them.
For who, being afflicted either by poverty or by long illness, would read this present passage and not be comforted?
For he had been in that illness for thirty-eight years, and every year he saw others being healed, yet he did not despair, nor did he go away.
Hear his words: how he said nothing with murmuring or with anger, but answered meekly. He did not even know who it was
who was speaking to him, or whether he intended to heal him. Now hear what the Lord said to him:
Gospel: Jesus said to him: "Take up your bed and walk."
Commentary: Some say, "This is the one
of whom Matthew also speaks." But it is not this one. That man had many helpers who brought him to the Lord, but this man had not even one.

That man said nothing to the Lord, but this one told him his whole life story. He healed this man on the Sabbath, but that one on another day. He healed that one in a house, but this one by the pool. To that one he said, "Your sins are forgiven";
but to this one he said, "See, sin no more!" Here the Jews murmured about the Sabbath, but there they accused him of blasphemy.
But you, see the incomprehensibility of the Lord's goodness: not only did he heal him, but he also gave him such strength that he could take up his bed and walk,
so that the deed might also be made manifest and they might not regard it as an illusion [?]. For the Lord did this often: in the case of the loaves too, so that they might not say:

"It was an illusion," for this reason he left a great quantity of leftovers; and to the leper he said: "Go, show yourself to the priest," so that his cleansing might also be known and so that he might shut the mouths of those who said: "He opposes the law of God." But see the faith of that paralytic: he believed at once and rose, took up his bed according to his word, and did not heed those who said to him:
"It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed." Instead he said to them:
"The one who healed me, he told me: 'Take up your bed and walk!'"
I consider it great courage that he listened to none of those many people, for he did not even know who it was that had healed him,
because Jesus had withdrawn. But see the wickedness of the Jews. They did not say to him: [?]
"Who is it who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?"

but: "Who is it that healed you?" For they always begrudged people their salvation. And why did the Lord withdraw? First, so that the testimony would be beyond doubt, since the Lord was not there; and second, so that their anger would not be stirred up further. They murmured, asking why he did such a thing on the Sabbath. They were not troubled about the breaking of the law, but about the healing of that paralysed man.

Teaching 37: On envy. See, then, what an evil thing envy is, and how it blinds the eyes of those it overcomes. Just as madmen often kill themselves, so the envious destroy their own life. These people are more wicked even than wild beasts. Beasts repay evil for evil, but these people do evil in return for good. So they are worse even than beasts and equal to demons, and perhaps even worse than demons,

for the demons wage an implacable war against us, but they do not fight one another. The envious, however, have no regard for their shared nature. Whoever commits this evil has no excuse, because we ought to grieve over our own evils, not over another person's good. The fornicator has desire as his pretext, the thief has poverty, and the murderer has anger. These pretexts are worthless and empty, but they are pretexts of some kind. But you, envious one, tell me: what pretext will you give?
You have no excuse at all except the great amount of your wickedness. If we have been commanded to love even our enemies, what answer will you give when you hate even those who love you?

As the Lord says, whoever loves only his friends is no better than the gentiles. Then what punishment will someone receive who does evil even to those who do him good? This passion is worse than fornication and adultery,
for those stay with the person who commits them, but the evil of envy has overturned great churches and ruined the world.
Through this Cain killed Abel; through this Esau sought to kill Jacob; through this his brothers sold Joseph;
through this the devil fights against all people.
And worst of all is this, that this sin is reckoned a light one, whereas it is heavier than all, even though you say, envious one:
"I do not kill, nor do I sell my brother." Yet if you are hostile to him and do not wish for his good and his virtue, you are in that same evil, and you are fighting against God, whom he pleases.
But see how it is worse even than fornication: for a certain man committed fornication in Corinth, and they were angry with him, and he turned to repentance.

Cain envied Abel and received no healing; rather, God spoke to him again and again, and he grew all the more angry. So this is the worse evil and hard to heal, unless we strive earnestly to uproot it, root and all. And we shall uproot it in this way: if we consider that we anger God if we envy our neighbor's good, and likewise that we make God well pleased with us if we rejoice over our neighbor's good. For this reason Paul commands us to rejoice with those who rejoice and to weep with those who weep, so that in both ways we may become great in spirit, and so that, even if we have not toiled ourselves, we may become sharers in the labor of those over whom we rejoice. Thus, then, let us strive to uproot envy from ourselves, so that we may attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 38
This passage: After this Jesus found him in the temple and said to him: "Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse may happen to you."
Commentary: Sin is evil and harmful to the soul, but often, when its evil grows beyond measure, it also touches the body,
for since we do not care much about the disease of the soul, whereas over even a small ailment of the body we make great haste to heal it,
for this reason God often punishes this lesser part, so that through it the superior part too, which is the soul, may attain some healing.
In this way Paul set right that sinner among the Corinthians, and through punishment of the body he healed the soul,
like a skilled physician.

And in the case of this paralytic too, Christ indicates this very thing, for he said to him: "Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse may happen to you." What, then, do we learn from this?

First, that this disease was born of sins; and second, that the mouths may be shut of those who say: "In one moment I killed a man, and at one time I committed fornication, and am I to be punished forever for that one moment?"
For behold, this man too did not sin for as many years as he was punished,
for sins are judged not by time but according to their nature.
And again, we understand this too from it: that even if we are severely punished for sins and afterward fall back into those same sins, a worse punishment will come upon us.
Even though we see many sinners living in luxury, let us not put our trust in that, but rather let us weep when it is so.
For then a harsher torment awaits us. Here, all torment is for our instruction, but the true torment is the one
that has no end. Some say: "This paralytic had been an accuser of Christ." But it is not so, God forbid! The disease had come upon him because of other sins. And if anyone should say:
"Why did he not say this word also to the other sick people whom he healed, but only to him?"
to this we say that in this man's case the disease had befallen him because of sins,
but in the case of the others it came from natural sickness.
And again I say this also:
that he saw great patience in his soul and knew that he was able to keep this teaching.

For this reason he commanded him and put fear into his heart, so that he would beware of sin. But see how he said to him: "Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, so that nothing worse may happen to you."
He showed him that he had not received the punishment his sins deserved, but that this thing had been done for him out of goodness.
For he did not say to him, "Behold, you have received punishment equal to your sins," but rather:
"Behold, you have been made well by grace and not because of merit; sin no more."
Let us also say this to ourselves, brothers, whenever punishment comes upon us for our sins and we are again relieved: "Behold, we have been made well; let us sin no more."
But if we go on sinning and are not punished here in this life, let us call to mind the saying of the apostle Paul,
that "the kindness of God leads us to repentance, but according to our hard and unrepentant heart we store up wrath for ourselves on that day of wrath."
Gospel: "The man went away and said to the Jews, 'It is Jesus who healed me.'"

Commentary: See how he stands firm in his earlier faithfulness, proclaims the healer, and draws others to him as well. For he did not say these words as an accusation; or how could he have done such a thing?
Even if he had been a wild beast, that benefaction and the fear with which the Lord frightened him would have been enough to make him submit.
But it is not so. Rather, these words show great boldness, and he proclaims his benefactor just as the blind man did, who said:
"He made clay and opened my eyes." In the same way this man said: "It is Jesus who healed me."
Gospel: "The Jews persecuted Jesus, because he was doing this on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered and said to them, 'My Father works until now, and I also work.'"

Commentary: When he was answering on behalf of his disciples, he brought David into the discussion and said, "Have you not read what David did when he and those with him were hungry?" But when he wished to answer on his own behalf, he turned to the Father, in order to show his equality with him in honor, since he works just as the Father does. And he wished to raise their minds, so that they would look upon him not as a man but as God and lawgiver. And if anyone should say, "What does the Father do?" let him hear how it is written: "God rested on the seventh day from all his works," and let him understand the manner of his working, how he works: for he governs, foreknows, sustains, and strengthens all created things.

And when you see the rising of the sun, the course of the moon, and lakes and rivers and springs and rains, and the courses of nature in seeds, in our bodies and in those of the irrational animals, and all those other works by which this whole world subsists, from all of them understand the perpetual working of the Father, for he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the righteous and on sinners. And again the Lord said: "Consider the lilies of the field, how he clothes them," and of the birds he said: "Your heavenly Father feeds them." For wherever he works a miracle by word alone, he stops their mouths by the deed itself; but here, since he commanded the taking up of the bed, he was showing the loosing of the Sabbath, and he carried his word up to the Father.

And whenever the discussion concerns the Sabbath, he speaks of it neither as a man only nor as God only, but sometimes in this way and sometimes in that. For he wished to make both credible: the lowliness of his dispensation and the honor of his divinity. Therefore he now answers as God, for if he had spoken to him in human fashion, he would never have received an understanding of his divinity. For this reason he brings in the Father and says: "What I do, my Father also does."
Gospel: For this reason they sought all the more to kill Jesus,
for not only was he loosing the Sabbath,
but he also called God his own Father and made himself equal to God. Jesus answered and said to them: "Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son can do nothing at all of himself."

Commentary: On account of this saying the speakers of vanity say: It was not that Christ called himself equal to the Father, but that the Jews suspected him of it. For this reason, they say, Christ dispels their suspicion and says: "The Son can do nothing at all of himself." But these words are vain and full of wickedness, for listen to how he said earlier: "My Father works until now, and I also work." What could be greater than this equality?
Behold, he left no distinction at all, and he did not say: "My Father works, and I assist him,"
but: "As he works, I also work."

Or suppose Christ was not making himself equal to God, as he is equal, and the Jews only suspected this. O you who speak lawlessness, would Christ not have made every effort to dispel their suspicion?

But look, we see that nowhere did he wish to dispel their suspicion. Rather, he confirmed it. Or, if it had been so, would the evangelist not have said that Christ did not mean this in that way, and that the Jews only suspected it? He does this in other places, when the Lord says one thing and they suppose another, as when he said:
"Destroy this temple, and on the third day I will raise it up," and they understood it to refer to that temple.
But the evangelist said: "Jesus was speaking of the temple of his body." And here too, if it had been so,

Would he not have said so, if the Jews understood it this way while Christ did not mean it so? But nowhere is this the case. And this saying which the Lord spoke, that "the Son can do nothing at all of himself," does not overturn the equality, O man, but rather confirms it. But listen attentively, for this saying, "he cannot of himself," is no small matter for inquiry. It occurs in many places, "concerning both the Son and the Holy Spirit," and we must learn well about this saying, so that no one may fall into sin because of it. For if someone understands it simply, just as it stands, see what evil would result. For he did not say: "Some things I can do of myself and some I cannot," but rather, "He can do nothing at all." So I ask my opponent to tell me: "Can the Son then do nothing of himself?"

And if he says, "No," I will answer him: "And did he not do of himself the chief of all good things?" And Paul also cries out: "He did not count equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself and put on the form of a servant."

And again he himself says: "I have authority to lay down my life and I have authority to take it up again, and no one shall take it from me." Do you see that he has authority over death and life, and that he carried out such a great dispensation of himself? And why do I speak of Christ, when even we, than whom nothing is lower, do many things of ourselves? We acquire evil of ourselves and we practice virtue of ourselves. Otherwise, if we did not have this power and did not act of ourselves, we would neither be handed over to hell for sin nor enter the kingdom for virtue. What then does this saying mean, "He cannot do of himself"? It means this: he cannot do anything contrary to the Father, and this saying rather signifies equality. And if you say: "Why did he not say, 'He does not do anything contrary to the Father,' but rather, 'He cannot do it'?"

But he says this to show that greater unity. These words do not testify to any weakness in him, but rather to great power. In another place Paul says of the Father: "so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie." And again he says:

"If we deny him, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself." These words do not testify to any weakness in him, but rather to indescribable power. What he is saying is that such a nature cannot admit anything of that kind. It is as if we were to say: "It is impossible for the Lord to sin." By saying this we do not testify to any weakness in him. Rather, we confess his inexpressible power. So also when he says:
"I can do nothing at all of myself," he is saying this: "It is not possible, nor fitting, nor can it come about, that I should do anything contrary to the Father."
And so that you may know that this saying is to be taken in this way,
Let us look at the words that follow, to see for whom Christ bears witness: for these words spoken by us, or for those spoken by you. For you say:
"This saying undoes his power and authority," but I say: "Rather, it shows his equality with the Father and that he does not differ from him in any way, and that he does everything as from one mind."
Let us then hear the word of Christ that follows this, and see whether he interprets this saying according to your suspicion or according to our word. Hear, then, what Christ says:
Gospel: "For whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise."
Commentary: Do you see how he has torn out your argument by the root and confirmed what we have said? For,
if the Son does nothing of himself, then surely the Father also does nothing of himself, since everything whatever he does, the Son does also.
Do you see how lofty the force of these words is? Yet you, from lack of understanding, bring it down to something lowly,
for he needs no help, since he is equal to the Father in every respect. For as the evangelist says:
"All things were made through him, and without him nothing at all was made."

Do you see how his authority is shown in every respect? If he speaks some words in a lowly manner, do not be surprised. When the Jews heard lofty words, they persecuted him and called him an opponent of God.
For this reason he brought his discourse down a little toward lowliness, and then raised it up again to loftiness,
and again brought it down to lowliness, and in this way he varied his speech, so that it might be acceptable even to those without understanding. For consider

how it goes: first he said, "My Father works and I also work," and showed his equality with the Father; and then he said, "The Son can do nothing at all of himself, unless he sees some work from the Father."
And then he again raised it toward loftiness and said, "For whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise," and again he brought his speech down to lowliness and said:
Gospel: "For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he does, and he will show him works greater than this."

Commentary: See again what kind of humility this is, and it is rightly so. As I have said elsewhere, I say now too: whenever he speaks a humble word, he speaks it in an exceedingly humble manner. He does this so that the very great humility of those words might convince those who do not understand, and so that they might realize it cannot be so, but that this saying has some other, lofty meaning. For when he says, "He will show him greater works than these," see what harm would follow if anyone understood this saying just as it sounds.
For he would be saying:

"There are still works that he has not learned." This was not said even of the apostles. When the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon them, they knew in an instant everything they needed to know. And what could be worse than for someone to say, "The Son of God is still learning"? But hear what this saying means. Since he had healed the paralytic and was about to raise the dead as well, he says this: "Do you marvel at this? You will see even greater things than this." Yet he did not say it that way, but in a humble manner, in order to calm their frenzy. So that you may know that he did not truly say "He will show him greater things than this" about himself, hear also the words that follow:
Gospel: As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.

Commentary: See, then, how the saying "He can do nothing of himself" does not undo his authority. For look, here he says, "He gives life to whom he wills." If he cannot act of himself, how does he give life to whom he wills? The saying "As the Father raises the dead" points to the unchangeable sameness of his power. And the saying
"to whom he wills" shows that his authority is equal.

Do you see that the word he spoke, "He can do nothing of himself," does not undo his authority, but reveals the unchangeableness of the power of his will? Understand in the same way also that word he spoke, "He will show him," for in another place he says, "I will raise him up on the last day," and again he shows that he needs no help, and says, "I am the resurrection and the life," so that you may not say, "He raises the dead and gives them life, but he cannot do other things in this way." For this reason he cut off every argument beforehand, for he said, "Whatever he does, the Son also does likewise." Whether you speak of the resurrection of the dead, or the creation of bodies, or the forgiveness of sins, or anything else, all of it is said to be alike. But those who hate their own life listen to none of these things. So evil is the desire for preeminence.

This gave birth to the heresies; this confirmed the impiety of the pagans. For God willed that we should understand his invisible things through the creatures of this world, but they did not wish to follow this teaching and found another way instead. For this reason they also fell from that true way, and the Jews did not believe, because they received glory from men and did not seek the glory of the only God.

Homily 38, on vainglory. But let us, beloved, flee from this disease with all zeal, for even if we should have myriads of virtues, the passion of vainglory is able to undo them all. For if we love praise, let us seek praise from God and not from men. Otherwise, the praise of others, whatever it may be, as soon as it appears, at once vanishes and perishes; and even if it lasts a short time, no profit at all comes to us from it. For what is wonderful about human glory,
which many harlots and robbers and evildoers possess?

But whoever is glorified by God is not glorified with them, but with the holy prophets and apostles and those who have shown forth an angelic life. If you love praise and glory from the people, make the angels your praisers and become terrifying to the demons. Desire nothing from men, but trample all human affairs underfoot like dung and clay, and then you will understand that nothing harms your soul so much as vainglory. And it is impossible for someone conquered by it to complete a good life, just as it is impossible, again, for someone who has conquered it not to trample down the greater passions as well. But you, beloved, listen: victory over it comes about in this way, if we always look toward the eternal glory, from which it wants to lead us away;
for if we seek heavenly glory, it will make us shine here as well, and it will go out with us to the eternal life,
and it will free us from all bodily slavery, which we now serve with great wickedness, having altogether nailed ourselves to the earth.

For wherever you go, whether to streets or houses or roads, or wherever else you go, in every place you will find care for the affairs of this world, and that each person is being tormented because of it.

What hope of salvation, then, could we have, when we dwell on God's earth and do not strive to serve God, but we who were commanded to be strangers to the world are strangers to heaven, and citizens of the world and not of the kingdom? What could be worse than this folly? For every day we hear words about the judgment and the kingdom, and yet we imitate the people of Noah's time and the Sodomites, as if so that all those evils might come upon us in actual fact. And all of this was written for this reason: that those who become unbelieving about what is to come might have, from what has passed, a testimony of what is to come. Let us therefore reflect on all of this, both past and future, so that in this way we may rouse ourselves a little from this bitter slavery and take care of our souls,

so that we may attain the eternal good things by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 39
This saying: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father."
Commentary: We need great diligence in everything, beloved, for we are to give an account of both words and deeds in that life
to which we are going, and before the throne at which we are to stand, to receive according to our deeds, whether we have done good or evil.
Let us therefore always remember that judgment seat, and in this way we will be able to remain in virtue.
For just as whoever casts that day out of his soul falls among cliffs and precipices, like someone without a guide,

For it is written: "His ways are defiled at all times," and then it also stated the reason for this: "Your judgments are taken away from before his face." Likewise, whoever always has fear lives in good conduct, as it is written:
"Remember your end, and you will never sin." For the one who now forgives our sins
is going to be our judge. The one who died for us is the one who will judge our nature. This is why he said:
Gospel: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,
so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father."

Commentary: When he says, "He has given all judgment to the Son," by "all" he means that he is Lord of both honor and punishment. For he saw that human nature lacks understanding, and that people are not moved so much by promises of good things as by fear of punishment. So he told them this, in the hope that fear might bring them to honor him.

The word "gave" is used so that you do not consider him unbegotten, and do not imagine two fathers. For all that the Father is, the Son is the same: begotten, and abiding in the Godhead as Son. So that you may know that the word "gave" means "begot," hear another saying and learn this from it as well. For he says, "As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself." What, then, does
this saying mean? Did he first beget him and only afterwards give him life? For whoever gives something gives it to someone who already exists. Was he, then, ever begotten without life?

But not even the demons would come up with this, for along with their lawlessness they also have great folly. Rather, just as the saying "He gave life" means "He begot Him," so too this saying "He gave judgment" means that He begot Him as judge. For He comes to judge, so that you may know that He is in every way equal to the Father. Whatever authority the Father has to punish and to honour whomever He wills, the Son is able to exercise it equally with the Father. Otherwise, how can you say that it is not as I say, but that He was first begotten and afterwards this authority was given to Him? Or for what reason was this given to Him after His birth?

By what progress did He come to this honour? Are you not ashamed to bring these mean human notions to bear on that incorruptible nature, in which there is nothing that was added later? But if you say:
"Why does He speak this way?", understand that He speaks this way so that His word may become acceptable and may prepare the way for those lofty words.

For this reason He mixes the lowly with the lofty and the lofty with the lowly. Listen from the beginning. He said, "My Father is working until now, and I am working," and by this He showed His equality, but they sought to kill Him. See, then, what He did next. He spoke a lowly word, but its meaning was the same: "The Son can do nothing of Himself." Then again He raised His word to loftiness: "Whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise." Then He brought it down again to lowliness: "The Father loves the Son and has shown Him everything that He does, and He will show Him works greater than these." And again He raised His word to loftiness: "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wills."

After this He again spoke a word that signified both lowliness and loftiness at once: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son." And again He raised it to loftiness: "so that all may honour the Son as all honour the Father." Do you see how He varies His discourse and weaves it with lofty and lowly words and terms, so that it might be acceptable to the people of that time, and later generations might suffer no harm from it?

For we understand that the reason for his lowly words is entirely befitting God and lofty, for he did this for our sake, so that we might learn humility and so that he might show us salvation, since salvation comes about through this, as he himself indicated in another place, saying:

"I say this so that you may be saved." For since he brought in the testimony of John and set aside his own, because this was not worthy of his majesty, he therefore states the reason for such great lowliness of speech:
"I say these things so that you may be saved."
But listen again to a word about His equality with the Father:
Gospel: "Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him."
Commentary: Do you see how the honor of the Son is joined with the honor of the Father? For he did not say:
"If they do not honor" only, but, "Whoever does not honor him in this way, as the Father, does not honor the Father."

For He speaks His words with wisdom, so that we may understand the reason and not fall into the heresy of Sabellius, and so that the weakness of the Jews might be healed in this way and He would not be regarded by them as an opponent of God. For they were saying:

"This man has not come from God." Lofty words could not have removed this suspicion as well as lowly ones could. That is why he spoke again and again of his being sent. He did not do this so that we would take his words to mean he is in any way inferior, but so that he might stop their mouths. For this reason he keeps referring what he says to the Father, and at the same time he also shows his own honour. If he had always spoken in keeping with his own nature and honour, they would not have accepted those words, since whenever they heard even small words of this kind, they persecuted him. And again, if for their sake he had spoken only lowly words, many people after him would have been harmed. For this reason he mixed lofty and lowly language in what he said.
For this reason he also said what follows:
Gospel: "Amen, I say to you: whoever hears my words and believes the one who sent me has eternal life."

Commentary: Do you see how he hastens to dispel the suspicion they held, that he was an opponent of God, and how by both frightening them and promising good things he restrains their opposition to him? And here too he lowers his speech, for he did not say, "Whoever hears my words and believes me," since otherwise they would again have accused him of boasting. For if after much time and many miracles they still did not understand this and said to him, "Abraham died and the prophets perished, and how do you say, 'Whoever hears my word and believes will not taste death'?" — then it was so that they might not become enraged now as well that he spoke in this way:

"Whoever hears my words and believes the one who sent me has eternal life." For this made his word not a little more acceptable, so that they might know that he was preaching faith in the Father; and if they had accepted this eagerly, they would have more easily believed the rest as well. And thus it is evident that the lowly words also assist the lofty ones, for he said:
Gospel: "He has eternal life, and he will not enter into judgment, but will pass from death to eternal life."

Commentary: In two ways he makes his word credible: first, because he presents the Father as the one to be trusted, and second, because he bestows many good things on those who believe. And as for "he will not enter into judgment," this means that he will not be punished. For by death he does not mean this death of the present world, but the eternal one, just as he also speaks of that immortal life:
Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you that the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the words of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."

Interpretation: He had said, "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills." So that this would not be a mere word that they might count as a falsehood, he also shows that it is true in fact, saying:

"The hour is coming." So that they would not expect it in the distant future, he says that it is even now, when the dead will hear the words of the Son of God and will live. See here too his indescribable authority, for as in the future resurrection,
so it will be now, he says; for then we shall rise by the command of God, and now too, he says,
while I am with you, this deed will come to pass. And then he introduces a saying that confirms this matter and says:
Gospel: "Just as the Father has life in himself, so also he has given to the Son to have life in himself."
Commentary: Do you see the unchangeableness, and that there is only one distinction, that of personal property?

For he is the Father and he is the Son. But everything else is equal and unchangeable, and by this it is known that he does everything with such power and authority as the Father does, and not in any other way,
for he has life in the same way as the Father. For this reason the following saying also comes next, so that we may understand this from it, for he says:
Gospel: "And he gave him authority to execute judgment as well."
Commentary: Why does he turn resurrection and judgment over and over in this passage?
Because these words, more than anything else, turn the mind around, for whoever believes this will become afraid and will hasten to appease that judge.
Gospel: "For he is the Son of Man; do not marvel at this."

Interpretation: That saying seemed unbelievable to those who heard it, and they had taken Christ to be a mere man. Yet those words were beyond men and even angels, and belonged to God alone. For this reason he said:

"Do not marvel at this, because he is the Son of Man." And as to how this would come about, he says: "For the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment."
And why did he not say: Do not marvel that he is the Son of Man, for he is also the Son of God, but mentioned only the resurrection?
Because above he said:
"They will hear the voice of the Son of God," while here he spoke of "a work that belongs to God alone," so that from it they might reason that he who does this is surely God and the Son of God.
For if he himself had said this repeatedly, the matter might perhaps have been met with opposition; instead, by means of signs he better kept that teaching safe from harm.
And earlier, when he alluded to the raising of Lazarus, he spoke thus: "The hour is coming and is now here, when the dead will hear the words of the Son of God,"

and there he kept silent about judgment; but here, when he was speaking about the resurrection of all, he also mentioned judgment: "Those who have done good will come out to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment." For since he had said above: "Whoever hears my words and believes him who sent me will not enter into judgment," so that no one might think that this alone is enough for life, he therefore spoke of deeds as well: "Those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment." Since, then, he said that the whole world must give an account to him, and that all will rise at his voice, a new thing, which even now is unbelievable to many, how could it not have seemed unbelievable to the Jews at that time?
Therefore listen to how he makes that saying credible and lowers himself to their weakness, and says:
Gospel: "I can do nothing of myself,
but as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, for I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me."
Commentary: For since it seemed to them that he was speaking some strange words, beyond those of the prophets, for they said:
"It is God who will judge the earth."
But Christ was saying: "The Father judges no one, but I judge all,"
and this saying troubled the Jews and persuaded them to call him an opponent of God. For this reason he spoke here a word of great humility,
so that he might heal their weakness and tear out that evil suspicion by the root. For this reason he said:
"I can do nothing of myself," that is to say: "It is impossible that you should see or hear from me any deed or word opposed to the Father."
And just as he said above, "What we have heard we speak, and what we have seen we testify," and was speaking of both with regard to true knowledge,
and not with regard to seeing and knowing, so also here, when he spoke of hearing, he indicates nothing other than this:
"It is impossible that I should will anything other than what the Father wills." Yet he did not say this in the following way:
"As I say," for otherwise it would not have been accepted, but he spoke humbly and in human fashion: "As I hear, I judge." He did not say:
"As I am taught," but "As I hear." Yet he does not say this as though he had need of hearing, for not only was teaching unnecessary for him,
but hearing was unnecessary as well. Rather, he was indicating the unity and unchangeableness of the judgment, as if he were saying:
"I judge just as the Father himself would, if he were judging."
And then he says: "My judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of the one who sent me." What are you saying? Do you have another will apart from the Father?

And how do you say in another place, "As I and you, Father, are one," speaking there of will and unity? But understand, brothers, that this saying means something like this: "It is not that my will is one thing and the Father's will another,
but just as there is one will of one nature, so also is it with mine and the Father's.

And I have no other will separate from the Father, but what he wills, that same thing I also will, and what I will, that same thing he also wills; and such as the Father's judgment is, such also is mine. For indeed the command of both proceeds from one mind"? But do not be surprised that he speaks this saying in so human a fashion, for as yet he was reckoned a mere man. And for this reason it is necessary in such places that we examine not only the things said, but also what mind those hearers had, and that we listen to them as things said with regard to their mind. For if anyone understands the words of scripture just as he finds them, he will fall into much evil.

And how would this be? If the Lord were saying, "My will is one thing and the Father's is another," which even men who truly serve God do not say! For if Paul so blended his own will with the will of God that he even said, "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me," how then would the King of all have said, "My will is another, and I do not seek it, but I seek the will of my Father"?

But he said this to suit the minds of his hearers and the suspicion of those to whom he was speaking at the time. Earlier he had spoken his words partly in a manner befitting God and partly in a human manner. Here again he speaks as a man and says, "My judgment is just," for this reason:

"For I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me." Among men, it is unfitting to say that someone judges unjustly if he is far from carrying out his own will and from love of himself. "In the same way, you cannot convict me now either. Someone who seeks to establish his own will might perhaps be suspected by many of perverting justice. But if someone does not seek his own will, what reason could there be for him not to judge justly?

"Apply this reasoning to me as well. If I were saying that I have not been sent by the Father, and if I did not give him the glory for these works, perhaps one of you might have suspected that I want glory for myself and am therefore not speaking the truth. But since I glorify him, what reason do you have to accuse me?" Do you see where he brought his argument? Do you see that, as I have said many times, the extreme lowliness of his words teaches the intelligent all the more? It teaches them not to understand his words only as they hear them and so fall into error, but to rise to the loftiness of their meaning and not be harmed.

Teaching 39: On the remembrance of wrongs and on mercy. But as for us, brothers, when we hear all this, let us not pass over these words in vain, but let us examine them well and carefully investigate the reason for what was said. And let us not think that ignorance and lack of learning are enough for us as a defense before God, for the Lord has commanded us not only innocence but also wisdom.
Let us therefore acquire wisdom along with sincerity, and let us judge ourselves here and now, so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
And let us be toward our neighbors such as we wish God to be toward us, for we say:
"Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."

And I know that when the soul is distressed by another, it does not bear this without distress and pain; but if we understand that it is not to the one who distresses us but to ourselves that we do good,

if we do not become angry, then we may be able to cast out the venom of wrath. For the one who tormented his fellow servant over the hundred denarii did not harm him, but made himself a debtor of the myriad talents, forgiveness of which he had previously received.
So when we do not forgive others, we do not forgive ourselves. Therefore let us not always say only to God:
Do not remember our sins; but let us also say to ourselves:
Do not remember the sins of your neighbor that he has committed against us. For you first write the law of forgiveness, and so God carries it out,
that is to say:
If you forgive others, he will forgive you.

Now then, others blot out their sins by keeping vigil, by lying on the bare ground, and by countless torments and hardships; but you are able, by this easy road, which is not remembering wrongs, to blot out all your sins.
Why then do you sharpen the sword and wound yourself like a madman, and drive yourself out of eternal life? We must make every effort so that you may attain that life.

For if life in this place of training is so desirable, what could anyone say of that life where there is no pain, no sorrow and no sighing? There is no fear of death there, and no worry that those good things will come to an end.

Blessed are they, three times blessed and ten thousand times blessed, who have been made worthy of that blessed life. In the same way, wretched are they, and ten thousand times to be pitied, who have fallen short of that blessedness. And if you say, "What deed is it that makes us worthy of that life?", listen to the Lord himself and what he says to a certain young man who said, "What shall I do to inherit eternal life?" The Lord told him about the other commandments, and last of all he came to love of neighbor, as the seal of them all. And if anyone should say even now, "I have not committed adultery, I have not stolen, I have not killed anyone," then along with these things he must also have achieved this: to love his neighbor as himself. For if someone has envied his neighbor, or spoken evil of him, or repaid evil with evil, or did not give him even what he needed, he has not loved him as himself.

Christ commanded not only this but something else as well: "Sell your possessions, give to the poor, and come, follow me." By "following" he meant becoming like him through deeds. What then do we learn from this? First, that whoever does not have all these things cannot reach perfection in that life. For he spoke as one pointing to perfection when he said, "If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor."

Again, we also understand this: he rebuked the young man himself for boasting in vain. For how could he, who lived in such wealth and disregarded others in their poverty, have loved his neighbor as himself? He was not speaking truthfully at all. But let us strive with all our strength to give away all our possessions and buy the kingdom of heaven. For if people give all their possessions for worldly honor, an honor that stays here, and often does not even stay with them for long here, what then shall we say, who will not spend even a little for that eternal honor? Is it not utter madness that we do not want to take with us what would otherwise remain here? What excuse do we have, then, when an easy life lies before us and yet we hurl ourselves down cliffs and walk where there is no path? Instead, let us wake up, come to our senses and order our life well, so that we may gain eternal life by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 40
This saying: "If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true; there is another who bears witness about me, and I know that his witness is true."

Commentary: Whoever searches for the veins from which gold is extracted and is inexperienced in that craft will find no profit anywhere, nor will he extract any gold, but will only take vain labor upon himself.
So too those who do not know the manner and usage of the Holy Scriptures, and yet search into their meaning,
they mix gold into the earth, and through ignorance they will never find the treasure that lies within them.
I have said this because in the present saying there is much gold, yet it is not plainly visible but hidden. Therefore we must labor until we find it.
For who would not be astonished on hearing Christ say, "If I bear witness about myself, my witness is not true,"
when he is seen in many places to bear witness about himself? For he said to the Samaritan woman:
"I am the Christ." And to the blind man he said, "He who is speaking with you is he." And to the Jews he said:

"How can you say, 'He blasphemes,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?" He does the same in many other places. What then does this saying mean, and how should we understand it? For again, further on, he says:
"If I bear witness about myself, my witness is true," while here he says, "If I bear witness, it is not true." What then? Which of these two are we to accept?
Unless we investigate the reason for this saying, why he said it and to what persons, how are we not to fall into temptation?
For if his testimony is not true,
What would our hope of salvation be? Rather, we must be watchful, so that we do not stop at the words alone, but also look into the force and sense of the word,
For this is how the heretics went astray: they understand the words of Scripture just as they heard them.
And if we do this, failing to investigate the time, the saying, and the mind of the hearer, we shall fall into great evil.
What then does this saying mean? The Jews were going to say to him, "You bear witness about yourself, and your witness is not true."
Therefore the Lord anticipated them and said this, as if to say: "Perhaps you will say to me, 'We do not believe you'; but the Father also bears witness about me."
For the saying "my witness is not true" should not be understood simply in this way, but rather as follows:
"My witness is not true in your eyes." Thus their suspicion is joined to the saying, and he did not say this as a statement of how things are, but answered with regard to their way of thinking.
And when he says, "My witness is not true," he exposes the wickedness of their mind and the opposition they were going to offer him.
But when he says, "If I bear witness about myself, my witness is true," he reveals the very nature of the matter: that they ought truly to acknowledge his word as that of one who is worthy,
even though he is speaking about himself. For since he had spoken of the resurrection of the dead and of judgment, and that "whoever believes in him does not go to judgment but to life;

And that he is the one who will sit as judge, and that he has authority and power equal to the Father's: he wished to prove all this. For this reason he first spoke this word, which was within their nature, as though he were saying: "I said that 'as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills'; and that 'the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son'; and that 'whoever honors the Son honors the Father'; and that 'honor is due to the Son just as to the Father'; and that:

'whoever hears my words and believes will not enter into judgment, but will pass from death to life'; and that 'the dead will hear my voice, some now and some at the last'; and that 'I will call all to account for their deeds.' And since all this is my testimony, and my testimony before you is not true, look to those other witnesses of mine." And in this way he made his word credible. For first he revealed to them what was hidden in their minds, and showed them this one sign of his power, and after that he brought in other proofs as well, for he offered three witnesses to his words: first, the works that he was doing; then, the testimony of the Father; and also the preaching of John. And first he told them the lesser one, that is, John's, for when he had said, "There is another who testifies about me, and I know that his testimony is true," he immediately added and said:
Gospel: "You sent to John, and he testified to the truth."

Commentary: Do you see how from this word too it is evident that the saying "My testimony is not true" was spoken with reference to their suspicion? And he said, "You sent to John," so that they could not say, "And what of it, if he testified to do you a favor?" For this reason he said, "You sent," and if you had not held him to be a very trustworthy man, you would not have sent to him. And indeed they did not ask him about Christ, but about himself: "Who are you?" This is a sign of greater trust, for if we accept someone's testimony about himself, would we not accept it all the more if he testifies about another? And those who were sent were not some contemptible persons, but priests and Pharisees. And he indicated all this by the word he spoke: "You sent to John, and he testified to the truth."
Gospel: "But I do not receive testimony from man."
Commentary: And why did he bring in John's testimony, since that too was not human? For he says, "He who sent me to baptize with water, he said to me."
and indeed John's testimony too was God's, for he had learned it from Him and spoke it,
but they did not know this; instead, they regarded John as speaking on his own authority.

And so that they would not say, "How can you say that you have learned everything from God and that you are from Him, and then again receive testimony from John?", he answered them according to their own way of thinking: "I do not receive testimony from man." And again, so that they could not say:
"If you do not receive testimony from man, why do you bring in John's preaching as a witness?"
For this reason, so that they could not say this, he added what follows as well and said:
Gospel: "But I say this so that you may be saved."
Commentary: Now this saying means the following: I have no need of his testimony, for I am the God of the nature of men,

but since you listen to John, and his word is credible to you, and you went to him as to a prophet, while you do not listen to me even on account of the miracles, for this reason I remind you of his testimony.
Gospel: "For he was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a time in his light."
Commentary: And so that they could not say: "He spoke, but we did not accept his word,"

he also shows that they accepted his words and rejoiced over his words. So much did they marvel at him, and they did not oppose his words. And this saying, "for a time," he spoke in order to show the lightness of their mind, that they quickly departed from him too.
Gospel: "But I have testimony greater than John's."
Commentary: That is to say: if you had wished to accept faith according to the truth of the deeds, I would have made you believe by means of the deeds.
Since, then, you do not wish it so, for this reason I lead you to John.
Not that I have need of his testimony, but I use every means so that you may be saved. And I have testimony surpassing John's, through my works,
but what I want is this: to bring you to faith by whatever means.
And he wished to expose their mind, that they were willing to rejoice in him only for a short time. And he indicated that unstable mind of theirs, and he gave John the name of lamp in order to show
that he did not have the light of himself, but from the grace of the Holy Spirit.

And by mentioning this, he convicted them: the same attitude with which they despised him (John) also kept them from believing Christ's [testimony], for for a time they had gained faith in him; if not [?]
Had it not been so, he would long ago have brought them to Jesus.
And he showed them in every respect that they are not worthy of mercy, and immediately he added and said:
Gospel: "I have testimony greater than John's, for the work which the Father has given me to accomplish, these works testify about me that the Father has sent me."

Commentary: Here he reminded them of the deed done for the paralytic and of the many other miracles. As for John's words, they might perhaps say that they were not true and that he spoke out of favour toward him. Even saying this would have been wicked with regard to John, a man so truthful and held in such esteem even by them, but with regard to the deeds it was utterly impossible even for madmen to say any such thing. Therefore he brought this in as a second testimony and said:

"The works which the Father has given me to accomplish, these works testify about me that the Father has sent me." Here he is also speaking about the breaking of the Sabbath, since they were saying, "He is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath."

For this reason he says, "which he gave me," although he did everything with authority; but in order to show with certainty that he does nothing contrary to the Father, he spoke this humble word. For why did he not say, "The words which the Father gave me, they testify that I am equal to the Father"? For through the works both of these things were made known: that he is equal to the Father and that he does nothing contrary to him. And why did he not speak thus, but said, "The works testify that the Father has sent me"? Because he was eager to persuade them of this, that he does nothing contrary to the Father; for if they did not believe this, how would they have believed that he is equal to the Father?

And for this reason he was eager to persuade them of this lesser thing, and he knew that if they became well convinced of this, they would afterward easily believe that as well. And he mentioned that higher testimony too, and he mentioned the lesser matter, so that they might accept that also.
Gospel: "And the Father who sent me, he has testified concerning me."

Commentary: And where did the Father testify concerning him? Once, at the Jordan: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." But it was necessary to show this, for the testimony of John was known to all and they could not deny it, and again the signs done by the Lord, these too were manifest and they could not deny them. But it was necessary that he also show the testimony of the Father and make it credible, and this is what the Lord wished to do. For this reason he said:
Gospel: "Neither have you ever heard his voice, nor have you seen his form."
Commentary: And how is it that Moses says concerning himself, "Moses spoke and God answered him with a voice," and David says:

"He heard a language which he did not know," and again Isaiah and Jeremiah and Ezekiel and many others speak of seeing him? What then is this saying of Christ? It is only this: he wished to teach them little by little to understand what is good, so that they might know that God has neither a voice nor a color that a person might hear or see, but that God is above such forms and words. For he does not say that God gives forth a voice, only one that cannot be heard, or that he has some color, only one that cannot be seen; rather he indicates this, that nothing belonging to these material things is with God. And this was so that they would not say that God spoke only to Moses, as they indeed said:
"We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from." Therefore he says:

"With God there is neither a material voice nor a form. Not only have you never heard his voice or seen his form, but even in the thing you boast of, that you possess his teachings, you have not managed even that." Therefore he added and said:
Gospel: "And his word does not abide in you."
Commentary: That is, the Law and all the prophecies: although God commanded them, yet none of them abides in you, since you do not believe in me.
For if all the Scriptures proclaim concerning me, and you do not believe me, then surely nothing of them abides in you. For this reason he also added and said:
Gospel: "For the one whom he sent, you do not believe him."
Commentary: But so that they might not say, "Since we have not heard his voice, how are we to believe the one whom he has sent?", for this reason he says:
"Search the Scriptures, for they testify about me." He means that the Father testifies about me through them,
and he also testified at the Jordan and on Tabor, yet he did not bring those voices into the discussion,
for otherwise they would not have believed it, since, first, they had not heard the voice on Tabor, and second, even though they had heard the other, they did not believe.
For this reason he sent them to the Scriptures, to show that the Father's testimony is in them,

And first he demolished the boasting of those who imagined that they had seen God and heard his voice, and in this way he sends them to search the Scriptures. Teaching 40 [?]: that the one who is perfect in virtue is the one who carries out all the commandments, and on almsgiving.
And let us too, whenever we speak with heretics, arm ourselves in this way, for "all Scripture is divine and profitable to the soul for teaching and for reproof,
so that the man of God may be perfect for every good thing," for
whoever has one good thing and lacks another is not perfect. For what profit is it if someone prays much but does not have almsgiving?
Or what if someone gives alms, but from what was stolen, or to make a show before men; or gives alms properly but is boastful; or is humble but has love of money, the mother of all evils?

For the love of money is the root of all evil, so let us flee from it, because it has thrown the whole world into turmoil. It separates us from the service of Christ, for it is impossible to serve both God and mammon. Christ commands us to show mercy, but it commands us to rob. Christ orders us to forgive our debtors, but it tells us to harm even those who have done us no harm. Christ says, "Be merciful," but it says, "Be merciless and hard-hearted, and pay no attention to the tears of the poor," so that on that day the Lord will be merciless toward us. For then all our deeds will be set before our eyes, along with those whom we afflicted and wronged, and they will hold us to account for every word [?].

For if Lazarus had suffered no harm from the rich man, but only because he had not received mercy from him became his accuser and the one who silenced him, what will become of those who seize what belongs to the poor, and who afflict and ruin orphans? If those who did not feed a hungry poor man fell into so great an evil, then what will those who have seized another's property be found worthy of?

Or what consolation would they find? Let us flee, then, from this evil. Let us remember the greedy who lived before us: do not others now have their wealth, while they themselves are tormented in the fire? How then is such wretchedness not madness, that we should be in toil and evil during this life, and, when we depart from here for eternity, should be terribly tormented? Let us practice mercy, so that we may find rest here and inherit the kingdom of heaven there. For just as sin, even before Gehenna, torments those who commit it here and now through the reproach of the mind, so also virtue, even before the kingdom, gladdens those who practice it with good hope. Let us also strive, then, to have such a way of life, so that we may find rest here and attain the eternal good things there, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 41
This saying: "Search the Scriptures, for you suppose that you have eternal life through them,
and they are the ones that testify about me, and you do not want to come to me, so that you may have eternal life."

Commentary: Beloved, let us make every effort to understand the divine words, and let us not read them so carelessly and without understanding. This is why Christ the Lord, when he was speaking to the Jews

about the Scriptures, did not simply tell them, "Read," but "Search." The words spoken about him were worth searching carefully, because from the beginning they had been spoken in a hidden way and in parables, for a better purpose.
For this reason he commands them to search well, so that they may find the mysteries hidden in their depth,
for the mystery did not lie on the surface, but, like a great treasure,
it was hidden in the depths, and whoever does not seek diligently will not find what is buried in the depth.
For this reason he said, "Search the Scriptures, for you suppose that you have eternal life through them." He did not say,

"You have life," but, "You suppose," for he shows that those who supposed they would be saved by reading alone gained nothing at all from them. And this saying amounts to the following: "Do you not say,
'The Scriptures are true and a cause of life'? So I too take testimony from them,
for they testify about me, and you do not want to come to me, so that you may have eternal life."

But since he had made many efforts so that they might believe him, and had mentioned the testimony of John, and that of his own works, and that which comes from the Father, and so that they could not say, "He wants glory from people,"
for this reason he speaks these words and brings them forward to lead them to faith in him. For this reason the Lord said to them:
Gospel: "I do not accept glory from people."
Commentary: That is to say, I have no need of it; my nature is not such that I would need glory from people,
for if the sun receives no addition of light from a small candle, should I not be all the farther removed from needing human glory?
But I say this so that you may be saved. And he also gave yet another reason for this:
Gospel: "But I know you, that you do not have the love of God in yourselves."
Commentary: Now since they were saying, "We love God, and that is why we persecute you, because you make yourself equal to God," and the Lord knew
that they are not going to believe him [?]. And so that no one could say, "If you do not need glory from men, why do you say such things?", he said:

"I say these things to convict you, to show that you are not persecuting me out of love for God. I have shown you that he testifies about me. So if you were persecuting me for his sake, and if you loved God, would you not now have come to me?"
But the love of God is not in you." And for this reason he showed them yet another sign of their not loving God, and said:
Gospel: "I have come in the name of my Father, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, will you receive him?"

Commentary: Do you see how he tried in every way to take away their excuse? This is why he said, "The Father sent me": so that they would have nothing left to say. And when he says, "[Another] will come in his own name," he is pointing here to the Antichrist and showing how extremely senseless they are. For if you were persecuting out of love for God, should you not rather have persecuted the Antichrist?
For he will say nothing like this, and will not claim to be sent by the Father. He will say the exact opposite. He will seize [?] by force, and he will call himself God in every way.
For this is what coming in one's own name means; but I have not come in this way, rather I have come in the name of the Father.

And since they did not receive the one who said he was sent by God, while the one who will come in his own name and say, "I am God," him you are going to worship, this is a sign that they persecuted him out of envy and hatred of God. For this reason he set down these two reasons for his words: first, their life: "that you may be saved," and: "that you may have life."

And since they were going to scorn this, he told them a second reason as well, one that exposes their wickedness. For Paul said about the Antichrist, prophesying: "God will send a power of delusion, so that all who did not believe the truth may be judged." But Christ did not say, "He will come," but, "If he comes."

For he was being considerate of those hearers, and for this reason he kept silent about the reason for his coming; but Paul stated the reason as well: "For he is the one who will take away every argument from them." And after this the Lord also stated the reason for their unbelief:
Gospel: "How can you believe, since you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory of the only God?"
Commentary: With this saying too he shows that they were not seeking the things of God,

but were using that as a pretext to do their own will. For they were not seeking the things of God but the glory of men. He had shown in many ways that they did not have the love of God, and he had openly proved that they had no argument left. Then he also brought forward Moses as their accuser and said:
Gospel:
"Do not think that I will accuse you before the Father; your accuser is Moses, in whom you hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me.
If you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?"

Commentary: What he is saying amounts to this: "By dishonoring me you insult him even more than me, for you have become more unbelieving toward Moses than toward me." Do you see how he took away every argument they had? For he says:
"You were saying, 'We love God,' and I will show that you do not love him, since you persecute me. You were saying,
'You break the Sabbath and transgress the Law'; I have exposed that accusation too. Or will you say, 'We listen to Moses,' and persecute me on account of his words?

I have shown that by persecuting me you dishonor Moses all the more. And he, more than anyone, has accused you." And so he shut their mouths, when he showed them that they did not believe even Moses, for Moses said:
"If someone comes and performs signs, and leads you to God, and speaks truly of all that is to come, believe him."
And Christ did all of this: he performed signs in truth, led everyone to God, and foretold all that was to come, and yet they did not believe. But if he also said:
"I do not accept testimony from a human being," and now he has brought forward Moses as a witness,
