do not be surprised, for he took as witness not Moses but the words of God, and he mentioned the person of Moses
in order to frighten them all the more. But consider how he has left them no argument, for they were saying:
"We persecute him for the love of God"; he showed that they were doing this out of hatred of God. Again they were saying:

'We believe Moses.'" He showed them that they did not believe Moses and that this was why they acted as they did. "For if you love God," he says, "you ought to love me as well. If you believe Moses, you ought
so that you might believe me too and worship the one about whom he preached. If you do not believe him, what wonder is it if you do not believe me either?"
And after all this they did not turn back, for such is wickedness: however much anyone may say and do, it does not bend but keeps its own venom.

Moral teaching: that nothing makes a person as wise as virtue does, and that every evil has its beginning in wickedness. So let us hurry to drive all wickedness out of our souls and never practise deceit. For the Lord God sends crooked ways to the crooked, and the Holy Spirit of God flees from deceit and from evil thoughts. Nothing drives a person as mad as wickedness does, and nothing makes a person as wise as virtue does. Virtue makes a person gracious, loving toward others, gentle and kind. What could be wiser than someone like that? Virtue is the spring and root of wisdom, just as the beginning of all wickedness comes from folly. The proud and the angry are overcome by their passions because they lack understanding. That is why the prophet also said:

"There is no healing for my flesh because of my folly." He said this to show us that every sin has its beginning in folly, and that the virtuous person who fears the Lord is the wisest of all. For "the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." Since wisdom is the fear of the Lord, and the wicked person has no fear of the Lord, he is indeed cut off from wisdom and is the most foolish of all. Yet many people call the wicked wise because they harm others skilfully.
And they do not know that this is great folly, for

the person who harms another does not really harm that other person. Instead he drives a sword into his own heart without realising it. This is a sign of great folly. So let us not call those who are afflicted and suffer at the hands of others wretched. Let us rather call wretched those who harm and afflict them. They are the ones who are truly harmed. They set themselves up as fighters against God, they open the mouths of countless accusers against themselves, and they prepare a great judgement for themselves in Gehenna. But those who were afflicted and endured it receive mercy from God and from everyone. In this world they show their wisdom, and in the age to come they find endless good things. May we all be found worthy to attain these by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory belongs to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 42
The text: After this Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias, and a great crowd followed him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.
And Jesus went up on a mountain and sat with his disciples. And the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near.
Commentary: Let us not clash too much with evil people, brothers, but, when our virtue is not being harmed, let us give way to their wickedness and withdraw from them,

for behold, the Lord, because of the great wickedness of the Pharisees and the other Jews, went to Galilee in order to quench their envy and anger. And now again he crossed the sea and went away toward the mountain.
And a great crowd followed him, because they saw the signs that he was doing.
However, the evangelist does not recount those signs one by one, for he was eager rather to relate to us the teachings of the Lord, which he spoke to the Jews.
And behold, of that year he told of no sign except only that of the paralytic and that of the son of the royal official,
for it was impossible to tell all his signs. Therefore he has related to us a little out of much.
But see the coarseness of mind of that crowd: after so many signs they still followed him because of the signs and not because of his words, which is the behavior of a coarse mind,
for a sign, it says, is for unbelievers, not for believers alone.
Why did he go up the mountain?

But he did this to teach us too to love the wilderness and to flee from turmoil, for the wilderness is good and lovely. That is why the Lord often withdrew alone to the mountain and prayed. He wanted to teach us that whoever wishes to draw near to God must stay far away from turmoil. But on this occasion only the disciples went up. The rest of the crowd did not go up the mountain with them because of their unbelief, but came afterwards.
Gospel:
"The Passover, the feast of the Jews, was near. Jesus lifted up his eyes and saw a great crowd coming to him."
Commentary: Why is it that at Passover everyone was going to Jerusalem, while the Lord went to Galilee?

Because, on account of the wickedness of the Jews, he had begun little by little to pass over their feasts. And he sat with the disciples in humility and, as I suppose, was teaching them certain mysteries. For this reason he had also turned toward them, and he lifted up his eyes and saw the people who had come. And the other evangelists say that the disciples came up and spoke to the Lord about the people.

But this evangelist says that the Lord asked Philip. Both of these are true, but they did not both happen at one time. Rather, what the other evangelists tell happened first, and this happened afterward.
But why did he ask Philip? Only because he himself knew which of the disciples needed more teaching.
For this is the one who was going to say later on:

"Show us your Father." And for this reason he had been strengthening and teaching him from the very beginning. And now too he asked him first, and he confessed the poverty they had, saying: "Two hundred denarii worth of bread is not enough for this people."
And when he had confessed with his own mouth how great the matter was, then Jesus performed the miracle.
Gospel: "But he said this to test him, for he himself knew what he was going to do."

Commentary: What is this saying, "he was testing"? What did it mean to say? For he knew everything before doing or saying it. But understand what this saying is from the Old Testament, for there it says, "God tested Abraham," and neither does it mean there that only after the test did he learn the outcome of the matter, whether Abraham would obey or not.
Far from it! For how could this apply to him who knows everything before it comes to be? Rather, both of these things are said in human terms.

For just as, when Scripture speaks of the one who searches the hearts of men, it does not mean that he does not know and is searching in order to find out, but points to his true knowledge, so also when it says, "He was testing him," it means nothing else but this: he knew well, and he wished that Philip too should be tested and made firm. And as with Abraham, so with this one: by his question he led him to understand that surpassing miracle. For this reason too, so that you would not imagine anything wrong because of the weakness of this word, the evangelist said, "He himself knew what he was going to do." For wherever an evil suspicion might creep in, the evangelist hastens to set it right.
And when the Lord had questioned Philip, Andrew answered him:
Gospel: "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. But what is this before so many?"
Interpretation: This one was higher in understanding than Philip, yet even he had not reached perfection. And what do you suppose? He had in mind the miracles performed by the prophets?
and how Elisha performed miracles with the loaves; yet he could not understand fully,
for he thought that he would multiply little from little and much from much, because he did not know
that it was just as easy for him to multiply the loaves from a little as from a lot.

And it was not that he needed material set before him, but rather so that no one might say, "Created things are foreign to his wisdom," as Marcion later dared to say. For this reason: "He took material from created things to perform this sign."
And once both of those disciples had given up hope of bread, then he began to perform the sign, and he showed the superiority of this sign over the one performed by the prophets.

And while the loaves were nowhere to be seen, so that you may know that what does not exist is before him as what exists, as Paul says: "who calls the things that do not exist as things that exist." For this reason here too, before the loaves were brought, he commanded the crowd to sit down, as at a table by the road, so that this might also benefit the minds of the disciples; and they had come to understanding through that question. Therefore, without doubting, they carried out his command and seated the crowd.

Nor did they say, "What is this? Nothing is to be seen, and you command the crowd to sit down?" But those who earlier had been unbelieving and were saying, "From where shall we buy bread?" now came to faith even before seeing. And why is it that when he healed the paralytic and performed other signs he did not pray, yet here he prays? To teach us to pray at mealtime; and again, because he prays over these lesser signs in order to show that it is not that he needs prayer. For if he had needed it, would he not rather have done so over those greater ones? And since he performed those great signs by his own authority, it is evident that here too he had no need of prayer; rather, the crowd was large, and he wished them to believe that he had come by the will of God.

Gospel: "And Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and gave them to those who were seating the people, and likewise of the fish, as much as they wanted. And when they were filled, Jesus said to his disciples: 'Gather up the leftover fragments.' And they gathered them and filled twelve baskets."

Interpretation: Do you see how great the difference is between the servants and the Master? For they had grace in measure, and so they performed miracles in that way, but God does all things with unstinting power. And the leftovers remained. He did not do this so that people would see it, but so that no one could say, "The thing was an illusion." For this reason too he did it from the material at hand. And why did the disciples carry the baskets? Because he wished them to be well taught, since they were to be the teachers of the whole world. And this was no small condemnation for Judas, for he too carried a basket. And so that you may know that he did it to teach them, hear how afterward he reminded them, saying:

"Do you not understand how many baskets you took up?" And indeed the baskets were equal in number to the disciples. But at another time, because they were better taught, they took up seven and not twelve, for he made the leftovers as many as he wished. In the case of the loaves there were leftovers, so that it would not be counted an illusion. But in the case of the fish there were no leftovers at that time. Instead, after the resurrection a fish was seen without any material at hand, so that you may know that even now he did not use that material out of need, but in order to stop the mouths of the heretics.
Gospel: But the people said, "This is truly the prophet."

Commentary: O, the excess of gluttony! He did countless things more wondrous than this, and they never took them to mind; and now, when they have filled their bellies, then they confess him to be a prophet.
Gospel: "But Jesus, perceiving that they were coming to seize him in order to make him king, withdrew and went away alone."
Commentary: See the fickleness of their natures. They no longer cared about the breaking of the Sabbath, nor did they call to mind anything of the Law, which they used to speak of before,
But when they had filled their bellies, they called him a prophet and were about to make him king. But Christ fled,
to teach us to despise the honours of the world, and to show that he needs nothing of the earth,
for he chose everything lowly: mother, house, city, upbringing and clothing. And he did not wish to be made known through earthly things,
for everything heavenly was radiant, and angels and a star and the Father proclaimed him greatly, and the Holy Spirit bore witness, and the prophets had spoken beforehand,
but everything earthly he held as lowly, so that in this way his power might be shown all the more, for he came in order to teach us contempt of the world.
For this reason he said to Pilate: "My kingdom is not of the earth."
And when the prophet says, "Behold, your king comes,"
he was speaking of the heavenly kingship and not the earthly. For this reason the Lord said:
"I do not receive glory from men."
Homily 42, that the glory of this world is nothing. Let us learn, then, beloved, contempt for the glory that comes from men, for we have a great honor,
compared with which this is insult and contempt. Just as the wealth of the world is poverty compared with that wealth, and this life without that one is death,
so too this glory compared with that one is reproach and shame, for "the glory of man is like the flower of grass."
And what is lower than a flower and grass? Even if it were not vain, what would it profit the soul?
Nothing! For it even does harm beyond measure, and makes those who seek it slaves of slaves.
But is not freedom better than slavery: freedom from men and slavery to God?

And if you love glory, love that immortal glory, whose benefit is great, for that glory is immortal. Which, then, is better: glory from men or from God, on earth or in the heavens? Is it better to be crowned for one day, or for those endless ages?
Give to the poor and do not give to the singer, so that you do not lose your soul along with your wealth, and his soul too. For you are the cause of his ruin, you who honour him for his wickedness.

For if poets and singers knew that their art was unprofitable, they would long ago have given up that occupation. But when they see that you love the thing and give a great deal for it, then even if they do not want to, the desire for money makes them do it. So let us turn away from that unprofitable spending. Let us know and understand where it is right to spend, so that we do not anger God on both counts, when we gather from where we should not and scatter where we should not. For how is it not lawlessness when you pass by the poor man and give to the harlot, even if you had acquired that wealth justly? This too was an evil deed: to give a reward for wickedness, and to honour someone for the very thing for which punishment was due.

But when you also strip orphans and oppress widows, and give it as payment to a sinner, understand how you are bringing fire upon your own soul. For if you praise the singer and his deed pleases you, you are worse than he is. For he, though he has no defense, still has poverty as an excuse; but what excuse will you state, other than the destruction of the soul? What will you say at that great judgment, where you will have to give account even for your thoughts? With what eye will you look upon the Judge? What excuse will you state for that deed of yours? There is no excuse that you could state, only eternal, unending torment. But may we all be worthy to attain his kingdom, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, whose is the glory, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 43
The passage: And when evening came, his disciples went down to the sea and got into a boat and were going across the sea to Capernaum.
And darkness had just fallen, and Jesus had not come to them. And the sea was being stirred up by a great wind.
Commentary: Not only when Christ was with them bodily, but also when he was far away, he arranged what was better.
And see what he did here too: for he left the disciples and went up onto the mountain.
And they went down to the sea when evening came. Until evening they waited for him to come to them, and when he did not come, they waited no longer, but began to seek their teacher.
So great was the love they had for him, and they shrank from nothing,
but embarked in a boat; for this is why the evangelist also mentioned the time.
But why did Christ leave them and then appear to them again? He left them so that their longing might grow,
and he appeared so that they might know his power, for it was fitting,
for they too had to see his miracles by themselves, they who were to become teachers of the world.
For this reason they saw miracles by themselves: the Transfiguration, and this one now on the sea, and those after the resurrection, and many others.
And they were going to Capernaum to seek the Lord.
"And it was evening, and the sea was stirred up, and they were about twenty-five stadia out on the sea."

"And they saw him walking on the sea, and they were afraid. But he said: 'It is I; do not be afraid.'" For he showed himself to them so that they might know that he is the one who delivers from that storm.

For this reason also, when they wanted to take him into the boat, they found themselves at the land where they were going. But he did not show this to the crowd, for that miracle was beyond their weakness. He showed it to the disciples, and at once he became invisible. This is a different event, and the one Matthew tells of is another, where Peter also said to him:

"Let me come to you." For he often performs one and the same miracle once, twice, and even three times, so that it may not seem strange to those who see it, but they may accept it in faith. For this reason, at that earlier time they took the thing for an apparition and believed in the power [?], but now, when they saw him, they knew at once that it was the Lord. And the Lord did not get into the boat, so that they might marvel all the more. For he allowed the storm to come so that they would seek the Lord, and he calmed the storm so that they would know his power, and he did not get into the boat so that the miracle might be all the greater.
Gospel: "On the next day the crowd that stood on the other side of the sea;
knew that there was no other boat there except one, the one the disciples of Jesus had entered, and that Jesus had not entered that boat with them."

Commentary: By these words the evangelist indicates that the crowd too, although not openly, yet suspected that marvellous deed of the Lord. For they knew, he says, that there was no other boat there, and they also knew this, he says,
that Jesus had not entered that boat with the disciples.
And when they found him in Capernaum, what else could they then have imagined, except that he had come by walking on the sea?

And in spite of all this, when they went and found him, they did not say to him, "How did you cross over?" but "When did you come here?" Unless this phrase, "When did you come," stood in place of "How did you come?"
But see how fickle their minds were, fixed on nothing. For those who had been saying, "He is a prophet," and who sought to make him king,
said nothing of the kind when they found him. Instead, they had forgotten that miracle and were looking to see another.
But he did well, for when he was coming to Capernaum, among those harsh people, he first performed that miracle of the loaves,
so that their hearts might be bent. But they did not turn; rather, they sought yet another miracle, so that they might again be filled with that bread.
Teaching 43: That we should ask God for spiritual things and not for the things of the world. Let us thank God for all these visible good things that he has given us,

and even more for the spiritual ones, for that is what he himself wants. For the sake of the spiritual he gives us the bodily things too, so that in this way he may draw and instruct those who are weak in understanding all the more.

Therefore we must always ask for what is spiritual, for if we have spiritual good, then even if we do not have bodily good, it will do us no harm. But if we have what is bodily and not what is spiritual, there is no longer any hope for our salvation. Therefore let us always ask God for what is spiritual. And this is also how he has taught us: if we consider the prayer that he taught us, we will find nothing bodily in it, but everything spiritual. Now hear how it is entirely spiritual: "Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day this our essential bread." This one small phrase he spoke concerning what is visible, and even this is spiritual and holy.

And immediately afterwards he says: "Forgive us our debts, as we have forgiven our debtors." He included no request for bodily glory, or wealth, or anything else of the kind, but everything is spiritual and heavenly.

How then is it not wretchedness if we ask God for what he has not commanded, when, even if we have something, we ought to give it up? For this is the "much speaking" in prayer: when we ask for anything belonging to the flesh. But if someone says, "How is it that the wicked become rich?", understand that it is not God who gives wealth to the wicked. They gain it themselves by robbery and greed. And if you say, "Why does God allow it?", understand that God let that rich man too become rich so that he might be punished all the more for his wickedness. That is why Abraham said to him: "Child, you received your good things in your lifetime." But may we not also hear the same words because of our luxury and our living in sins.
Therefore let us acquire that true wealth, so that we may attain eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ,
to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 44
This passage: Jesus answered and said to them, "Amen, amen, I say to you, you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.
Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life."
Commentary: Gentleness and refraining from rebuke are not always good, but in some circumstances severity also befits a teacher, for when a disciple is negligent and slack,
then he needs a goad, so that he may be raised a little out of his negligence.
And the Son of God did likewise in many other places, and here too.
For when the people came and said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?"

The Lord wanted to show that he does not seek the glory of men but seeks only the salvation of their souls. So he spoke to them in reproof, in order to set their understanding right and to bring into the open what was hidden in their minds. For he said to them:
"Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me not because of the signs, but because you ate and were filled."

he rebuked, yet gently and not harshly, and showed them that "it is not because of the sign that you marvel, but because you were filled." And for this reason, a little later, their mind became evident, for they said to him: "What sign do you show me? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness," for they were again seeking bodily food. But the Lord did not stop at rebuke alone, but also began to teach them, and said to them:
Gospel: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you, for on him God the Father has set his seal."
Interpretation: What he says here means this: "Do not be seekers of this food, but of that spiritual food,"
But those who love ease and idleness use this saying as a pretext. It is good to address a word to them as well, for they also bring forward the saying that the Lord spoke:
"Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many matters, but Mary has chosen the good portion," and again where he says: "Do not be anxious about tomorrow."
But it is good that I speak about all of this, so that those who say these things may also be silenced, and so that we may not introduce disturbance among the divine words,
For the apostle Paul says: "I beseech you not to be idle, but to walk becomingly in work. And let the thief steal no more,
but let him labour with his own hands, so that he may have something to give to others who are in need." For see, Paul commanded not only work, but work with toil and sweat as well.
And again the same man says: "These hands served my needs and those who were with me," and again it is said of him:
"He stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, and worked."
It is right, then, that we also give the interpretation of this saying, and not only state what opposes it. This, then, is what I say:
that taking no thought does not mean not working,
but that we should not nail our mind to the affairs of the world, that we should treat the business of the flesh as a side matter, and that we should not store up for tomorrow,
for it is indeed possible to labor and not to store up for tomorrow, since labor and anxiety are not one and the same,
but there can be labor without anxiety. And
as for what he said to Martha, he was not forbidding work, but rather telling her not to waste the time of teaching and prayer in care for the body, but to do everything in its proper time,
and he was not teaching idleness, but to listen well to teaching, as he said to her:
"I have come to teach you what is better, and are you anxious about the table? For this is the table I desire: that you listen well to my words, as, behold, your sister is doing."
He was not forbidding hospitality, far from it!
He meant rather that at the time of teaching she should occupy herself with nothing else. And as for this saying:
"Do not labour for the food that perishes" does not mean that idleness is right. For idleness is rather the food that perishes,
"which has taught men all evils." Rather, it means that we should work and give to others.

For this is the food that does not perish. But if anyone is idle, only indulging himself and filling his belly, he labours for the food that perishes. If, however, someone toils and clothes and feeds Christ, that is, the poor, who would be so mad as to say of him, "He labours for the food that perishes"? For to this the eternal good things have been promised. Those people, though, had no care at all for spiritual things, and did not ask by what power the Lord did those works. They sought only to fill their bellies. So the Lord rightly called such food "the food that perishes," as if he were saying: "I fed your bodies so that you would come to seek spiritual food, and do you still seek earthly things? Therefore I tell you not to seek this worthless thing, but that which is not temporal,"

…but the eternal, which nourishes not bodies but souls." But since he had said a great thing about himself, namely, "This the Son of Man will give you," he added a word about the Father, so that they would not take offence at what he said. For when he said, "The Son of Man will give you," he at once added, "for on him the Father, God, has set his seal." That is, the Father sent him for this purpose: to bring you such food. This phrase also carries another meaning. For Christ says in another place, "Whoever has heard my words has set his seal that God is true." That is, he has shown it and confirmed it by his own testimony. The Lord could also reveal himself, but when he spoke to the Jews he would bring in the testimony of the Father.

Homily 44. That the good things of this world are nothing.

So let us also hurry, beloved, to ask God for such things as it is right to ask of him. The things of this passing world do us no harm, even if they come to us with hardship. If we become rich for a short time, we will be among those riches only for a short time. If we become poor, that poverty does us no harm. The good things of this passing world are no cause for joy, and its hardships are no cause for mourning. Both are worthless and quickly pass away. This is why God called this life a "way": one way broad, and the other narrow and hard. But everything that belongs to the eternal state of the soul remains forever, both torment and reigning. So let us strive to escape the torments and find rest. For what profit is there in the pleasure of this passing world? Today it exists, and tomorrow it does not. Today it is a bright flower, and tomorrow it is dust that has passed away.

Today it is a blazing fire, and tomorrow it is cold ash. But nothing spiritual is like this. It always stays bright, blooms beautifully, and grows brighter every day. That wealth never runs out. It does not pass to anyone else and is never used up. It never brings worry, envy, or slander. It does not destroy the body or corrupt the soul, for all these things are found in the wealth of this world. That glory does not lead to arrogance or cause pride, and it never fades away. In the same way, that heavenly rest stays unchanging and undying, and it has no end forever. So let us seek that life. For if we seek it, we will count the things of this world as nothing,

Instead, let us despise it and laugh at it. Even if someone were to give us an earthly kingdom, let us not accept it, if we have this hope. In this world nothing better than kingship is found. Yet to those who desire heavenly things, even that seems contemptible and nothing, worth nothing. For anything that soon comes to an end is not to be desired, and anything that exists today and is gone tomorrow is very small and nothing, however great it may be. So let us not cling to those fleeting things that pass away like a river. Let us instead acquire the firm and unshakable good things. May we all be [?worthy] to attain them by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 45
This passage: "They said to him, 'What shall we do, so that we may perform the work of God?'
Jesus answered and said to them, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'
And they said to him, 'What sign do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What do you do?'"

Interpretation: Nothing is worse than gluttony. It makes the mind thick; it makes the soul flesh. It blinds and does not allow one to look upward. See, then, how this happened in the case of the Jews as well,
for since they were eager for gluttony and wholly lovers of the world, they understood nothing spiritual.
For this reason Christ spoke many words to them to reprove and shame them, and still they did not rise up but remained sunk below, for he said to them:
"You seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled."
And he wounded them with that reproof and showed them what kind of food one ought to seek, when he said to them: "Do not work for food that perishes, but for food that abides to eternal life."
And he remedied their objection by saying:

"On this one the Father has set his seal." But see their lack of understanding: as if they had heard nothing from him, they speak to him thus: "What shall we do, so that we may perform the work of God?"

But they said this not in order to learn and do good. For the words that follow show that they were not asking for this reason, in order to learn and do it, but for this reason: that they might bring him back to give them food and fill them. But see how the Lord answered:
Gospel: "'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'
And they said to him: 'What sign do you do, that we may see and believe? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness.'"

Interpretation: Nothing is more foolish than they are, or more brutish. The miracle was still in their hands, and yet they spoke to him as if nothing had been done: "What sign do you do?" When they asked, they posed the question themselves and did not leave the choice of the sign to him,
but they thought to drive him into a tight spot, so that nothing else would be done except what had been done for their fathers. That is why they say to him:
"Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness." For they thought that by this word they would persuade him also to do such a sign, and bring him to desire that deed, so that he would feed them bodily.
For why did they not mention some other of those earlier wonders, which are many,

such as the wonders that were done in Egypt and again at the Red Sea, but passed over everything and mentioned the manna? Only because they were gluttons and sought that by which the belly was filled, for they were slaves of the belly.
Or how is it that you, who were calling him a prophet when you saw that sign and wished to set him up as king,

have now become so ungrateful and wicked, as though you had not seen a single sign from him, and ask for a sign of the gluttonous kind? And the manna is marvelous in your eyes, and not the food of the soul.
And see what they did: they did not say, "Moses did this sign; what do you do?"
For they thought that he would become angry.
Rather, they still speak to him with honor, in that expectation of food, and they do not speak thus: "God did this; what do you do?" so that they would not make him equal to God,

nor did they bring Moses into the discussion, so that he should not count it a humiliation. Instead they set the matter in the middle and said, "Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness." And it would have been well even if he had said:

"I have done a greater wonder than Moses, I who used no rod, nor do I need prayer, but I do everything as I wish. If, then, you speak of manna, behold, here I will give you bread." But his one concern was to bring them to desire that spiritual food. And see his immeasurable wisdom, how he answers them:
Gospel:
"It was not Moses who gave you bread from heaven, but my Father gave you the true bread from heaven."

Interpretation: Why did he not say, "It was not Moses who gave to you, but I"? Why instead did he name God in place of Moses, and himself in place of the manna? Because their weakness was great. This is clear from the words that follow: even when he spoke this way, he still could not hold on to them, although he had already told them before, "You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled." For this reason he taught them afterward too, and even so he could not turn them away from that way of thinking. But when he promised to give water to the Samaritan woman, he did not mention the Father. Instead he said, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, 'Give me water to drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water." And again he says, "The water that I will give." But now, here, he mentions the Father, so that you may know how great the faith of the Samaritan woman was and how great the weakness of the Jews was. But since the manna came from the clouds and not from heaven, how can it be called heavenly?

It is like the way we speak of the "birds of heaven," which fly in the air, and "the Lord thundered from heaven"; this is the same. He calls it "true bread," not because the wonder of the manna was false, but because it was a type that foreshadowed the truth, and not the truth itself. And when he mentioned Moses, he did not name himself in Moses' place, because they did not yet honor him more than Moses; they still held Moses in greater esteem. That is why, when he said, "It was not Moses who gave," he did not add, "I give to you." Instead, he names the Father as the giver. But when they heard this, they said:
Gospel: "Give us this bread to eat."

Commentary: For they supposed it to be some visible thing, and they expected the filling of the belly, and for this reason they quickly ran toward the matter. But Christ wished to lead their minds up to the heights little by little. For this reason he said, "It is the bread of God, which comes from heaven and gives life to the world, not to Judea only, but to the whole world." And he did not say simply "food" and nothing more, but called it "a wondrous and glorious life." And he calls it "life" because through him all people who had previously been dead were made alive. But they were still bent downward in their minds, and they said to him:

"Give us this bread." And he himself wished to expose them: how, as long as they thought that food was visible, they sought it, and when they learned that it was spiritual and invisible, they did so no longer. Therefore he said to them:
Gospel: "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst. But I said to you: you have seen me and do not believe."

Commentary: John also did the same, when he first said: "What he knows he speaks, and what he has seen he testifies to, and no one receives his testimony." And again he himself says: "What we know we speak, and what we have seen we testify to, and you do not believe me." He did this in order to show beforehand that nothing can trouble him, that he does not long for human glory, and that he is not ignorant of the hidden things of the mind, nor of things that will be and are to come.
Gospel: "I am the bread of life."

Interpretation: Behold, now he intends to bring them to an understanding of high mysteries, and first he speaks about his divinity, saying: "I am the bread of life." For this is not said about his incorruptible flesh, since about that he says further on: "The bread that I will give you is my flesh."
But for now he is still speaking about the divinity. For that, because of God the Word, is bread, just as this bread of the offering becomes heavenly bread because of the Spirit who comes upon it.

But here he does not make use of witnesses, as he did in that first teaching, for he had the matter of those loaves as a witness, and because they still professed faith, whereas there they murmured and contradicted. For this reason he makes a firm declaration here.
And since they were expecting to find bodily delight, they were not troubled, until afterward they gave up hope.

And even so he did not keep silent, but spoke many words of reproof to them, for those who, while they were eating those loaves, called him a prophet, here take offense and call him the son of a carpenter.

But when they received those loaves, they did not behave this way then, but said: "This is the prophet," and wanted him as king. Here, however, they claim to be angry because of the word he spoke, namely:

"I have come from heaven." But the true cause of their anger was not this, but rather that they no longer expected to see a bodily table. For if they had truly taken offense at that word, they ought to have asked
how he is the bread of life, or how he has come from heaven.
But now they do not do this, but only murmur. And that it was not this that made them stumble, his saying "I have come from heaven," is evident from the following: when he said,
"My Father gives you the bread." They did not say to him, "Entreat him to give it to us," but:

"Give us this bread." And he had not said, "I will give you," but "My Father gives you," he says. But they, because of their craving for that food, took him to be the giver of that nourishment and able to do this thing.

And those who held him able to give such bread, how could they have stumbled afterwards, and all the more when they heard from him, "The Father gives you"? What, then, is the cause of their stumbling?

It is this: when they heard that "the eating of it will not be bodily," for this reason they stumbled and became unbelieving, and as a cover for their unbelief they seize on the loftiness of his word. Therefore he says to them:
Gospel: "You have seen me and do not believe."

Interpretation: And by "seeing" he meant, first, the miracles that he performed before them, and second, the testimony of the Scriptures, for "they," he says, "are the ones that testify about me," and also:
"I have come in the name of the Father and you do not receive me. How can you believe, you who receive glory from men?"
Gospel: "Everyone whom the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out."

Interpretation: See how he does everything for their salvation, for he added this saying so that he would not be reckoned as speaking in vain. But what is this saying of his, "Everyone whom the Father gives me will come to me," and "I will raise him up on the last day"? For why does he speak of the general resurrection of all, which even the lawless receive, as some great gift to be given to those who believe in him? It is because he is not speaking of resurrection simply, but of a resurrection of a particular kind. For first he said, "I will not cast him out," and "I will not destroy him," and then he said:

"I will raise him up." For at the resurrection some are cast out, as it has been said: "Cast him out into the outer darkness." And again some perish, as he says: "Fear him who has power to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna." And again the saying, "I give eternal life," signifies the same thing, as does "Those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of destruction." Here too, then, he spoke of this good resurrection, meaning: "I will raise him up on the last day with the good resurrection and not with the one that brings condemnation." But what does he signify by saying, "Everyone whom the Father gives me will come to me"? With this saying he rebukes their unbelief and shows that whoever does not believe in him transgresses the will of the Father. Yet he did not say this so openly, but in every case he acts by way of parable and covertly, to show that those who do not believe in him anger not him alone but the Father as well.

For if this is his will, that he should save men, and if he has come for this reason, then those who do not believe transgress his will. This means: "When the Father leads someone to come to me, nothing any longer hinders him from coming." And elsewhere he says: "No one can come to me unless the Father brings him." And the apostle Paul says that he gives to the Father, for "when," he says, "he gives the kingdom to God and the Father." So just as when the Father gives, it is not that he expels from himself the one he gives to him and hands him over, and himself no longer has him (may it never be!), so also when the Son gives the kingdom to the Father, it is not that he removes himself from that kingdom. May it never be! Rather, it is called giving because through him we have found access to the Father and acceptance by him, and he has offered us to him. And this "through whom" he applied to the Father as well, as it has been said: "through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son," and "by the will of the Father." And again he says:

"Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you." What this signifies is this: faith in me is not so slight a matter; rather, help from heaven is what is needed. He confirms this throughout his whole discourse, to show that this faith needs a courageous soul and a compunction given by God. But perhaps someone will say: "If everyone whom the Father has given us comes to you, and those whom he brings, and if no one can come to you unless it has been given to him from heaven, then are those whom the Father has not brought free of all blame?" But such words are vain and worthless. Our own will and zeal are also needed, for the receiving of teaching and believing come about from the will.

Here, by this saying, "All that the Father gives me," he signifies nothing other than this: faith in me is no small matter, nor something achieved by human reasoning; rather, revelation from heaven is needed, and a good soul to receive that revelation. And the saying, "He who comes to me will be saved," means that he will find great help, for it was for this that I came and became flesh and put on the form of a servant. After this he went on to add:

Gospel: "I came down, not to do my will, but the will of him who sent me." What are you saying? "Is your will one thing, and the will of him who sent you another?" But so that no one should imagine this, he set the saying right again with the following words, saying: "This is the will of him who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life."

What are you saying? Is your will not in this as well? And how do you say in another place, "I came to cast fire upon the earth, and I wish that it were already kindled"? But if you also wish this, and the Father too, it is clear that there is one will of both, for in another place also he says:
"As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills." What then is the will of the Father?
That he should not lose even one of them. And this you also will, Lord!

So your will is not one thing and the Father's another. For further on he says: "How often I wished to gather your children, and you would not." What, then, is this saying that he speaks? It is this: I have not come in order to do something else that the Father does not will, nor do I have some other will that the Father does not have, for "all that is the Father's is mine, and what is mine is the Father's."
Now if all that belongs to the Father and the Son is common, he rightly says, "I did not come to do my will," for, he says, I have no will that the Father does not will.
But he did not say this here, that all that is the Father's is mine,
but he says it toward the end, for, as I said,
he was still concealing those lofty matters and not declaring them, and he wishes to show that if he had said, "This is my will," his word would have been held in contempt.
For this reason he says, "I too do his will," so that he might wound them the more, as if he were saying to them: What do you think, that it is only me you anger by your unbelief?
No, rather you anger my Father as well, for "this is the will of him who sent me, that of all that he has given me I should lose none."
And here he shows that their obedience is of no benefit to him, and that he has not come for his own sake but for their salvation, nor for honor from them, as he said earlier:
"I do not receive glory from men"; and again he says: "I say this so that you may be saved."
For his effort was always directed to this: to convince them that he had come for their salvation, and to ascribe the glory to the Father,
so that in this way it might be beyond doubt. And that he was speaking for this reason he indicated by these following words, for:
"He who does his own will," he says, "seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no falsehood in him.
And this is the will of the Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
But why does he keep turning the resurrection over like this, again and again?

For this reason: so that they might not perceive God's providence in the affairs of this world only; so that, even if they do not receive their recompense here, they might not on that account become careless and negligent, but might look forward to the age to come; so that they might neither, in the afflictions of this world, fail to look forward to the rest to come, nor, in the ease of this present life, be unconcerned about the torments to come, but might look forward to another life.

Teaching 45: On the remembrance of the judgment. But they gained nothing from the repeated mention of the word about the resurrection. But let us profit, brethren, from hearing often about the resurrection to come. Whether we desire covetousness, or robbery, or to do some other evil, let us at once call to mind that fearful day and picture that fearful tribunal among us. Such a thought, stronger than any bridle, will hold back that evil impulse. Let us always say to one another and to ourselves that there is a resurrection and that a fearful judgment awaits us. If we see someone puffed up and delighting in the good things of this world, let us say this to him too and show him that everything here is to be left behind. If we see someone else afflicted and made despondent by tribulations, let us likewise speak to him and show him that the tribulation will last only a short time. If again we see someone in sloth and laxity, let us teach him in the same way and show him that he will surely have to give an account for his sloth. This word about the resurrection alone is enough, more than any medicine, to heal our souls. For there is indeed a resurrection, and that resurrection is not far off but is at the doors,
for in a little while the one who is coming will come and will not delay.
And all of us, both good and evil, must stand before the fearful throne of Christ,

...the wicked, so that they may be put to shame before all, and the good, so that they may shine before all. For just as the judges of this world punish the wicked and honor the good before all, so it will be there too, so that the shame of the former may be greater and the splendor of the latter more glorious. Let us therefore picture all this every day in our minds.

Let us always remember this within ourselves, and not one of the affairs of this world will harm us, for "the things that are seen are passing away, but those that are unseen are eternal." For this reason, then, let us continually say to ourselves and to one another that there is a resurrection and a judgment and a repayment for deeds; and let all who say that there will be no resurrection say this word and be delivered from that disease. If there is a resurrection and a judgment and a repayment for deeds, how can anyone be unbelieving about the resurrection? Yet I am ashamed to speak about the resurrection to Christians, for whoever needs teaching about the resurrection and is not fully convinced that these matters are not so vain, but that there will be a resurrection, is not a Christian. Therefore I implore you, brothers, let us purify ourselves from all evils and strive in every way to find mercy on that day and to have something to say in defense at the tribunal of that day. But perhaps someone may say: "And when will the end and the resurrection be? Look, so many ages have passed and nothing of the kind has happened." But it will happen, believe me. For before the Flood too they spoke in the same way and laughed at Noah, but the Flood came and overtook those unbelievers, and it saved Noah the believer.

And again, the people of Sodom did not expect that wrath from God until the thunderbolt and the fire with brimstone came upon them and wiped them all out. And neither in their case nor in Noah's did any events take place beforehand that foretold that wrath; rather, the wrath came upon those who were reveling and raging and living lawlessly. So too will the resurrection be. This is why the apostle Paul said: "When they say, 'Look, peace and security,' then suddenly destruction will come upon them, like the pain of a woman giving birth when the hour of delivery overtakes her, and they will not escape." And this is because that day is coming unknown, so that we may always be in fear and never become careless. What do you say: do you not expect the resurrection and the judgment? The demons acknowledge the resurrection, and are you unbelieving? For hear what they say to the Lord: "Have you come here before the time to torment us?" And those who acknowledge torment also know of the resurrection and the judgment.

Let us not, then, anger God by this wicked thing, being unbelieving about the resurrection on top of our other evils. For just as Christ became a beginning for us in other matters, so also in this one, for it is on this account that he is called "the firstborn of those who have fallen asleep."
For if there were not going to be a resurrection, whose firstborn would he be, since no one would be going to rise?
If there were no resurrection, where would God's justice be? For so many wicked men are prospering in this world, and so many righteous men are in affliction and end their lives in affliction,
for where will each of them receive according to what they deserve, if there is no resurrection?
But none among good and righteous men disbelieves in the resurrection; rather, they constantly pray this holy saying and say:
"Your kingdom come." And who are those who disbelieve in the resurrection, if not those who walk in a foul way and an unholy life, as the prophet says:

"His ways are foul at all times, and his judgments are removed from his sight." For it is impossible that anyone who led a good life should disbelieve in the resurrection, since those who have done nothing deserving punishment believe all the more, and rejoice that they will receive the reward of their good deeds. Now therefore let us not anger him, O brothers, but let us listen to his word, which says: "Fear him who has power to destroy souls and bodies in Gehenna," so that through that fear we may turn to what is good, depart from destruction, and become worthy of the kingdom of heaven, by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 46
The text: The Jews grumbled about him because he said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven," and they said:
"Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then does he now say, 'I came down from heaven'?"

Commentary: "Whose god is the belly and whose glory is in their shame," as the apostle says about the Jews; and this is evident both from those earlier words and from these present words, when they came to Christ,
For when he gave them bread and filled their bellies, they called him a prophet and sought to make him king; but when he was teaching about the spiritual food and about eternal life,

When he was raising them up from the visible things of this earth, speaking to them about the resurrection and purifying their minds, at the very time when they ought most to have marveled at him and worshipped him, they murmured all the more. But tell me, O Jews: if this is that prophet of whom you used to say:
"This is the prophet about whom Moses said: 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me;
listen to him,'" and since you said this and counted him a prophet, you ought to have listened to him and believed the word he spoke: "I came down from heaven."

But see their lack of understanding, how they did not believe him but grumbled, and yet still held back; for the miracle of the loaves had only just been done for them, and for this reason they did not openly contradict him at that time, but grumbled and in this way showed,
that they were angry because he did not set for them the table they craved, and they murmured and said:
"Is this not the son of Joseph?" And from this it is evident that they were ignorant of his wondrous birth; for this reason they called him the son of Joseph.
But he was not angry with them, nor did he say to them, "I am not the son of Joseph." He did not refrain from saying to them,
"I am not the son of Joseph," because he was his son, but because they were not yet able to bear and understand that wondrous birth.

And if they were not able to hear of his birth in the flesh, how much less would they have been able to hear of his ineffable birth from the Father? If the lower had not been revealed, how would he have told them the higher?

This offended them even more: that he was called the son of so poor and lowly a father. Even so, he did not reveal the truth to them about any of this. He did not want them to fall into a greater offense while he was trying to correct the one offense. But see what he says when they were offended at him:
Gospel: "No one is able to come to me unless my Father who sent me brings him to me."
Commentary: The Manichaeans fall upon this saying and declare that
"Nothing is in our power." Yet this rather shows the freedom of our wills. But they say:

"If someone comes to him and is able to come of his own will, why does he need to be drawn?" But this saying does not take away our free will. Rather, it shows that we need help. Here it makes us understand, not that the Father draws a person against his will, but that we need help from God.
And next he shows us the manner of his drawing as well. So that no one would again imagine something visible about God, he added this and said:
Gospel: "Not that anyone has seen God, but he who is from God, he has seen the Father."

Commentary: And if someone says, "And how does he draw?", let him hear the words of the prophet, who said long ago: "They shall all be taught by God." Do you see the dignity of faith? It does not come from human beings or through human beings. It is taught by God himself. For this reason too, to confirm his own word, he sent them to the prophets. But if all are taught by God, how is it that some do not believe?

Because that saying refers to the great number of believers. And again, the prophet tells all of them, all who are willing, that he sits as a teacher, ready to give the good things that come from him to all who are willing to receive them.
Gospel: "And I will raise him up on the last day."

Commentary: The honor of the Son is shown to be no small thing here, since we hear that the Father draws people to him and he raises them up. This is said of the Father, for how else could it be? [?] But it shows the equality of their power. When he said, "The Father who sent me bears witness concerning me," he showed them the words of the Scriptures, so that they would not look for a voice that was not human. In the same way here, so that they would not imagine any such thing, he sends them to the prophets. He turns the matter over again and again, up and down, to show that he himself is not opposed to the Father.

And if someone should say, "How were people before him? Were they not taught by God? So what is greater now?" What is greater now is this: back then the teaching came through human beings, but now it comes through the only-begotten Son of God and through the Holy Spirit. Then he said next:
Gospel: "No one has seen the Father except the one who is from God."

Commentary: He says this not in the sense of cause but in the sense of nature. Otherwise, if he were speaking in the sense of cause, we are all from God, and then where is the superiority of the Son and his distinction from all? Or why did he not say it to them more plainly? He did this only because of their weakness, for if, when he said, "I came down from heaven," they stumbled even at that,

if he had told them this, what would they have done? And he designates himself as the bread of life, for he is the one through whom our life subsists, both the present life and the life to come. And he says, "Whoever eats this bread will live forever." By bread here he means either the life-giving teachings and faith in him, or his flesh, for both of these strengthen, sustain and nourish the soul. See, then, from what he draws his distinction from the manna: from the outcome. One must look at both foods, for in order to show that he was doing nothing strange, he said:
Gospel:
"Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and perished."

Commentary: And further he prepares his discourse to show that they have been made worthy of far greater things than their fathers, such as Moses and those like him, those wondrous men; therefore he said:
Gospel: "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and died, but whoever eats of this bread will not die but will live forever." And this expression too, namely:
"in the wilderness," he did not say idly, but to show that the manna neither lasted a long time, nor remained with them and entered the land of promise.
But this bread is not of that kind, and "the bread that I will give is for the life of the world."
At this point it must be asked what the occasion was for these words, which were the undoing of many, for it says:
"Many of his disciples went away and said, 'This word is harsh; who can listen to it?'"
For it would have been proper to say these things to his disciples privately, as Matthew also said: "Privately he would speak to them."
What then shall we say about this? Why were these words needed? There was great need and great reason for them,
since they were pressing him and asking for bodily food,

and were recalling the food given to their fathers and regarding the manna as a great thing, for this reason he wished to show that all of that was a type and a shadow, whereas his own works are the truth. For this reason he mentioned that spiritual food. But someone may say: "He ought to have said:
"Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness,

but I have given you bread." But there is a great difference here. The wonder of the manna was thought to be greater than the loaves, because it had come from heaven, while this sign was done on earth.
Since, then, they were seeking food coming from heaven, for this reason he kept telling them: "I have come down from heaven."
And if someone should further inquire why he began at that time to speak of the mysteries of his flesh and blood,
let us say this to him: that it was very much the right time for those words of his, for the obscurity of things said always makes the hearer attentive and causes him to listen well.

And therefore there ought to have been no offence, but rather questioning and inquiry. But they went away. Yet if they had counted him a prophet, they ought to have believed his words. For this reason too it is evident that the offence came from their own folly, and not from any obscurity or difficulty in what he said. But you, see how little by little he leads them toward himself, for here he speaks of himself as the giver of the bread, saying: "The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world." But someone may say: "That teaching was strange and altered." Yet John indicated this from the very beginning, when he gave him the name of Lamb. And if anyone says that, although John said this, they still did not understand it,

I know this as well, but neither did the disciples understand it. For if they as yet knew nothing about the resurrection, for that reason they also did not understand the saying: "Destroy this temple, and on the third day I will raise it up." And since they did not understand that, would they not much more fail to understand these things, for these were far more difficult than those? And again for this reason too: they knew that other prophets had also risen, but that anyone had eaten the flesh of the Son of Man they had never heard anywhere, for none of the prophets had ever said this anywhere. Yet in spite of all this, although they did not understand, they still followed him and confessed that he had the words of eternal life.

For this is the task of a disciple: not to scrutinize the doings of his teacher, but only to listen and believe him, and to wait for the proper time when he will be able to understand those words. But as for those who opposed him and went back from him, this came about from their wickedness and lack of understanding. For when inquiry enters in, asking "How is this?" and "How is that?", unbelief also enters together with that inquiry. So likewise Nicodemus too was astonished and said: "How can a man enter his mother's womb?!" And these men too were troubled in the same way and said: Gospel: "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?"
Commentary: For if you seek the 'how' concerning the loaves, why did you not do this then and say: "How did he multiply those five like this?"

But this happened because at that time you looked only to being filled, and not to the sign. If, again, you say this: "At that time the deed itself taught us, and we were fully convinced," then since at that time you saw it in deed and were convinced, you ought to have believed this too on that account. For this is why he first performed that great sign: so that you might learn from it and no longer be unbelieving toward him.

Homily 46, on Communion. But they at that time bore no fruit from those words of the Lord, whereas we have received his beneficence in very deed. Therefore it is good that we should understand what this wonder of the mystery of Communion is, why it was given to us, and what the benefit of the matter is. Hear, then, and understand: we are one body, and members of his flesh and of his bones. And you who are baptized and have understanding, hear this word and understand it, since we are his members. He wished this to be not in word only, but that we should be united with his flesh in deed as well. And this came about through the mystery that has been given to us, so that he might show us the love he has toward us. For this reason he also united himself with us, so that we might in this way become one with him, as the body is one with the head; for this is the mark of the deed of great love.

And Job indicated this when he spoke of the servants to whom he was greatly beloved, how out of their great longing they said to him: "Who will grant us to be filled with his flesh?" For this reason Christ also did this, so that he might bring us to a greater love of him and show his own love which he has toward us. He deems us worthy not only to see him, but also to touch him and eat him, to chew his incorruptible flesh with our teeth, to be united with him, and to fulfill that desire of ours. Now therefore, brothers, let us go away from his table like lions from whom fire pours. Let us be terrifying in this way to the devil and his angels, and let us forget ourselves and remember the love which he has shown toward us, he who says to us:

"Fleshly parents often give their children to others to be reared, but I do not do so. Rather, I nourish you with my own flesh and set myself before you, for I desire that you all become rulers and nobles.
"And I give you good hopes concerning the age to come. For I who here have given myself to you, shall I not do this all the more in that age,
"I who chose to be a brother to you, who became a partaker of flesh and blood for your sake, and who in turn give you that flesh and blood of which I became a partaker?"

Now then, brothers, this blood beautifully forms the royal image and makes it shine within us. It does not allow the nobility and sovereignty of the soul to dry up and wither, but waters it continually and nourishes it. This goodness is beyond telling, for the blood that increases in us from bodily foods does not become blood immediately,
but is first changed into another substance and only then becomes blood. This, however, is not so; rather, as soon as we receive it, it immediately waters the soul and gives it great power.
This blood of the mystery drives away the demons and puts them far from us, and it summons to us the angels and the King
of the angels, for wherever they see that royal blood, the demons flee and the angels hasten there.
This blood, when it was poured out, washed the whole world. Blessed Paul speaks with great wisdom about this blood in the Epistle to the Hebrews:
"This blood has sanctified the invisible things and the Holy of Holies."

And if its type had so much power in the temple of the Hebrews, and in Egypt too when smeared on the doorposts, then this blood of his, made in truth, of which all these were the type, how could it not be exceedingly and inconceivably great?
This blood sanctified the golden altar. Without it the high priest did not dare to enter the inner temple. It purified sins in those former types and figures.
And if in those types and figures it had so much power, if death trembled at the shadow, how would it not tremble beyond measure at the truth?
This is the life of our souls. By this the soul is washed, by this it is adorned, by this it is set aflame. This makes our mind brighter than fire,
this makes the soul purer than gold. This blood was poured out and made the heavens a road for human beings to travel.
Truly awesome is this mystery.
A spring went up out of paradise and sent forth visible rivers, but from this table a spring goes up and sends forth spiritual rivers.
Beside this spring are planted not fruitless willows, but trees that reach up to heaven, always full of ripe and unwithering fruit.
So whoever is distressed by heat, let him draw near to this spring and cool his heat,

for this spring dispels parching drought and comforts all who are scorched by heat, not the heat of the sun but the heat of the enemy's burning arrows. For its beginning is from heaven and its root is there, from where it is watered. Many are the streams and nectars and channels of this spring, which the Spirit, the Comforter, sends forth, and the only-begotten Son is the mediator. He does not use a mattock or cut a furrow, but opens up our minds by his power. This spring is a spring of light, sending forth the rays of truth. Before this spring stand the powers of heaven, gazing at the beauty of its waves, for they see more clearly than we do the power of the mysteries set before us and their brilliance, which eyes cannot withstand. For just as when gold is melting in a furnace, if someone dips a hand or a tongue into it, it immediately turns the color of gold.

The holy mysteries do the same to the soul. For this stream is hotter than fire, yet it does not burn. It only purifies, and it makes indestructible whoever comes to it. From the very beginning this blood was always prefigured on the altars and in the slaying of the saints. This is the price of the whole world. With it Christ purchased the Church, and with it he adorned her on every side. A man who buys slaves pays in gold, and if he wants to adorn them, he does that with gold as well. In the same way Christ bought us with his own blood and then adorned us with that same blood of his. Those who partake of this blood stand with the angels, the archangels and the heavenly powers. I do not say this with respect to rank but with respect to holiness. They have put on the royal garment and the spiritual armor. But why do I speak this way? They have put on the very King of all himself. Do you see how great and glorious this thing is?

So know this: this thing is as great and wonderful as that. If you approach it in holiness, you have come to it for the life of your soul. But if you approach it with an evil and defiled mind, you receive it for your own condemnation and destruction. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks it to his own condemnation. Those who defile and soil the royal purple are punished like those who tear it. So it is not at all unreasonable that those who receive the body and blood of Christ with an impure mind will be punished like those who nailed him to the cross. See, then, how fearfully Paul set out the judgment of the unworthy, when he said: "Anyone who despises the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses."

"How much greater a punishment, do you think, will he be deemed to deserve who tramples on the Son of God and counts as common the blood of the covenant by which he was made holy?" Therefore let us take heed to ourselves, my beloved brothers, to whom such good things as these have been given. And when we wish to say something evil, or are carried away by anger and wrath or by some other passion, then let us remember what things we have been made worthy of and what kind of Spirit has been given to us. And let this thought be a bridle upon those evil passions. For how long will we be nailed to these passing things? How long will we not wake up? How long will we take no care for the life of our souls? Let us understand what good things Christ has made us worthy of. Let us give thanks to him and glorify him, not by faith alone but also by deeds, so that we may be made worthy of those eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 47
This saying: "Jesus said to them: 'Amen, amen I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.
But whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.'"

Commentary: When we speak of spiritual matters, let there be nothing of worldly affairs in our souls at that time, let nothing of dust and earth be found there; rather, let us at that time drive all such things away from us, and let us direct our ears and our hearts to the hearing of those divine words.
For if a king arrives somewhere, all tumult is quieted in the places to which he comes.
Should we not all the more create quiet when the Holy Spirit is speaking to us, and listen to him in stillness and with trembling? For these words are indeed worthy of great trembling, since he says:
Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life."
Commentary: For since they were saying, "It is impossible to do this," he shows that not only is it not impossible, but it is even indispensable for anyone who desires life.
Gospel: "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
Commentary: For since he had said, "Whoever eats of this bread will not die for ever," and they were opposing him and saying:
"Abraham died, and the prophets, and how do you say, 'He will not die'?"
For this reason he spoke here of the resurrection, in order to resolve that question of theirs and make them understand that, although one may die for a short time, it is not for ever.
And he repeatedly returns to this word about communion in the holy mysteries, in order to make them understand and to show the greatness of this matter, and that it must be done without any excuse.
But what is the meaning of the saying, "My flesh is true food and my blood is true drink"?

For either he said, "It is true food and drink," because it nourishes the soul, or he said it in order to make them understand and convince them that his word was not spoken in a parable, so that they might not look for a figure and a parable, but understand that his flesh must truly be eaten. Then, accordingly, he says:
Gospel: "Whoever eats my flesh abides with me."
Commentary: And he was saying this in order to make us understand that whoever receives him, if worthily, is wholly united to the Lord, for he says, "He abides with me, and I with him."

But what follows this appears to be out of keeping with the preceding saying, if we do not understand the force of the saying. For what connection is there, or what is the point, one may ask, in that after he had said:
"Whoever eats my flesh abides with me, and I with him," he immediately added to this:
Gospel: "As the living Father sent me, I also live because of the Father."
Commentary: Yet this saying has a close connection, for he was speaking both above and below about eternal life, and then he said, "He abides with me."
For this reason he also said what follows, as if he were saying: "Whoever eats my flesh abides with me, and I am living," and so it is evident that he too will live. And then he says:
Gospel: As the living Father sent me
Commentary: But this belongs to equality and likeness, and this saying means the following: "I live just as the Father does."

And so that you might not suppose him to be unbegotten, for this reason he said "because of the Father." He does not indicate by this that he needs some power from another in order to live, for he already removed this notion from us earlier when he said:
"As the Father has eternal life, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself, just as the Father does."
Since, then, he has life in this way, just as the Father does, he can in no way need another helper for life. But what is this saying that he spoke: "I live because of the Father"?
For in this place he indicates the cause, and this saying means the following:
"As the Father lives, so I live, and whoever eats of me will also live because of me." Here he speaks of the higher, divine life, not of this ordinary life,
which everyone has. This makes it clear that he is not speaking of human life but of the divine and holy life, since everyone is alive with this human life,
even unbelievers and those who have not eaten of his flesh.

Do you see how he was not speaking of this life, but of that eternal life? For his saying means the following: "Whoever eats my flesh, when he departs from this world, will not perish, nor will he be tormented." And again, when he said, "I will raise him up on the last day," he did not speak of the general resurrection of all, for all will rise, but of that chosen and good resurrection, which will have its reward in abundance.
Gospel: Your fathers ate manna and died, but whoever eats this bread will live forever.

Commentary: See, he says this word many times so as to fix it firmly in their minds, and to assure them of the resurrection and of eternal life. That is why he also mentions the resurrection and promises eternal life: to show that this life is not now, but will come after the resurrection.

But if someone should say, "How is this known?", let him listen to all the Scriptures. For in every place he sent them to the Scripture and commanded them to learn the truth from it. And when he said, "This bread gives life to the world," he wanted these words to make them jealous, so that they would envy others their entry into life and would not stay outside themselves. He keeps reminding them of the manna, to show them how different the gift he gives is from that manna, and to bring them to faith. For if he was able to feed them in this way for forty years, without labour and without sowing, would he not do such a thing all the more now, if he wished, since he has come with greater love for mankind? For if all that was a type and was done so easily, would the deed not be done all the more now, where the power of the truth is great, the power of never coming to an end and of existing in that true life?

He speaks of life in every place, because people long for life and nothing is so sweet as not dying. For in the Old Testament too this was the good thing: length of days and a long life. But now it is not only length; it is life without end. On top of all this, he also wants to show that he means to do away with the punishment that came upon us, cursed because of our disobedience. Now he undoes that sentence which leads to death, and in its place he brings in eternal life, the opposite of that first sentence.
Gospel: "He said these things in the synagogue, as he taught in Capernaum."

Commentary: All this he said, it says, at Capernaum, where the greatest number of mighty works had been done, and for this reason they ought to have believed his words. And he taught in synagogues and in the temple, first, so that the multitude of the people might listen to him and be converted, and also so that he might show everyone that he is not opposed to the Father.
Gospel: "Many of his disciples who heard this also said: 'This word is hard.'"

Commentary: "How hard it is": that is, it is difficult and laborious. And why did they say this? He was saying nothing of that kind, since he was not teaching about bodily virtues but about faith.
