They were stripped of their homeland, their freedom, their rest and the worship of God, were cast out from every good thing, and became slaves and captives.

Teaching 51, on not doing evil. But let us, who know all this, never plot evil against another. For be assured, you who do this: you are sharpening a sword against yourselves, and you are wounded more grievously by your own hand. But if someone afflicts you and you wish to pay him back, do not repay him with evil, and you have paid him back. But if you do him evil in return, you have not paid him back. And do not think that I say this word idly, for it is true.

And if you say, "How can this be?", hear how. When you do him no harm, then God becomes the one who does evil to that evildoer of yours. But when you yourself begin to do him evil, God is then no longer hostile to him but to you, for you have annulled that word of Scripture which says, "Judgment is mine, I will repay," says the Lord.
For if our slaves were to quarrel with one another, and were not to come to us for a just judgment to be made,

But if they themselves were to pass judgment, would we not be distressed? And if we are like this, will God not be so all the more, who has commanded that all judgment be left to him? For is it not folly if we do not show such wisdom and obedience to God? And how much we demand from our own servants! I say this about ourselves, who are eager to do evil to one another. Is this not the true course: not only to do no evil, but to forgive completely and, even more, to do good, so that we too may be given that great recompense for this good, which is the finding of forgiveness? For tell me, if you are angry at the one who has sinned, why do you also sin and fall into the same evil? For if he has reviled you, do not revile him in return; otherwise you revile yourself. If he has distressed you, do not distress him in return; otherwise you no longer have any difference from him. If he has harmed you in some way, do not harm him in return; otherwise what profit will you have?

But then you are altogether like him. This is how you are able to put him to shame: if you endure everything with meekness. In this way you will be able to calm his anger, for no one can cure evil with evil, but evil is cured by good. Even some of the philosophers among the pagans kept to this practice. Are we not ashamed, then, if we are found inferior in virtue even to those senseless pagans? For many of them suffered evil from another and endured it; many were slandered and did not retaliate. There is reason to fear, then, that they too may be found to have done better than we have, and that a heavier judgment may come upon us for this reason. For when we, who have received the Holy Spirit, who await the kingdom of heaven, who do not fear Gehenna, who have been commanded to be angels, to whom such mysteries have been given, cannot attain even to their virtue, what hope can we still have? For if we must surpass the Jews in virtue, since the Lord says:

"Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." What will become of us if we are found worse than the gentiles? Will we not be cast out of the kingdom all the more, when we do not surpass even those utter unbelievers in virtue? Therefore I beseech you: let us root out from ourselves all anger and wrath. And again I say to you: let us root this out from ourselves. For it does not weary me to say the same word many times, if only by all this you may learn what is good. Physicians too use the same medicine many times, and we also will not cease always to teach and cry out about what is good, for many are the affairs of this world that make us forget what is better.

And therefore constant teaching is needed. But so that our gathering here may not be vain and empty, let us therefore make haste to do good in deed as well, so that we may attain those eternal good things by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ,
through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 52
This saying: The servants of the chief priests and Pharisees came, and they said to them: "Why did you not bring him?"
The servants answered and said to them: "Never did a man speak like this."
Commentary: Nothing is clearer than the truth, nothing is better, if only we do not undo it; and again, nothing is worse or more difficult than an evildoing man,
for see, the scribes and Pharisees, who thought themselves wise, kept constant company with Christ for this reason: so that they might do him harm,
and they saw the signs and read the Scriptures, and from all this they gained nothing,
but rather suffered harm. The servants, however, who were unlearned, gained from a single teaching alone, and those who had gone to bind him and bring him returned bound themselves by that wonder.
And I marvel not only at their understanding, that without a sign, by teaching alone, they were thus won over, but also at their boldness,
how they spoke to the Pharisees who had sent them, who were always fighters against the good, for it says that:
"The servants came," it says, and the Pharisees said to them: "Why did you not bring him?" Yet coming back was far superior to staying away,
for if they had not come at all, they would have escaped their harshness and blame; but now they become preachers of Christ's wisdom and show great boldness,
and they did not say: "We could not because of the people, for all regarded him as a prophet," but they spoke as follows.
Gospel: "Never did a man speak like this."
Commentary: For they could also have said this: "We could not because of the people," but they displayed that upright mind,

for these words that they spoke were not only wonder at his wisdom but also an accusation against the Pharisees, because they had sent men to arrest him whom it was right to obey; and indeed they had not heard any long teaching, but only a brief one.
For when the mind is good, long words are not needed, for such is the truth.
But see what the Pharisees did: for they ought to have become humble, but they grew even angrier and said: "Have you too, then, been led astray?"

Yet they do not speak to them with wrath, for they were afraid that they might follow Jesus altogether, but he only reproaches them. For he ought to have asked what Jesus had said and to have marveled at his words. But they did not do this, for they knew that they were always defeated by his words; instead they adopt a very foolish line of argument and say:
Gospel: "Surely none of the rulers has believed in him?"
Commentary: What do you say, wretched men? In this too do you blame Christ, and not those who became unbelievers? And you say:
Gospel: "As for how the people believed, those who do not know the law are accursed."
Commentary: But this is your great indictment, that the people believed, who did not know the law, and you did not believe.
And how are they accursed, who, although ignorant of the law, did what those learned in the law ought to have done?

For it is you who are accursed, you who do not keep the law, and not those who have believed the law. And you ought not to have blamed and accused the Lord on this account, that the rulers did not believe in him, for this is not a matter of justice, since you too became unbelieving toward God, as the apostle says: "What then, if some have become unbelieving toward God, will their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God?" Far from it! For the prophets continually reproached them and said to them: "Hear, you rulers of Sodom," and again: "Your rulers are unbelieving," and again: "Is it not yours to know judgment?" And they continually reproached them with this. What then is to be said?

Who will blame God on this account, that some were unbelieving? Far from it! For this blame belongs to those who did not believe, not to him in whom they did not believe. Or what other, greater sign could anyone find of your lack of learning, and of how you do not know the law, than this, that you do not believe in him? But since they said: "Has any of the rulers believed? But only this people, who do not know the law," for this reason Nicodemus reproaches them and says to them:
Gospel: "Does our law condemn a man unless you first hear from him?"

Commentary: For he shows that they neither know the law nor do it. For if the law says not to condemn a man before hearing from him, and these men have condemned before the law, then they are indeed transgressors of the law. And since they said, "None of the rulers has believed in him," for this reason the evangelist makes it known and says, "He was one of them," so that they might know that rulers too believed in him. For although they did not show the boldness that was fitting, yet they believed in Christ. But see with what caution he makes this rebuke, for he did not say: "You seek to kill him, and you condemn him without trial and call him a deceiver?" He did not speak in this way, but spoke gently, so that he might calm their great rage and murderousness. For this reason he directs his word toward the law and says:
Gospel: "Unless it first hears him and knows what he is doing."
Commentary: And this saying means this:

That it may know what he is doing, what he intends, or why and how, and whether he does it to break up the strife [?] of that people, or not. But they were stunned, since they had said, "None of the rulers has believed in him," and for this reason they speak to him neither with anger nor with mildness. For what coherence did their words have, when he said, "The law condemns no one," and they said:
Gospel: "Are you also a Galilean?"
Commentary: For they ought to have shown that they were not condemning him without trial, or else that they ought not to speak a word; but they make their speech in folly and anger.
Gospel: "Search and see, for no prophet has arisen from Galilee."

Commentary: But what had that man said — that "he is a prophet"? Or did he not rather say this: "It is not right to kill him without a trial"? And they, although they did not say to him so openly, "You do not know the Scripture; go and learn," nevertheless say this very thing in a veiled way, for this is the meaning of "Search and see." But see what Christ did: since they were turning over Galilee and the prophets, up and down, in order to free them from such a thought and to show them that he is not one of the prophets, but the King of the whole world, he therefore said to them:
Gospel: I am the light of the world
Commentary: Not of Galilee only, and of Palestine and Judea, but of the whole world. But hear that saying of the Jews: "You testify about yourself." What, then, did he testify about himself?
Gospel: I am the light of the world

Commentary: This saying is great, and truly great, yet it still did not bend them, for in this place he does not make himself equal with the Father, nor did he say, "I am his Son," nor, "I am God," but he said only this: "I am the light of the world." And they wanted to refute this saying of theirs [?] as well, but far more exalted than this is the saying that:
Gospel: Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness
Commentary: By darkness in this place he means the error of unbelief, as if to say: "He will not remain in error,
and here he also draws Nicodemus and praises him for his boldness, and he also praises those servants
who spoke thus to them, and he also rebukes those others, because they were devising their plots secretly and in darkness,
but they will not overcome the light." And he also reminds Nicodemus of the words he had spoken to him earlier, namely:
"Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his deeds may not be exposed." For since they were saying, "None of the rulers has believed in him," he therefore said:
"Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come," in order to show that this failure to come does not arise from any weakness of the light, but from their crooked and perverse mind.
Gospel: The Pharisees said to him, "You testify about yourself, and your testimony is not true"
Commentary: But hear what the Lord said to them:
Gospel: "Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I have come from and where I am going"
Commentary: What, then, is this saying? It is this, namely:
"I am from God, and I am God and the Son of God; and God is a trustworthy witness of himself, but you do not know," he says.
"For you desire evil, and you who know that I am God pretend ignorance and say everything with a human mind, since you do not wish to understand anything greater than what is visible."
Gospel: "You judge according to the flesh"
Commentary: Just as living in the flesh signifies an evil life, so judging according to the flesh means judging unjustly.
Gospel: "I judge no one; and if I do judge, my judgment is true"

Commentary: Now this saying that he speaks is of this kind: for he said, "You judge unjustly," and they would have said, "If we judge unjustly, then why do you not judge us and punish us, if you are God?" And for this reason he said:
"I judge no one, for I have not come for this; and if I do judge, my judgment is true." That is to say:
"If I had judged, you would have been found condemned, and justly too,
but now is not the time of judgment,"
and he also gave a sign of that eternal judgment when he said: "I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me are."
But here he showed that not he alone will condemn them, but the Father as well, when he said to them:
Gospel: "In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true."

Commentary: By this saying he reveals his unity with the Father, for he named no one else but the Father, in order to show us that consubstantiality. Otherwise, why did he not speak of John and say, "I testify about myself, and John also testifies, or the angels, or the prophets," since all of these testified about him? But he was not saying this only to point out witnesses, but to reveal his consubstantiality with the Father.
Gospel: The Jews said to him:
"Who is your father?" Jesus answered and said to them: "You know neither me nor my Father."

Commentary: Since they were speaking of a well-known matter as though it were unknown, and of what they knew as though they did not know it, and were testing him, he did not consider them worthy of an answer. For this reason he began to say everything openly and with great boldness, when he also brought testimony from his signs and his teachings, for his crucifixion too was near, for he said to them: "I know where I come from and where I am going."

Yet this saying did not touch them strongly; rather, they were frightened more by the saying that he added when he said: "Where I am going, you cannot come," for he showed that he was not going to remain in death. But why did he not say, "I know that I am God," but instead said to them, "I know where I come from"? Only because he always mixes lowly words with lofty ones and conceals the latter. For when he had said, "I testify about myself," and had shown this, he came back again to lowly speech, as if he were saying to them: "I know by whom I have been sent and to whom I am going." For in this way they could no longer contradict him, once they learned that he had been sent by him and was going to him.
For he shows this: "How could I tell a lie, I who have come from him and am going to him, the true God? But you do not know God; therefore you judge according to the flesh."
For they, to whom so many signs and reproofs and parables had been offered, still said, "This is not true," and held Moses to be more trustworthy. But Christ said to them:

"I judge no one," but just as he first said, "The Father judges no one," so here too he says, "I judge no one, and if I do judge, my judgment is true, for I am not alone." Yet again he answers according to their suspicion, that is to say: "My judgment is the Father's, for the Father would not judge otherwise, if he were to judge, but just as I do, and I do not judge otherwise than as the Father does." But why did he also mention the Law? For this reason: because they would not have believed him unless he had brought forward the testimony of the Father. And further, that saying would not otherwise hold, for among men, when two men testify about a matter that is not their own, then it is true, for this is the testimony of two; but when someone testifies about himself, then they are no longer two.

Do you see how he said this for no other reason than to show his unity with the Father, and then by this to show that he is in no way inferior to the Father? See then his lordship, for he says: "It is I who testify about myself, and the Father who sent me testifies about me." And so that you may not think this was said for the sake of the number, see the authority, which has nothing altered in it. For a man testifies when he is himself considered trustworthy, and not when he needs testimony, and this too in a matter not his own; but in his own matter, when he needs the testimony of another, he is no longer trustworthy.

But here everything is the opposite, for he testifies in his own matter, and speaks of testimony being brought by another, and thus makes his word trustworthy in every respect, in order to reveal that his testimony is given with authority.

For why, after he had said, "I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me," and, "The testimony of two men is true," did he not keep silent, but added and said, "I am the one who bears witness about myself"?
It is clear, then, that he is pointing to his own authority. First he spoke of himself: "I am the one who bears witness about myself," and then of "the Father," saying:
"The Father who sent me bears witness about me." And here he shows his equality in honour with the Father, and that it profits nothing to those who say,
"We know the Father," when they did not know him; and that the reason for this is that they did not wish to know him.
For he says: "It is impossible to know the Father without the Son," so that perhaps by these words he might draw them to understanding,

For since they were rejecting him while always seeking the Father, he shows concerning knowledge that "it is impossible to do this without me," he says. So it is now clear that those who blasphemed the Son blaspheme not him alone but the Father as well.

Moral Teaching 52: On virtue. But let us flee from these deeds and glorify the only-begotten Son of God, not only with this glory of right confession but also by good works. For right belief alone, without good works, is of no profit, for
"If you are called a Jew, and rest upon the law and boast in God": now then, you who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who boast in the law, you dishonor God by transgressing the law.

So then, brethren, let us look to ourselves as well, lest we boast of the righteousness of faith but fail to do the works that befit that faith of ours, and so provoke God to anger against us, and his name be blasphemed because of us. For the Christian ought to be a teacher of the whole world, and a light, a salt and a leaven of good works, as the Lord says. And what does being a light mean? It means a radiant and good life, in which no darkness at all arises. For light is not useful to itself, nor is salt, nor leaven; they show their usefulness toward others. In the same way, God seeks from us not only our own profit but that of others too. For salt, if it does not salt, is not salt.

Understand this also: if we carry out good works, others too will come to our good; but if we fail, how can we be of profit to others? So let there be among us, O brethren, nothing crooked, and no sign of laxity and folly. For such are the affairs of the world; such are the cares of this vain life. This is why those virgins were called foolish: they were turned toward the affairs of this world and gathered where it was not right to gather, and where riches were a good thing, there they were poor. So there is fear and trembling that we too may depart from here clothed in a defiled garment, where all the righteous will have radiant and glorious garments. For there is nothing more foul and more loathsome than sin. This is why the prophet set forth the nature of sin, saying:

"My wounds have grown foul and festered." And if you wish to know the stench and loathsomeness of sin, consider what it is like after it has been committed. When a man has turned away from that evil desire and the fire of desire no longer burns, see how loathsome it appears to him. Consider anger, too, once it has calmed down. Consider avarice, when one is free of that passion: nothing is more loathsome than it. I tell you all this over and over, not to weary you but to profit you greatly and wonderfully. For whoever does not achieve the good after hearing once may perhaps achieve it after a second or third hearing. May we all be found worthy, freed from evil deeds, to attain the fragrance of Christ, for to him belongs the glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and ever and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 53
The text: These words Jesus spoke by the treasury and taught in the temple, and no one seized him, for his hour had not yet come.

Interpretation: O, the foolishness of the Jews! Before the Passover they were seeking him, and then after the Passover they found him, and many times they wished to seize him, both by themselves and through others,

and they could not, and even so they did not marvel at his power, but they constantly added to their wickedness and did not cease. And so that you may know that they were constantly fighting against him, hear what the evangelist says:
Gospel: These words Jesus spoke at the treasury, and he was teaching in the temple, and no one seized him.
Commentary: He was speaking in the temple and in the manner of a teacher, which was all the more able to embitter them,

and he was speaking words at which they grew angry, when he was showing that he is equal with the Father, for the saying "The testimony of two men is true" indicates this. Yet he said all this at the treasury, in the temple, and in the guise of a teacher.
Gospel: And no one seized him, for his hour had not yet come.

Commentary: That is, it was not yet the fitting time at which he willed to be crucified. And from this it is evident that, since they could not seize him when he did not will it, and when they did seize him,

was that too, then, by their own power? No, it was the work of his dispensation, for they had wanted to from the very beginning but were not able. And even then they would not have been able, had he himself not permitted it.
Gospel: Jesus said to them again: "I am going away, and you will seek me.

Commentary: Why then does he say this word to them again and again? Only for this: to frighten and terrify them. For see how much fear this word brings upon them, since those who were striving to kill him so as to be rid of him now ask where he is going. So great a matter did they consider it. And he also wished to teach them something else: that this affair does not come from their tyranny, but was ordained by him from the beginning. And further, by these words he foretold the resurrection as well:
Gospel: The Jews said to one another: "Will he perhaps kill himself?"
Commentary: But the Lord wished to dispel this suspicion of theirs and to show how evil that deed is. Therefore he said to them:
Gospel: "You are from the earth."

Commentary: This saying means the following: that it is no wonder that such thoughts are devised by you, who are from the earth and wholly flesh, and in whom nothing spiritual is found. And as to his saying: "I am not of this world":
Gospel: You are of this world.

Commentary: By this saying he indicates fleshly thoughts. For from this it is evident that when he said, "I am not of this world," he does not say it to mean, "I did not become fully and completely man," but he speaks about human thoughts, as if to say: "I am far from such wickedness as you have." For he said to the apostles, "You are not of this world," and yet they were in the flesh; just as Paul too says, "You are not fleshly," and he did not say this because they were without flesh. Likewise, when he said to the disciples, "You are not of the world," he testifies to nothing other than their estrangement from the affairs of the world.
Gospel: "I said to you:
'If you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins.'"

Interpretation: But if he came for this, that he might take away the sins of the world, and this thing does not come about without the laver of baptism, it is evident that whoever is an unbeliever is to depart clothed in the garment of the old man. For whoever does not wish to put himself to death for the sake of faith in God and to bury the old man completely will die with him and go into that age to receive judgment for his sins.
For this reason the Lord said: "Whoever does not believe is already condemned", not only because he did not believe, but also because he departs with the burden of his former sins.
Gospel: "They said to him: 'And who are you?'"
Commentary: O the blindness and lack of understanding! After so much time and so many miracles and teachings they ask: "Who are you?" But see what the Lord answered:
Gospel: "First, that I am speaking to you."
Commentary: This saying means the following: even this, that you are made worthy to hear my words, is a great thing, let alone that you should know who I am,
for you say everything in order to test me, and you never listen to my words sincerely, and I have the power to expose all of this.
For this reason he said: "I have many things to say and to judge concerning you", that is, not only to expose you but also to punish you.
Gospel: But he who sent me, that is, the Father, does not wish this, for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world, as it says:
The Lord did not send his Son to judge the world, but to save the world.
Commentary: Now therefore, it is for this that he has sent me: truly and justly, I judge no one now, but only speak these words of life and not of reproof.
He said these words to them so that they would not say: "Out of weakness he is unable to repay these insults of ours, or he does not know our thoughts and these reproaches and testings."
Gospel: "They did not understand that he was speaking to them of his Father."

Commentary: O this lack of understanding! He did not cease speaking to them about the Father, and still they did not know. But since he had shown them so many miracles and signs and had taught them so much, and could not turn them to the good, from this point on he begins to speak about the crucifixion and says:

Gospel: "When you lift up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and that I say nothing of myself, but as the Father taught me, so I speak. And he who sent me is with me and has not left me alone."
Interpretation: He shows that he rightly said to them:

"First, since I tell you this: do not listen in this way to the things that are said. When you lift up the Son of Man, do you not think that then you will be rid of me and will have killed me? But I tell you that:
'Then you will know all the more that I am he.'" Because of the signs, the resurrection and the captivity of this city.
For all this was enough to show his power. And he did not say, 'Then you will know who I am,' but, 'Then you will know that I am he.' That is: 'When you see me, that I was not harmed by death,
Then you will know that I am the Christ, the Christ, the Son of God, who holds all things, and who am not opposed to the Father."
And for this reason he also added and said: "I do not speak of myself"; that is to say, so that you may know both things: both my power and this my unity which I have with the Father.
For this saying, in which he said, "I speak nothing of myself," signifies his indivisibility, for he says nothing apart from the counsels of the Father.

For when you have fallen from the worship, when you are not permitted to serve him well as you did before, then you will know that he is seeking vengeance for my sake and that it is from him that this is done to you, and that he is angered at all who will not listen to me. It is as if he were saying: "If I were a stranger to him and his opponent, why would he have brought such great wrath upon you for my sake?" So too Isaiah the prophet says: "I will give over the wicked in place of his burial," and David says: "Then he will speak to them in his wrath," and he himself said: "Behold, your houses are left to you desolate." And his parables also signify the same thing, when he said to them: "What will the lord of the vineyard do to those laborers? For he will wickedly destroy those wicked men." Do you see that in every place he spoke these words, because they did not yet believe him? And if not, if he himself is going to destroy them, as indeed he is, for he says: "Bring here those who did not want my reign over them, and slay them before me."

And since he himself has authority over their destruction, why does he assign this not as his own act but as the Father's? It is clear, then, that it is because of their weakness, for they were not able to understand everything, and again because he honored the Father. For since, in the face of all my good deeds, you did not wish to come to understanding, therefore when you are being punished, then you will know who I am.
Gospel: And the Father is with me.
Interpretation: So that they would not suppose that the word he spoke, "He sent me," he said because of his inferiority, he therefore says:
"He is with me," for the one belongs to his dispensation and the other to his divinity.
Gospel: "He has not left me alone, for I always do what is pleasing to him."

Interpretation: Again he has brought his speech down to a humbler form, and by this he opposes that saying of theirs, when they said, "He does not keep the Sabbath." For this reason he says, "I do what is pleasing to him," in order to show them that the abolition of the Sabbath is pleasing to the Father. So likewise at the time of his crucifixion he said, "Do you think that I cannot entreat my Father?", he who only said to them, "Whom do you seek?"

and he cast them down upon the ground. But if you were to say, "And why did he not say, 'Do you think that he has not given me power to destroy you?'", understand that he did this thing by deed, but kept silent about it in word because of their great weakness. For this was always his earnest concern: to fully assure them that he is not opposed to the Father and does nothing outside his will. And for this reason he speaks this human word here. And just as he said, "He has not left me alone," in the same manner he also said the word that follows: "I always do the things that are pleasing to him."
Gospel: As he was saying this, many believed in him.

Interpretation: When he had brought his speech down this way to lowliness, then many believed in him. And do you still ask, 'Why did he speak with such lowliness?' For the evangelist made this clearly known and said:

"As he was saying these things, many believed in him." It is as if the theologian were crying out openly: "Do not be troubled, O man who hears these words, if you hear something lowly. For with those who had not believed, despite so much teaching, that he is truly from the Father, he spoke in a lowly manner so that they might be convinced." And again he said this also on account of the words that followed, which he was about to say and which the Lord spoke in a lowly manner. For they believed, but not as they ought to have; they only found a little rest in the lowliness of his words.

For the evangelist shows by the following words, which they spoke to him with reviling, that they did not believe as was fitting. And that those who reviled him again after this are the very ones who now believed is evident from what the evangelist says after this.
Gospel: Jesus said to the Jews who believed in him: "If you abide in my words"

Commentary: He shows that they did not accept his word, but only listened to the words. For this reason he spoke to them more painfully. For there he said thus simply, "You will seek me," but now he added something more and said, "You will die in your sins." And he shows them how: for "you cannot come there and entreat me."

Homily 53, that it is necessary to be diligent in the reading of Scripture and in church. But if we thus examine the Scriptures carefully and not superficially, we will be able to find the life of our souls,
if we always listen to the words of Scripture. In this way we will acquire both the firmness of the right faith and a good life.
Even if someone is very harsh and unbending and bears no fruit at those other times,
yet at the time of hearing the divine books he will undoubtedly bear fruit and gain some profit for the soul, some much and some little, but all receive it.

For if anyone passes by the shops of perfume sellers or sits near one, whether he wishes to or not, he catches the scent of those perfumes. Will not the one who goes to church much more receive the scent of spiritual fragrance?
For just as negligence is born of negligence, so also is diligence born of diligence.

Therefore I tell you: even if you are full of many evils and impure, do not flee from going to church. And if anyone should say, "What benefit is there in going there and hearing the words of Scripture, if I do none of those words?", I say that it is no small benefit to blame oneself.
This fear is not useless; this trembling is not unprofitable,

if only you listen to those words of Scripture, and sigh, and blame yourself, and say, "How is it that, behold, I always hear the words of God and never do them?" And when you are in such a frame of mind, know that at some time you will also come to the doing of the divine words, for it is not possible for a person to converse with God and hear the words spoken by God and not benefit.
For when we merely take a book into our hands, we at once become reverent and wash our hands.

Do you see how much reverence comes about through the reading of a book? And if we should desire a deeper understanding of those words, we will gain great benefit. For if it did not also bring the soul to reverence, we would not wash our hands. And a woman, if she is bareheaded, immediately covers her head when she is about to take a book in hand; and a man, if his head is covered, takes off the covering and bares his head. Do you see how that outward form becomes a herald of the inner reverence? And then, when he sits down to listen or to read, he often sighs and blames this vain life. Let us therefore listen to the words of Scripture, O beloved. Even if we should grow cold toward any other book, let us at least listen to the Gospel and read it continually. For as soon as you open the book, you will see the name of Christ written there, and you will at once hear it saying: "The birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way,

for his mother Mary was betrothed, and she was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit." And whoever hears this, does he not at once become a lover of virginity, and marvel at that lofty birth, and rise above the earth? And all these things are not small, when you see how the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin and how the angel spoke to her; and you will learn all this with only a brief glance. If you read everything through to the end, then you will despise every affair of this vain world and condemn the whole world. If you are rich, you will count wealth as nothing when you hear that she who lived in the house of a carpenter and poor man became the mother of your Lord and King and of all creatures. And if you are poor, you will no longer be ashamed of your poverty when you learn that the Creator of all was not ashamed to be in that lowly dwelling. When you reflect on all this, you will not become greedy, nor a robber, nor one who seizes the possessions of another, but rather you will love poverty and despise wealth.

And when you have accomplished all this, then you will have driven out all evils. Again, when you see him lying in the manger, you will no longer wish to adorn your children with gold and silver, and you will be delivered from the acts of greed that come upon you because of this. Much other profit will also be found, which I cannot now describe one by one, but those who have been proved in it will know it. Therefore I implore you that we acquire books, and understanding from them as well, so that we may understand their words and write them in our minds. For we must establish their words in our hearts, so that in this way we may be able to make this life of ours holy and become worthy of those eternal good things. May we all be worthy to attain them by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen!
Chapter 54
This saying: Jesus said to the Jews who believed in him:
"If you abide in my words, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
Commentary: We have need of great endurance, beloved.
But endurance comes about when those divine teachings have been firmly rooted in our minds, and, as with a great tree,
strongly established by its root, which no wind is able to uproot, so also the soul nailed to the fear of God,

nothing is able to bend, for being nailed is firmer than being bound by roots. For this reason the prophet also prayed and said: "Nail my flesh to your fear." So then you too nail yourselves, as those fastened with a nail. For as one nailed to the fear of God cannot be bent, so one who is not nailed is quickly and easily carried away, as indeed the Jews were. For when they heard and believed the words of the Lord, they became unbelieving again. But Christ wished to establish faith among them, so that it might not be weak and as nothing. For this reason he undertakes, with more painful words, to establish those souls of theirs in faith.
And if they had been true believers, they would have endured that rebuke, but they hardened all the more and became savage. But see how the Lord spoke to them:
Gospel: First he commands and says: "If you abide in my words, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."

Interpretation: It is as if he were saying to them, 'I am about to heal the wounds of your souls, but do not be alarmed.' And even more, by these words he was quelling the arrogance of their souls. But why was he freeing them from sins? Just listen to the words of those arrogant men, who said:
"We are the offspring of Abraham and have never been slaves to anyone."

Their mind at once fell away because of that arrogance. He himself said to them, 'If you abide in my words,' for he was revealing the thoughts of their hearts: that although they had believed, they did not abide in his words and in those promises, that great thing, which is to be his disciple. For earlier also some had departed from him, and therefore he says to them: 'If you abide in my words, you will be my disciples. For they too believed, but since they did not abide in my words, they departed from me.' As it is written: 'Many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.'
Gospel: "You will know the truth."
Interpretation: That is, you will know me, for I am the truth.
And everything belonging to the Jews was a figure, but you will know the truth from me, and the truth will set you free from sins. For just as he said to the others that
"You will die in your sins"; in the same way he says to these, "[If the Son] makes you free." But listen to what they were saying:
Gospel: "We are descendants of Abraham and have been slaves to no one."

Interpretation: And if it had been proper to become angry, they should have become angry at that first saying, when he said to them, "You will know the truth," and they should have said: "Do we not know the truth now? Or is the Law false, and this understanding of ours?" But nothing of this troubled them; rather, they were pained over worldly matters when they heard of slavery. For there are many even now who are ashamed of slavery to men, but if they are slaves of sin, it does not seem shameful to them, and they would choose to become slaves to sins ten thousand times rather than once a slave to men. Such were these people too, and they did not know that there is also another slavery, that of God, but only this human slavery, and they said: Are we, these descendants of Abraham, who are freeborn, being named slaves?
And it was not right for you to call us slaves, for we have never been enslaved.
Such was the boast of the Jews: "We are descendants of Abraham," "We are Israelites," and they never made mention of virtues and good deeds.
For this reason John also said to them: "Do not say, 'We have Abraham as father.'"
But why did the Lord not rebuke them for that statement they made, "We have never been slaves to anyone," since they had many times been slaves to the Egyptians and the Babylonians and many others?
For this reason: because he was not speaking about human slavery, but about their life; otherwise he would have mentioned those four hundred years, and again the seventy,
and again what came upon them under the Judges, sometimes for twenty years, sometimes for seven years, and sometimes for two years, and how they never ceased from slavery.

But his own concern was not this, to single them out for having become slaves of men; rather, his concern was this, to show that they are slaves of sin, which is the evil slavery, from which God alone is able to deliver and not man,
for the forgiveness of sins belongs to no one else but God alone, and they too acknowledged this.
And since they too acknowledged this, that the forgiveness of sins is the work of God, for this reason he said this to them:
Gospel: "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin."
Interpretation: In order to show that he was speaking to them about this freedom, which comes about from such slavery, for this reason he said to them:

Gospel: "The slave never remains in the house forever, but the son remains forever." See how, little by little, he lowers even the Law and alludes to those former times, so that they might not say, "We offer the sacrifices that Moses commanded us, and they are able to save us." For this reason he added this saying, because "all have sinned and have fallen short of the glory of God, but they are justified freely," even the priests themselves. For this reason also the apostle Paul says of the priest, "He must first offer for himself as well as for the people, since he too is subject to weakness." And this is what he alludes to by the saying, "The slave never remains in the house."

And in this place he also shows his equality with his own Father and the difference between the slave and the free man. This parable is an image of that. That is, "he does not have authority," for this is what "he does not abide" means. But why is it that, while speaking about sins, he mentioned the house? He did so to show that, just as the master of a house has authority over the house, so he has authority over all created things. And "he does not abide" means that whoever is not the master of the house has no authority to grant [freedom]. But the Son is the master of the house, for this is what "he abides forever" means. And so that they could not say to him, "Who are you?", he showed them by means of human affairs that:

"Everything is mine, for I am [the Son] and I abide in my Father's house." He calls power and dominion the house of the Father. That is why he said to them, "In my Father's house are many mansions." Since his discourse was about slavery and being set free, he rightly used such words, to show that no one [else] was able to set them free and forgive their sins. Therefore he said to them: Gospel: "If the Son makes you free"

Commentary: Do you see how he reveals this unity of his with the Father? He shows that he has the same authority as the Father has. And this is what "If the Son makes you free" means: there will no longer be anyone who can speak against you, but you will hold that freedom firmly. For "if it is God who enlightens [?], who is the one who condemns?"

Here he shows that he is able to cleanse them from sin and set them free, and that this freedom is higher than bodily freedom. Even men give bodily freedom, but this freedom belongs to God alone. For this reason he teaches them not to be ashamed of bodily slavery, but rather to be ashamed of the slavery of sins. He also wanted to show that if they are freed from the slavery of sins, they are no longer slaves. And he gave them to understand that they are still in slavery by the word he spoke, "You will be free," for this word indicates that the freedom they have is not true freedom. He also did this so that they could not say, "We have no sin," for given their senselessness it would not have been surprising for them to say this.
Therefore see how he points out their sin. He passed over their other deeds, for which he might have reproached them, and spoke only of the one they held at that time and wished to carry out.
Gospel: "I know that you are descendants of Abraham, but you seek to kill me."

Commentary: Do you see with what skill he leads them away from their descent from Abraham, so that they may not boast of it in vain? He shows that, just as slavery and freedom come from deeds, so does kinship. He did not say to them at once, "You are not the seed of Abraham, you murderers of that righteous man." Instead, he first concedes the point and says, "I know that you are the seed of Abraham, but none of you is being asked whether you are the seed of Abraham." Then he says something more painful to them: "You seek to kill me." And again, so that they could not say, "What does it matter, if we seek to kill you justly?", he also tells them the reason:
Gospel: "My word finds no room among you."

Commentary: How then has it been said: "They believed in him"? But, as I said: "They believed and turned away from the faith again." For this reason this saying touched them deeply, for he was telling them: "If you boast of kinship with him, you must also do his deeds." And he did not say to them: "You will not keep my word," but: "My word finds no room among you," for he was indicating the loftiness of his teachings. And why, then, did they need to kill him for this? For rather it was incumbent on them to worship and honor him for telling them his words openly, but because of their evil and wickedness they were thus doing evil in return for good. And here too, then, they wanted to say: "You speak those words of yourself; what need is there to know them?" For this reason the Lord added and said:
Gospel:
"I speak what I have seen from my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father."
Commentary: That is to say: just as I reveal my Father by words and by truth, so you show your father by deeds,
for I have not only the same essence that the Father has, but also the same truth that he has.
Gospel: The Jews said to him: "We have Abraham as our father."
Jesus said to them: "If Abraham were your father, you would do his deeds, but now you seek to kill me."
Commentary: In this place he repeatedly mentions their murder-loving will, and he also mentions Abraham, in order to show
that they are far from kinship with him,
and in order to scrape away that vain boast of theirs and persuade them no longer to place hope of salvation in their fleshly kinship with him, but to seek kinship by deeds,
For this was what kept them from coming to Christ: they thought that descent from Abraham alone was enough for their salvation. And as for the truth that he speaks of here:
"You seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from the Father." This, then, is the truth for which they sought to kill him: that he said, "I am equal to the Father."
For this reason he tells them here that this saying is not opposed to the Father, but that it is the Father's will in this matter.
Gospel: They said to him: "We were not born of fornication; we know one Father: God."
Commentary: Since he had estranged them from kinship with Abraham and they had nothing to say, they now ventured upon a higher matter and called God their Father,
they who were seeking to kill Christ because he called God his own Father in truth. But the Lord estranged them from this claim too, and said to them:
Gospel: "If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came forth from God and have come,
and I have not come of myself, but he sent me. Why do you not understand my words, and why are you unable to hear my words?
You are of your father the devil, and you want to do the desire of your father,
for he was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because the truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own heart."

Commentary: First he estranged them from kinship with Abraham, and since they dared to claim something higher, he then brought down on them the wound of his words and showed that not only are they not Abraham's,

but they are even the devil's. And since they shamelessly called God their Father, for this reason he too brought on them the wound of a rebuke matching their shamelessness. Nor did he leave his rebuke without proof, but he convicted them from their deeds and showed
that murder is the work of the devil. And he did not say:

"the deeds" only, but: "You want to do the desires of the devil as well," in order to show that they are eager with all eagerness for murder, just like the devil, and that envy was the cause of all this,
For he too had no complaint against Adam, as though Adam had done him any harm,
but he did what he did only out of envy. He points to this here as well: "You too act in likeness to him."
Gospel: And he did not stand in the truth.

Commentary: Since they repeatedly accused him and said, "He is not from God," for this reason he says to them: "That too is the counsel of the devil, for he first begot the lie and said: 'On the day that you eat of that tree, your eyes will be opened.'" He made use of lying from the very first, for when men lie, they do not do it as their own proper work, but when he lies, he does his own proper work.
Gospel: "But I tell you the truth, and you do not believe me."

Interpretation: What is the meaning of this, that you wish to kill me without cause? It is because you are enemies of the truth that you persecute me. If that is not so, tell me my fault. For this reason he said: "Which of you will convict me of sin?" And they said: "We were not born of fornication." How so? For many of them had been born of fornication, since they did not contract proper marriages. Yet he did not rebuke them even for this, but stayed with that one statement. For he had shown that they were not of God but of the devil because of their deeds, since murder is of the devil and lying likewise is of the devil, and they were doing both. And he showed them: "Since you hold to these deeds, you do not belong to God."
Gospel: "Why do you not know my words?"

Interpretation: Since they were always astonished and said, "Who is this who says: 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?", he therefore says to them: "You do not know my words, and you do not know them because you do not have the word of God." And this is because your mind is once again nailed to the earth, while these words of mine are lofty; and since your souls are constricted by evils, the loftiness of my words therefore finds no room in you. And if someone should say: "If they were unable to understand his words, what were they to do?", the answer is that here he calls unwillingness inability. That is to say: "By your own will you have made yourselves foolish and incapable of understanding anything." For since they were persecuting him and saying, "We love God, and that is why we persecute," he himself showed that persecuting him is the mark of those who hate God, whereas faith in him is the mark of those who love him. For is not your unbelief, he says, a sign of estrangement from my Father, showing that you do not know God, but do the will of the devil, and are wholly flesh, and wish to carry out the desires of your father, and are eager for that?

Do you see how he calls unwillingness inability? For Abraham did not do this; rather, his works are simplicity, meekness and goodness, whereas you are harsh and savage. And why did they say: "We know one Father, God"? For this reason: because he had cut them off from kinship with Abraham and had exposed their murderousness. Then they named God as their Father, and this in order to make it appear as if to say: "It is out of love for God that we seek to kill you, for we are zealous for God." But he himself showed that this very deed was what was provoking God's anger against them. And when he said, "I came forth from God," he shows that he is from him, and by "coming forth" he means his coming to us. And since they were going to say, "You are saying strange things, that 'I have come forth from God,'" he therefore said to them:
"Rightly you do not understand and do not listen to my words, since you are of the devil; for why do you seek to kill me?

"What is my guilt? And if you find no error, why do you not listen to my words?" So he showed from their lying and their murderousness that they belong to the devil, and he estranged them both from Abraham and from God: first, because they hated one who had done them no harm, and again, because they did not listen to his word. And he shows, both earlier and later, that he was not opposed to God, and that this was not the reason they did not believe his words, but rather that they were estranged from God. For when someone has committed not a single sin, has come from God and been sent by him, and speaks the truth, and when many were witnesses of his truthfulness, it is clear that those who do not believe such a one fail to believe because they have been taken captive by the devil and the passions.

For sins are able to bring down the soul more than anything else. Therefore he says to them: "Since you have become so negligent and slack that you are unable to despise earthly things, how could you be able to hear heavenly things?"

Homily 54. That we should be eager to seize the kingdom of heaven and not the things of the world. Therefore I beseech you, beloved brothers, let us strive with all our heart and soul to direct our life toward what is good, so that our mind may become pure and there may be no defilement in us, for it is said,
"Enlighten yourselves with the light of understanding, and do not sow upon thorns."

For whoever does not understand that covetousness is evil will not understand anything higher. Whoever does not depart from sin, when will he begin to do righteousness? Seizing is a good thing, though not the seizing of these perishable and destructive things, but of the kingdom of heaven. For it is said:
"The violent seize it." Yet it is not gained through negligence and slackness, but through great eagerness. And what does "the violent" mean?
It means that one must use great force on oneself, for the way that leads there is narrow, and a courageous soul is needed. For robbers strive
to outrun everyone; they pay no attention to anyone, nor to blame, nor to accusation, nor to punishment,
but their one concern is to seize what they desire, and they pass by everyone. Let us then seize the kingdom of heaven,

for seizing this is not blameworthy but praiseworthy, whereas seizing the things of this world is what is blameworthy. But the seizing of the kingdom is not like that, where our enrichment comes about through the impoverishment of another.
Let us then strive to seize it. Even if anger or desire presses hard upon us, let us force our nature; let us become gentle and kind, and let us toil a little, so that we may rest forever.
Do not seize gold. Instead, seize that wealth which shows gold to be dross.
For tell me: if [?] and gold were set before you, which would you choose to seize? Would you not choose the gold?

But here is something astonishing. Where the one who seizes gold is punished, there you choose the gold, because it is more precious. Yet where the one who seizes is greatly glorified, you do not seize the more precious thing. Even if punishment were set before you for both, would you not choose the same thing? But since blessedness is to be given for seizing this wealth, is that why you are negligent? And if you ask, "How can it be seized?", I will teach you: leave behind the vain affairs of this world, because as long as you hold on to them, seizing it is impossible. Consider a man whose hands are full of silver. While his hands are full of that silver, could he seize gold unless he first emptied his hands of it?

For a robber must be freed from every bond, so that he may be able to flee from his pursuers. For even now there are hostile powers opposed to us who pursue us, so that they might seize the good things we have taken. So let us flee from them. Let us flee, and let us carry no bond of this world. Let us cut its ropes and strip ourselves of these vain affairs. What profit is there in garments woven with gold? How long shall we keep hoarding gold? I would like to stop saying such things, but you do not let me, for you always give me reason to say them. So let us turn away from this kind of vanity, O beloved, so that you may be able to teach others too by your good deeds. And may we find those eternal good things by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 55
This passage: The Jews answered and said to him: "Did we not say well that 'You are a Samaritan and have a demon'?"
Then Jesus answered them and said: "I do not have a demon"

Commentary: Wickedness is shameless and harsh, and when it ought to feel shame, then it becomes all the more shameless, as also befell the Jews. For they ought to have been softened and amazed at those words and at his boldness, but instead they even revile him and call him a Samaritan and demon-possessed, and say: "Did we not say well that 'You are a Samaritan and have a demon'?" For whenever he says some lofty word, those utterly blinded men call it madness. Although the evangelist has nowhere said earlier that they called him a Samaritan, yet from this word that they speak, "Did we not say well?", it is evident
that they had many times called him "Samaritan" and "possessed by a demon." And who is the one possessed by a demon:
the one who honours God, or the one who dishonours and reviles him who honours God? But hear the word of Christ, which is wholly meekness and sincerity:
Gospel: I do not have a demon, but I honor him who sent me

Commentary: For where it was necessary to teach them and to humble that arrogance of theirs which they had over their descent from Abraham, there he was severe in his words; but here, where it was fitting to endure their abuse, he shows great gentleness. And when they said to him:
"We have God as Father, and Abraham," then he struck at them forcefully.

But when they called him demon-possessed, he did not become angry, but frames his speech with kindness, in order to teach us that when we hear some blasphemy spoken against God we should seek vengeance, but should not become angry over abuse against ourselves. For if he who by a word made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in it, endured all this, who are we, we who are nothing, that we should not endure contempt from our neighbors? Hear, then, what the Savior says:
Gospel: "I do not seek my own will"
Commentary: That is to say: I said all this that I have said for this reason, that you should not call God the father of yourselves, you who are murderers and liars.

And whatever I have said, I have said it all for the honor of the Father, and for his sake I hear all this, and for his sake you treat me with contempt. But I am not concerned about that abuse of yours, for from him you will receive the recompense for all this for which I endure contempt from you; but I do not seek my own glory.
Therefore I do not punish you, but I teach you and counsel you, that you may do these deeds by which you will not only escape torments but will also become worthy of eternal life.
Gospel: "Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will not see death forever"

Commentary: Here he speaks not of faith alone, but also of good deeds. And above he said, "he has eternal life," but here he says, "he will not see death." And along with this he also intimates another matter, that they are able to do nothing to harm him. For if he who keeps his word does not die, how much more will he himself not die? And they understood this, that this is what he was intimating. Therefore they said to him:
Gospel: "Now we know that you are demon-possessed. Abraham died, and the prophets"
Commentary: That is to say: those who heard the word of God died, and will those who hear yours not die?
Gospel: "Surely you are not greater than our father Abraham?"

Commentary: O this vainglory! Again they fled back to that descent of theirs! And at this point they would have had more of an argument if they had said: "Surely you are not greater than God?" or, "Are those who have heard your word greater than Abraham?" But they do not say this, for they considered him even inferior to Abraham. He himself, however, had earlier exposed their murderousness, and in this way made them strangers to that descent from him.

And as they persisted in the same thing, he himself again began to speak to them in another manner, in order to show them that they were laboring in vain. He said nothing to them about death; he neither revealed nor told them which death he was speaking of, but for the moment he only persuades them that he is above Abraham, so that perhaps in this way they might yield. And he says to them: "Even if I were some worthless man, it would not be right to kill me, since I bear no guilt at all. But since I also speak the truth, and have no sin, and am sent from God, and am greater than Abraham, are you not mad, and do you not labor in vain, you who seek to kill me?" But see their words, what they say:
Gospel: "Now we know that you are possessed by a demon."

Interpretation: But the Samaritan woman did not speak like this. She did not say, "You have a demon"; she only said, "Are you greater than our father Jacob?" This is because these men were revilers and apostates, but she wanted to learn the truth. That is why she was amazed, answered him in fitting measure, and called him Lord. For it was not right to revile one who was promising things far more exalted; it was right to marvel at his works. But these men revile the Creator of all and call him possessed by a demon.
for the words of that Samaritan woman came from wonder, but theirs from unbelief and wickedness.
Gospel: "Are you perhaps greater than our father Abraham?"

Commentary: It is evident, then, that this shows him to be above Abraham, for he himself said: "When you see me departed from here, then you will acknowledge that I am superior." For this reason he said to them: "When you lift me up, then you will know who I am." And behold his incomprehensible wisdom,
for first he separated them from kinship with Abraham, and then he began to show them that he is above him,
so that he might be seen to surpass the prophets by a great height. For since they always called him a prophet, he therefore said: "My word finds no room among you," and earlier he said:
"He raises the dead," but here he says:

"Whoever has believed in me shall not see death," which is far higher, not to see death at all, than to rise from death. For this reason they grew all the more harsh and said: "Whom do you make yourself?"
And this too is a word of reviling, that is to say: "You make yourself great." But Christ answered them in response to this word:
Gospel: "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing."
Commentary: He heard: "Are you perhaps greater than our father Abraham?"

And in keeping with their great weakness he did not say to them, "Yes, I am superior," but he framed his word skillfully. But what does this saying mean: "My glory is nothing"? How is his glory nothing?

But it is nothing with respect to them. For just as he says in another place, "My testimony is not true," and said that on account of their blinded mind, so likewise he gave this answer on account of their way of thinking, saying: "There is one who glorifies me, the one of whom you said:
"He is our God, and you do not know him." For he wished to show that they do not know him, not only as Father, but not even as God; but I know him.
"And if I say, 'I do not know him,' I will be a liar, like you." He makes known that it is not this that is a lie, "I know him," but rather this:
"I do not know" is the lie. And you, even though you say, "We know him," are lying. So too, if I were to say:
"I do not know," [I would be lying]. Rather: "As I know him in truth, so you are ignorant of him." And just as concerning Abraham he did not overturn everything they said, but said:
"I know that you are descendants of Abraham," so that by this word he might bring a greater accusation upon them, so too he did not show them to be wholly foreign to God, but said:

"of whom you say that he is our God." By these words he granted them their boast, and by this he made their sin greater. For he said to them: "You say it, and you do not know him. And you do not know him in this way: you revile the one who glorifies and honours him in every way, and you persecute the one sent by him." This word seemed unbelievable to them, but the next one silences them: "I keep his words." For at this point, if they had had anything to say, they could have refuted him, but they had nothing. For this saying is a greater testimony to him than the earlier one:
"He sent me." Therefore he says:
Gospel: "Abraham, your father, rejoiced that he would see this day of mine; he saw it and was glad."

Commentary: First he showed them to be foreign to him, for what he was joyful over, these men were grieved over. "But he saw my day and was glad": he speaks of the day of the crucifixion, which he prefigured beforehand in the offering of the ram and of Isaac, when he was offering Isaac and saw the ram hanging on the plant of sabek, and was glad, for it was a type of Christ's crucifixion. And it is of that day that he says, "He saw my day and was glad," that is, when he saw the type of the crucifixion. But hear what they say:
Gospel: "You are not fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Jesus said to them:
"Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am." The Jews took up stones to stone him

Interpretation: Do you see how he showed that he is greater than Abraham? Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and seeing it seemed a great thing to him. So it is clear that he regarded that day as the day of the one who gives life and of the one who is greater than he. They were saying, "He is the carpenter's son," and understood nothing else, so he leads them up little by little to a loftier understanding. When they heard that they do not know God, they were not so hardened. But when they heard, "Before Abraham was, I am," they became enraged, as though their own dignity had been made worthless, and so they were throwing stones at him.

"He saw my day and rejoiced" shows that he does not go to his passion unwillingly. He praises the one who rejoiced to see his crucifixion, because this was the life of the whole world. But they wanted to stone him. In this way they were always ready to kill, and they did such things without any inquiry. And why did he not say, "Before Abraham was, I was," but "I am"? Because just as the Father used this expression, "I am who I am," so did he himself. This expression signifies eternal being, outside all time. For this reason they considered the saying blasphemy. If they could not bear his equality with Abraham, which was small compared with his glory, what would they have done if he had kept making himself equal with the Father? Would they have stopped fighting him and stoning him? But again, in a human way, he flees from them and hides himself. He had set out much teaching for them and had finished his task, so he went out of the temple and went to heal the blind man, so that he might also prove by deed that he exists before Abraham.

Someone might ask why he did not take away their strength, so that they would believe that way. But consider this: he healed the paralytic, and they did not believe. He performed countless other miracles, and they did not believe. At the time of his passion he threw them down on their faces and darkened their eyes, and they did not believe. So how would they have believed now, even if he had taken away their strength? Nothing is worse than a soul that has given up hope. Whether it sees miracles or signs, it stays in the same shamelessness. Pharaoh also received countless plagues. Whenever he was being tormented, he would repent for that day only, and then he went back to the same wickedness. In the end he pursued the people he had let go. That is why the great apostle Paul cries out:

"Let none of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin." A body that is gripped by many diseases and made senseless by a high fever cannot get up. In the same way, when a soul is gripped by many sins, it becomes dead to virtue. Whatever you say to it, it understands none of the teaching at all. Whether you speak to it of torments or of the Kingdom, it remains unmoved.

Homily 55, on envy. For this reason I entreat you that, while we have the hope of life, while we are able to turn back in every way, let us hasten to save our souls; for those in despair, like ship captains,
are those who have cut off their hope and pitiably given the ship over into the hands of the wind, and who show no effort at all to save the ship.

So too are these people: for the envious man looks at nothing else but this alone, how he may fulfill his desire. Even if torment lies before him, or even death itself, he strives only to fulfill his passion; and so too the lover of fornication, and so too the lover of money.

But if the passions have such great tyranny, would not virtue have greater power, if only we were willing? And if we despise death for the sake of sin, shall we not all the more despise it for the sake of virtue?
If lovers of evil disregard their own lives in order to do evil, is it not all the more fitting to disregard ourselves for the sake of the life of the soul?

For what word shall we have before God, when we see that those who are perishing strive so eagerly by every means for their own perdition, while we do not strive for the salvation of our souls, but remain always in envy and spite [?]?
Nothing is worse than envy, for the envious man strives to destroy the other and to cast himself down with him into hell.
The eye of the envious man melts away with grief; he is in perpetual death; he regards as enemies all those who have done him no harm.
He grieves when God is honored, and he rejoices where the demons rejoice. "Such a one has been honored by men," he says.
But do not envy, man, for that honor is no honor. But if he has been honored by God, emulate him and become like him. Or do you not want this?

Why then do you want to destroy yourself as well? Why do you throw away even what you have? If you cannot be equal to him and acquire what is good, why then do you acquire what is evil? You ought to rejoice over your neighbor's good, even if you cannot become a sharer in his labors; yet by this you will gain a share, that you rejoice over the labors and good things of another, for often the will alone suffices to accomplish a great good. For Ezekiel the prophet says that the Moabites were to be punished for this, that they rejoiced over the affliction of the Israelites, and of certain others he says that they were to be saved for this, that they sighed over the evil of others. Now if merely sighing over another's evil brings such consolation, will it not do still more good to those who rejoice over another's honor?

And he accused the Moabites because they rejoiced at the punishment of the Israelites, even though God was the one punishing them. For even when God brings punishment upon someone, even then it is not right to rejoice, but rather to be grieved at their punishment. For it is not that God wishes them to be punished. But if it is right to grieve with those who are punished, is it not all the more right to rejoice for those whom God has honored? In this way the followers of Korah and Dathan perished: those whom they envied they made all the more illustrious, while they gave themselves over to destruction. For envy is a venomous beast and an unclean wickedness that has no defense, the cause and mother of all evils. Therefore let us tear it out by the root, so that we may be separated from all evils and attain those eternal good things by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom glory befits the Father together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 56
The text: And as Jesus was passing by, he saw a man who had been blind from birth. His disciples asked him, saying, "Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?"

Interpretation: He who is exceedingly loving toward humankind and who seeks our life, and who wished to stop the mouths of those ungrateful people, therefore left undone no deed that it was right for him to do, even though they did not understand.
That is why the prophet also knew this and said: "That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you judge." For this reason here too,
since they did not accept the loftiness of his words but even began to revile him and wanted to kill him, for this reason, when he went out of the temple, he healed that paralyzed man:

first, so that by his departure he might soothe their anger, and second, so that by performing that sign he might soften their harshness and inflexibility and make his words credible, and perform a sign not so ordinary, but one done only then, which had never been done before.

For "from the beginning of the age it has not been heard," it says, "that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind." For the eyes of a blind man may perhaps have been opened, but those of one blind from birth have never been opened.
And it is evident that when he went out of the temple, he went deliberately to heal him, for it was he who saw the blind man, and not the blind man who approached him,
and he looked at him so intently that even the disciples realized that he was looking at him, and for this reason they asked.
For when they saw him looking at the man so intently, they asked: "Teacher, who sinned, this man or his parents?"
Their question is mistaken, for how could he have sinned before birth? Or if his parents sinned, how could he have been punished?

Why, then, did they come to ask about this matter? Because before this, when he had healed the paralytic, he said to him: "Behold, you have been healed; from now on sin no more." And they understood that he had been paralyzed because of sins, and therefore they said here:

"Behold, that man was paralyzed because of sins. What, then, do you say about this one? Did this man also sin?" But this is impossible, for he is blind from birth. "Or is it because of the sin of his parents?" But this too is unfitting, for punishment is not brought upon a child on account of the parents. For just as we, when we see a little child in suffering, say with wonder: "What fault can this one have?", so the disciples asked this question in amazement. And the Lord answered them: Neither did this man sin, nor his parents, that he should have been born blind. Yet this word that he spoke does not show that they were without sin, for he did not say only this: "They did not sin," but:

"They did not sin so that he should be born blind," but "so that the Son of God may be glorified." For both he and his parents did sin, but his blindness does not come from this. He said this, however, not to show that this is so in this case while certain others became blind because of the sin of their parents, for it is impossible that one person should sin and another be punished for his sin. Otherwise, if we say this, we should also say that he sinned before he was born. For just as he said that this man was born blind neither because of his own sins nor because of his parents', so it is in every case. And for this reason Ezekiel removes that suspicion and says: "As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be, which is spoken: 'The fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth were set on edge.'" And Moses says: "A father shall not die for a son."

But if anyone should say, as it is said, "who repays the sin of the parents upon the children to the third and fourth generation," we say about this that the commandment does not apply to all, but was spoken about certain people, those who came out of Egypt. And the saying means this: since those who came out of Egypt, after so many signs that had been done in the time of their parents, became worse than those who had never seen a sign at all, therefore he says: "What came upon them, the same shall come upon these also, for they have done the same deeds." And whoever reads it will truly know that it was said about them. But why was he born blind?

"so that the glory of God might be revealed in him." Behold, here another difficulty appears, for someone might say: "What is this? Was it not possible for the glory of God to be revealed without his suffering?"
But it is not said in the sense that it was impossible, for it was possible for the glory of God to be revealed even without him; rather, it was so that it might be revealed in him as well.

But if anyone should say that this suffering came upon him unjustly so that God might be glorified, then let the one who says such a thing tell me: what harm would have come upon him even if his eyes had never been opened at all?
For I say that a greater good came to him through blindness, for his inner eyes were opened. For what did the Jews gain from their eyes?

Did not a greater judgment come upon them, because eyes had been given to them and they became blind? But what evil came to this man from blindness, since because of it the eyes of his soul were opened?
For just as the evil things of this world are not evil, so also the good things are not good; rather, only sin is evil, whereas blindness is not evil.
And he who brought him from non-existence into existence had the power to leave him thus.
But some say: "This statement that he makes, 'that God may be glorified,' does not express the cause but the outcome," as when he says:
"For the judgment of this world I have come, that those who did not see may see, and those who saw may become blind"; and again Paul says:
"What can be known of God has become manifest to them, so that they may be without excuse," yet he did not show it to them for this purpose, that they might be without excuse;
