But here he did not expose them, so as to teach us not always to rebuke those who do evil to us, but to endure everything with gentleness, since their actions were the actions of folly: for the deeds were proclaiming, and they were looking for words.
So listen to how he answered them. First, he wanted to show that they were asking with guile and not in order to learn. Second, he wanted to make clear
that he had preached by deeds more than by words, for he answered: "I told you, and you do not believe.

The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me." This is just as the more reasonable [?] among them said: "How can a sinful man do such signs?" and "How can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" And again they said: "Is this not the Christ? When the Christ comes, will he do more signs than these?" So when they were not convinced by such great works, did they claim that a few words would convince them?

See how he shames their wickedness, saying, "If you do not believe the deeds, when would you be convinced by words?" "But you do not believe," he says, "because you are not of my sheep." That is to say: "All that it was fitting for me to do, I have done. If you still do not follow me, this is not because I am not a shepherd, but because you are not sheep."

Gospel: "For my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and I will not let them perish for ever, and no one will snatch them out of my hands. For my Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of my Father's hands. I and my Father are one."
Commentary: "See how skilfully he calls them to follow him. For he says, 'You do not listen to me because you are not sheep,' and then he stirs in them a desire for this, when he said:

'Whoever comes to me I will not cast out.' And he revealed his own oneness with the Father. When he said, 'No one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hands,' he wanted them not to think that he himself could not do this and that the work was done only by the Father's power. So he added, 'I and the Father are one,' that is, one in power and in essence. Since the Jews had many times wanted to drive out those who believed in him, he said, 'You strive in vain, for my sheep are in the hands of the Father, who gave them to me.' This word, 'gave me,' is also said for their sake, so that no one could say that he is 'opposed to the Father.' And when you hear 'hand,' do not understand anything visible. By 'hand' he means power and authority, which is one and the same for the Son and the Father.
Gospel:
"And the Jews had stones in order to stone him."
Commentary: This was because he said, "I and the Father are one." Oh, the wickedness! The same people who had been asking him,

"Tell us, are you the Christ?" now stone him. But he confirmed his word all the more and said to them, "I have shown you many good works from my Father. For which of those works do you stone me?" The Jews answered and said to him:
Gospel: "We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you are a man and have made yourself God."
Jesus answered and said to them: "Is it not written in the Law: 'I said, You are gods'?
If he called them gods to whom the word of God came, how do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, 'He blasphemes,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
Commentary: Now this saying means the following: "If you do not blame those who received that name by grace and not by nature, how am I to be blamed, who have this by nature?"
But first he said:
"Whom the Father sanctified and sent," so that by this word of humility he might bend their anger, and so he introduced that open declaration. For he spoke humbly
so that his word might become acceptable to them, and only afterward did he raise his word and say:
Gospel: "If I do not do the work of my Father, do not believe me. And if I do, even if you do not believe me, believe the works."

Commentary: Do you see how he brought his word to completion and firmly showed that he is in no way inferior to the Father, but is equal to him in every respect? For since they were unable to see his essence, he therefore did everything through the equality of the works,
[?] the showing of his inseparability from the Father and his equality with him; and he also told them the faith, how they ought to hold it.
Gospel: "That the Father is in me and I am in him."
Commentary: This means: "I am nothing other than what the Father is. I am the same, abiding in sonship. And he is nothing other than what I am. He is the same, abiding in fatherhood.

For he is Father and I am Son, but in everything else, what he is, I am the same, and what I am, he is. The property of each is this: he is Father and I am Son, distinct in person and united in nature. If anyone knows me, he has also known the Father, and if anyone knows the Father as is fitting, he has also known the Son, who is of one essence with the Father and equal to him."
Gospel: "They sought again to seize him, and he went out from their hands and crossed the Jordan, to the place where John first used to baptize, and he stayed there.
And many came to him and said, 'John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man is true.' And many believed in him."
Commentary: Whenever he said something lofty, something concerning his divinity, he would go away from there so that their anger might subside, just as he did now.

And why did the evangelist also state the name of the place? So that you may know that he went there for this reason: to remind them of the words John had spoken there about him, and of his testimony.
For this reason they also remembered when they went there, and they said, "John did no sign, but all that he said about this man was true."
So far is this man superior to John, for John did no sign,

And he does this, and again, it was for this reason that that one [John] bore witness, and through this his testimony too was shown to be true. And many believed in him, for they remembered the words of John,

how he had called him mightier than himself, and light, and life, and truth. They also remembered the voice that came from heaven, and the appearance of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, which showed him to everyone, and his other signs, which they saw and by which they were strengthened. And they said, "If it was right to believe John without signs, is it not more right to believe this man, who also performs signs, and to whom John also bears witness?"

Do you see how much benefit came from withdrawing from those wicked men? For this reason he repeatedly withdrew his disciples from them, just as he had earlier removed the people of the Jews far from the wickedness of the Egyptians.

Homily 61: On not adorning the body. For this reason it is right for us also to do likewise, and to flee from tumults and disturbances and to live in quietness. For just as a ship that has escaped from fierce winds sails well, so the soul removed from the disturbances of the world is lifted up toward God. Let us therefore flee from disturbances and adorn our soul with virtue, with the fear of God and with mercy and purity,
and let us not adorn our bodies with gold and beautiful ornaments.

For this adornment even length of time destroys, and many other causes ruin it, but the adornment of the soul is far removed and pure from all this. Bodily adornment sows envy and [?] in the hearts of others, but that of the soul is pure from all this, when gold does not lie on our body and fingers but is given to the poor. For what is the profit of being clothed in gold-woven garments, since all flesh is grass and all human glory is like the flower of grass? All this I say in order to teach you to put on that adornment which the great apostle Paul taught us:
"Not gold or silver, but works of godliness, which endure forever and clothe those who acquire them with a shining crown."
But if you seek glory from people,

even so, acquire divine works. No one praises you for bodily adornment; even if the foolish and lovers of the world should praise you, rather even they do not praise you, but rather envy you. But for divine works both the good and the wicked praise you, and you will receive great praise from people and a reward from God on that day of judgment.

Let us therefore put on such adornment, so that we may fare well here too and find eternal good things there, which may we be worthy to attain by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom glory befits the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
Chapter 62
This saying:
"There was a certain sick man, Lazarus of Bethany, from the village of Martha and Mary, his sister.

And this was the Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment." Many people, when they see one of those pleasing to God in some affliction, bodily sickness, or poverty, or anything else, stumble and do not know
that such things come especially upon those who love God, since Lazarus too was a friend of Christ and was ill; for it says:
"There was a certain sick man, Lazarus in Bethany."
Not in vain did he also mention the place Lazarus was from, but for the reason that he states below. But now let us speak about what lies before us, how he also makes known his sisters:
Gospel: "For this was the Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment."

Commentary: At this place some say, "How did he endure this from a woman?" First, then, it is good that you should know that this is not the harlot whom Matthew speaks of, nor the one whom Luke speaks of, who anointed the Lord with ointment. For those were harlots, full of much wickedness, but this one was zealous and honorable and served Christ exceedingly well. And the evangelist shows that he loved the sisters very much as well; yet, despite all this, he allowed Lazarus to die. But why did they not go to Christ themselves,
as the centurion did, and that nobleman, but instead sent to him?
Because they greatly trusted in Christ and had great intimacy with him.
It is clear, then, that Mary was not one of those harlots, as I have said. And if someone should further say, "And why did the Lord receive those women?" It was for this reason:
so that he might loose sin and show his love for mankind, so that you might know

that there is no disease that could overcome his goodness. And do not look only at this, that he received them; look also at how he converted them. For why does the evangelist mention the matter of the ointment at this place? For this reason: to show that she loved the Lord greatly. And he says many times that:
"Jesus loved Lazarus and his sisters," in order to teach us not to lose heart when some sickness comes upon zealous and God-loving people.
Gospel: "His sisters sent to Jesus and said to him: 'Behold, Lord, he whom you loved is sick.'"
Commentary: They wanted to bring Christ by moving him to compassion, and they still thought of him as a man. This is evident from the word they said, namely:
"If you had been here, he would not have died." And they did not say, "Behold, Lazarus is sick," but, "Behold, lo, he whom you loved is sick." But hear what the Lord said:
Gospel: "This sickness is not unto death."

Commentary: Since he intended to stay there two days, he sent them this message. Because of this one must marvel at Lazarus's sisters: how, when they had heard his word, that "This sickness is not unto death,"
and afterward saw him dead, they did not stumble, but came to the Lord still with faith, and did not count him as having been proved false. And here too, then,
where he said, "that God may be glorified": this word "that" does not express cause but outcome, for that sickness came about for another cause, but he did not [?] use it for the glory of God.
Gospel: "And when he had said this, he stayed in that place two days."
Commentary: Why did he stay? For this reason: that he might die and be buried, so that no one could say that
he did not raise him from the dead. For this reason too he stayed so long, until they said, "He stinks."
Gospel: "And after this he said to his disciples: 'Arise, let us go again to Judea.'"
Commentary: Why did he never consult with them before, and now consults them? For this reason:
because they were greatly afraid. And so that he would not go there without their knowing and they be terrified, for this reason he consults them.
Gospel: "The disciples said to him: 'Rabbi, just now the Jews were seeking to stone you.'"
Commentary: For they were afraid for him too, but more for themselves. But see how Christ gives them courage:
Gospel: "Are there not twelve hours of the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world."
Commentary: Either he is saying this: "He who has done no evil walks in the light and has no fear of evil,
and likewise it is not right for us to fear, for I have done nothing evil and worthy of death?" Or he is saying this: "He who sees the light of this world does not fear falling, nor does he fall;

now then, if he who sees the light of this world [is so], will not all the more he who is with me and does not part from me remain without stumbling?" He said all this in order to dispel their fear, and he told them the necessary reason for going there, and to show them that he was not going to Jerusalem but to Bethany. For this reason he said to them:
Gospel: "Lazarus, my friend, has fallen asleep, but I will go and wake him."
Commentary: That is to say: "I am not going there in order to contend with the Jews again, but to wake my friend."
Gospel: "But they said to him: 'Lord, if he is sleeping, he will recover.'"

Commentary: They said this in order to prevent his going there, as if to say: You say that he is sleeping? Then there is no need for you to go there, for he will wake up by himself. Since, then, they did not understand, he therefore said to them:
Gospel: "Lazarus has died, and I rejoice for your sake."

Commentary: What does "for your sakes" mean? That is, that he was not there, and that he told them beforehand, and that he would raise him and root out every doubt from their hearts. Do you see how the disciples were still in weakness and did not know the power of Christ as they ought? It was their many fears that caused this. And when he told them, "He is sleeping," he said, "I am going to wake him," for he did not wish to announce beforehand in words what he was about to do in deed, and also so that he might teach us not to boast about anything.

But if someone should say, "Why did the disciples understand it as sleep and not realize that he was speaking of death, since he said, 'I am going to wake him'? For it would have been foolish for them to expect that he would travel so long a road to wake him." To this I say that the disciples supposed he was speaking in some figure, as he often did. For they were all afraid of the Jews, but Thomas more than all the rest; and for this reason he said to the others:
Gospel: "Come, let us go too, that we may die with him."
Commentary: For he was weaker than all the others. And some say that

"he too desired to die, and for this reason he spoke that word." But it is not so, for this word comes from fear. Yet Christ said nothing to him and did not rebuke him, for he bore with his weakness. In the end, however, he became stronger and firmer than all. And this is the wonder: he who before the crucifixion was so weak, once the Lord had been crucified and he had believed in his resurrection, became, as we see, more fervent than all. And he who did not dare to go to Bethany with Christ traversed the world alone without seeing Christ, and lived among peoples and cities that sought to kill him.

But how did the Lord find Lazarus four days dead? It was like this: on the day his sisters sent word to the Lord, on that same day Lazarus died. Behold, the first day! And when Christ heard, he stayed where he was two more days, and on the fourth day he came.
Gospel: "Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away; for this reason many Jews had come there."

Commentary: For it was fifteen stadia away, which is two miles; for this reason everyone knew of it, and many Jews had come to console them. Those who consoled them were people who were not very wicked, because they were friends of Christ; and others came because of the greatness of the trials that had befallen them, or else they showed them honor as noble and honorable people. But Martha met him first and did not bring her sister with her,
so that she might tell him about the matter by herself. And see what she says:
So since the Lord had brought her to good hope, for this reason she went and called Mary as well.
This is the Mary of whom he said: "Mary has chosen the good portion."

And although she was the more fervent, she had not learned of it, and that is why Martha came first. For it is not that Mary knew and did not come; rather, she did not know, whereas Martha came. And when she came, she said to the Lord:
Gospel: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."

Commentary: Do you see the wisdom of the women? Although they did not yet have perfect understanding, they nevertheless showed altogether great wisdom, for when they saw Christ they were not moved to mourning or to wailing,
as we do when we see one of our acquaintances who has come to us in our mourning. Rather, when they saw him,
they immediately glorified the Teacher and believed in Christ, but not as they ought to have, for they did not recognize that he was God,
or that he did everything by his own authority and power. And the Lord then taught them both of these things, for they did not yet know that he is God, and for this reason they said:
"If you had been here, our brother would not have died." And again, they did not know that he was saying all this by his own authority. For this reason Martha said to him:
Gospel: "And even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you."
Commentary: For she was speaking as if of some virtuous and God-loving man.
Gospel: "But Jesus said to her: 'Your brother will rise.'"
Commentary: He turned that word back. She had said, "Whatever you ask of God, he will give you." But he did not say, "I will ask," but rather:
"Your brother will rise." And when she said, "He will rise on the last day," he then revealed his power more fully and said:
Gospel: "I am the resurrection and the life."
Commentary: He shows her that he has no need of other help, since he himself is the resurrection and the life.
For this reason he also added: "Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, shall live," to show that he is the giver of good things and that one ought to ask from him.
Gospel: "Everyone who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live."

Commentary: See how he raises her mind. For what was being sought was not only that he should raise Lazarus. It was also necessary that the woman, and the others who were there, should learn about that resurrection too, about which he said:

"I am the resurrection." He said this so that she might know that, since he is the resurrection and the life, the life that comes from him does not depend on place, but wherever Jesus is, he is able to heal. For if they had said to him, as the centurion did, "Say the word and he will be healed," he would have said it. But since they had summoned him, he did this and went, so that he might teach them good understanding. For when he went to that place, he shows them that he was able to heal even without coming. For this reason he also delayed, so that the body would begin to stink, so that his grace might be spread abroad all the more. But where did the woman know about the eternal resurrection from? She had often heard Christ speak about the resurrection, but now she longed to see it. And see how she was still lying low in her mind. For she heard Christ say, "I am the resurrection and eternal life," and even so she did not say, "Raise him," but said to him, "I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God." And for this reason the Lord said to her:
"Everyone who believes in me, even if he dies, will live."

Here he is speaking of this bodily death. But when he says, "Whoever believes in me will never die," he is speaking of that eternal death. For this reason he says to Martha: "Since I am the resurrection and the life, do not be afraid. For even though your brother has died, he will live." For in that situation he consoled her and gave her hope with the words he spoke to her: "He will rise," and "I am the resurrection," and:

"Once he has risen, even if he dies again, nothing will harm him." And therefore we must not tremble at death. The saying he speaks means this: "Neither has this man died, nor will you die, you who believe in me."
Gospel: "'Do you believe in me?' Martha said to him: 'I believe, Lord, that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into the world.'"

Interpretation: I think the woman did not understand the saying. She knew that it was something great, but she could not properly understand what it was. That is why Christ asked one thing and she answered another. Still, she gained this much: her great grief was relieved, because such is the power of Christ's words. That is why Martha went ahead and Mary followed, for their love for the Teacher was driving away their grief.
So, along with the grace given to them, the understanding of those women also deserves praise.

Homily 62. It is not right to mourn the dead beyond measure, because this is what unbelievers do, and we should give alms for those who have died. Now, among our other sins, this too is an evil: mourning the dead beyond measure. Some wail aloud, tear their faces and pull out their hair. Some do it out of grief, and some for show. O believer, why do you do what unbelievers do? You gather choirs, stage an organized lament, and bring in women who weep aloud and to a tune. Is all this not madness?
Will the pagans not laugh at us, count every mystery of the Christian faith a fable, and say: "Look, the words written in your books are lies,
for otherwise, if you were expecting a resurrection, what is all this mourning? If you hoped that in the age to come there is a higher life, to which this departed person has passed over, why mourn?"
"So all their preaching must be empty. If the chief of their blessings is not believable, what else could be believable?" Do not do this, or we will become an object of reproach to the pagans.
Not all of them do this either. Many of them have shown wisdom.

For a certain woman's son was killed in battle, and when they told her, she not only did not weep, but rather began to ask about the other news of the city. And another philosopher had a crown on his head, as the other philosophers did, and they told him:
"Your son was fighting for this city of ours and has been killed," and he at once took off the crown and asked
which of his two sons it was. And when he learned that the one he loved was the one who had died for the city, he at once put the crown back on.
And for this reason I am ashamed that pagans prove more courageous than we are, and that
those who do not know the word of the resurrection act like people who know, while we who know about the resurrection behave
as if we did not know; and that those who have no fear of God, but do this for the sake of human concerns,
do what we do not do for the fear of God. And are we not worthy of great judgment? For the Lord says:
"Blessed are those who mourn." Yet no one mourns with that kind of mourning for the life of his own soul. And this other mourning,
which we were never commanded, is the one we practise? But some people say:
"Who can keep from weeping for his father, or son, or brother, or someone else like that?"
I am not forbidding anyone to grieve, nor am I saying, "It is not right to feel pain." What I condemn is that unseemly behaviour.
I am not so like a beast, nor so pitiless; I know that nature is under constraint and that it is impossible not to be grieved,
for Christ showed this when he wept over Lazarus,
and so you too may weep, but with the fear of God, and with quietness and dignity.

If you weep in this way, it is no sign of unbelief, and you are not mourning as one who disbelieves in the resurrection, but because you cannot bear the separation; for when our own people go away even on a journey, we are sorrowful. In the same way you too may weep, as if you were sending someone off on a distant journey. And even this I do not lay down for you as a law, but I make allowance for you and say that it is no fault if you do this thing in such an orderly manner. But if the one who has died was a sinner, grief and weeping are fitting for him, and rather not weeping alone, for this benefits him nothing, but that we should perform acts of mercy and offerings and liturgies for them, and that we should give thanks to the Lord, who knew that he would not come to repentance and for this reason took him away early, so that he might sin no more.

And if he was righteous, even so one ought to rejoice, for he has escaped the snares of the world and has entered the harbor without being drowned. And if he was a young man, let us rejoice in the same way, for he has been removed from the evils of the world. And if he was old, God gave him much time for doing good and only then took him away. But you consider none of this; instead you gather mourners, as though you were honoring the dead person, when this is the utmost dishonor. For the honor of one who has gone to his rest is not tears and the voices of mourners, but hymns and prayers and psalms. And if you wish to honor the dead person, honor him in another way: give alms. Otherwise, what benefit will come to him from so much lamentation? How long are we earth and ashes, how long are we blood and flesh? Let us look up to heaven, let us understand the spiritual matter. How shall we console the pagans, how shall we speak to them about the resurrection, when we ourselves behave like this?

Or how will we ourselves fare? For immoderate grief darkens the eyes of the soul and does not allow it to see anything better; we grieve God, we can do nothing to benefit the dead person, and we harm ourselves. But if we act as I have said, we shall both please God and benefit ourselves. And if anyone should say, "How can I not grieve for a son or a father?"

I do not say, "Do not be grieved." I say, "Do not lament beyond measure." If we understand that it was God who took them from us, and that our father and our son were mortal, then we will find comfort. A human being was born mortal, and as a mortal he died. So why are you sorrowful over something natural?

Surely you are not sorrowful that your son eats, which is a natural thing? Death is natural in the same way. Do not look for immortality in what is mortal, and do not lament. Instead, accept the law laid on human nature, and lament for your sins. That mourning is good. That is the mark of great wisdom. Let us take up this mourning, so that we may find joy there, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.
Chapter 63

This saying: "Jesus had not yet come to Bethany, but was still in the place where Martha had met him. But the Jews who were with Mary in the house and were consoling her, when they saw that Mary rose quickly and went out, followed her, thinking that she was going to the tomb to weep for him."
Interpretation: Wisdom is a great good, and by wisdom I mean divine wisdom,
But the wisdom of the pagan philosophers is vanity and a fable, for they did everything for the sake of human glory.

But spiritual wisdom is great; it makes a person honored both before God and before people. For whoever has despised the affairs of the world finds good even here, because he is freed from vain cares. And again, whoever tramples on the glory of the world finds rest even here, because he no longer needs to be a slave to people but has true freedom. For see, this woman too showed wisdom,
for many were sitting around her, and she was mourning and lamenting, and she did not expect the Teacher's coming to her,
but he was coming to meet her, as the Evangelist says:
Gospel: Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still there, in that place

Commentary: For he was walking slowly, so that no one might think that he was hurrying toward that miracle, but rather so that they might entreat him; or again the Evangelist indicates this: that Mary came so quickly that she found him in that same place.
But she came not alone, but with many Jews, and the others did not know where she was going, for this is why her sister spoke to her secretly, so that the others would not know.
But they followed her in order to carry out the mourning with her, and by this he again confirms the death of Lazarus.
Gospel: Now Mary, when she saw the Lord, fell at his feet

Commentary: This one was more fervent than her sister, for she was neither wary of that crowd nor of the suspicion they held concerning Christ, for some of his enemies were wicked, who were even saying:
"Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind man, have done something so that this one also would not have died?"
But she drove away all human concerns and sought one thing only, the honor of the Lord, and she said to him:
"Lord, if you had been here, that brother of mine would not have died."
But why is it that the Lord said nothing to her, as he had earlier to her sister? Because a great crowd was there, and it was not the time for such words,
but he begins to humble himself and to show his human nature, and he showed no great deed,
but he wished to lead them there, so that there he might show those crowds that great miracle, for he had not yet done one so great, from which great benefit would be given to the people.

For this reason he also led many there as witnesses of that deed by his humility, for this is why he began to act thus in human ways, so that they would follow him and not go away. And he reveals his human nature, for he weeps, and then he rebuked that mourning, for when it says, "He was troubled in spirit, as if with anger," it indicates this: that he checked that agitation of mourning. And thus he asked:
Gospel: Where have you laid him?

Commentary: So that the question would not be with tears. But why did he ask? Because he did not wish to go to the matter by himself, but to learn of it from them and be entreated, and only then to act, so that he might remove them from all suspicion.
Gospel: They said to him, "Lord, come and see," and Jesus wept

Commentary: For he was not yet showing any sign of raising him, nor did he go in such a way that others might think that he would raise him, but they thought that he was going in order to weep. For this reason some were saying:
Gospel: "'See how he loved him.' Some were saying: 'Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man have done something so that this one also would not have died?'"

Commentary: Not even at such a time did they stop their wickedness. See how they use this matter to slander the earlier miracle as well. For they said, as it were, "They would discredit that miracle too, for could he not [?] have made it so that this man would not have died either?" They wanted to discredit that miracle too, because what they were saying amounted to this:

"If he had done that, could he not have done this?" And they do not wait for the end to see what he will do. Yet raising a dead man was far greater than keeping a living man from dying. Do you see how corrupt their minds were?

Gospel: "Then Jesus, again groaning as if with indignation within himself, came to the tomb." Why does the evangelist say over and over, so insistently, that "he wept" and "he was indignant"? So that you may know that he truly put on our nature. Since this evangelist speaks of lofty and divine things about him more than the others do, he showed great lowliness here. For about the death he did not say, as the others did,

"he was sorrowful." Instead he said the opposite: "he threw them down on their faces." So he speaks here in this lowly way because he did not do so there. About the death he speaks this way: Jesus said, "I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again," and he says nothing human there. Therefore here he does something very human, to confirm his humanity. Matthew points to his human nature through his sorrow, fear and sweat, but this evangelist does it through his grief. If he had not truly been of our nature, how could he have been overcome by grief once and even twice? But he said nothing to the Jews who were accusing him, for what need was there for words, since he was about to act [?] by deed? Gospel: "Take away the stone."
Commentary: But why did he not call him from a distance and bring him out? Or why did he not raise him while the stone was still on him?
For he who made the lifeless body of a dead man alive and sent out a man who was still bound: could he not have raised him even if the stone had been on him? Why then did he not do so?

So that they themselves would be witnesses of that wondrous deed, and could not say, as they did about the blind man, "It is he," while others said, "It is not he." Or they might have considered the event an illusion, or one person put in place of another. But the going to the tomb, the removal of the stone, the rising of the bound man, the command to untie him, the presence there of people who knew him, the recognition by the grave clothes too, and the sight of the sisters, and also Martha saying, "Look, he already stinks": all this shut the mouths of those wicked people and bore witness to that miracle.
For this reason too he commands that the stone be taken away from the tomb, and for this reason too he first asked:
"Where have you laid him?" So that those who said, "Come and see!" could no longer say that
it was not he whom he raised; so that both their word and their hands might bear witness: the word that was spoken to him, "Come and see!"
and the hands, which took away the stone and loosed the bonds, and the eyes, which saw him coming out, and the nostrils, which the stench struck.
Gospel: But Martha said: "Lord, he stinks, for it is the fourth day."
Commentary: I might well say that the woman did not know what that saying of Christ meant, the one in which he said: "Even if he dies, he shall live."
For see what she says here, as though about an impossible thing, since the raising of a dead man four days decayed was indeed something strange. But the Lord said to her:
Gospel: "Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?"
Commentary: To the disciples he said, "That the Son of God may be glorified by it," but to Martha he speaks of the Father: "That God may be glorified," he says.
Do you see how the weakness of the hearers was the reason for the change of words?
And he reminded her of his word and reproved her for not remembering it, and said to her: "Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?"

Instruction 13, on faith. For faith is a very good thing and the cause of great good things, so much so that through faith people become able to do the works of God in his very name, for the Lord says:
"If you believe, you will say to this mountain, 'Move!' and it will move," and: "Whoever believes in me will do greater things than I."
And what is this "greater"? For the shadows of the apostles worked miracles, by which Christ was glorified,
for it is not so great a thing for Christ to work miracles while he was in this world, as for greater wonders to be done by others in his name after his death,
For these were the undoubted signs of his resurrection.

So faith is a great good when it comes from a fervent mind and a good soul. Faith makes us appear great. It covers the worthlessness of human beings, draws the mind up to heaven, and finds what human wisdom cannot find. So let us follow it well. Why could the pagans not know anything? Had they not found all human wisdom? And why, then, could they not overcome fishermen and tax collectors? Because they tried to do everything by human wisdom, while the apostles did everything by divine faith. That is why the apostles trampled down Plato, Pythagoras and all the other erring philosophers. They scattered like dust the power of the astrologers, geometers, arithmeticians, rhetoricians and all the rest. They became as much better than these men as a true philosopher is better than a madman and an ignorant man! At once they said, "The soul is immortal." And they did not only say it; they also convinced everyone.

But those others at first did not know at all what the soul is. Then, when they did learn of it and distinguished it from the body, at once the same thing happened to them again, for some of them said, "It is bodily," and some said, "It is twofold and not simple," and some said, "It is dissolved together with the body." And again, concerning heaven, some of them said, "It is a living being and it is a god." But those fishermen, the apostles, preached in harmony, taught by God, and they taught everyone. And if the pagans are in error, what wonder is that, since even those who think themselves believers fall into such evils?

That is a reproach and a stumbling block to themselves. For this reason they went astray, and some of them dared to say: "We know God just as he himself knows himself," which none of the apostles said or preached. And again, some of those who had gone astray said:

"A good life and godly conduct are of no benefit, but only faith." But this is known to all: that faith without good works is of no benefit. Both Christ and the apostle Paul confirm this, as the Lord says:

"Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does the will of my Father in heaven." And again he says: "They will say to me on that day: Lord, did we not prophesy in your name? And I will say to them: I do not know you." And again he says: "Do not rejoice when demons obey you, for those who do not guard themselves easily turn aside to wickedness, even if they have right faith." Rather, let us flee from evil deeds, for it is impossible to see Christ without good deeds, as the apostle says: "Pursue peace and holiness, for without this no one will see the Lord."

For this reason I constantly command you to chastity, so that each person may be content with his own spouse, whom he has lawfully married, and not defile himself with the filth of adultery. For everyone who commits adultery finds no mercy but is liable to perdition, even if he has countless other virtues.
For no adulterer will see the rest of the kingdom of heaven, but he is given over to Gehenna, and of such people God says: "Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched,"
and he has not a single mercy,

he who has a spouse and defiles himself with others. Since some keep themselves even from their lawful spouse at the time of fasting and prayer, what mercy will there be for the one who is not content even with her, but brings in another?
And whoever leaves his lawfully married wife and joins himself to another is reckoned an adulterer, as the Lord says:

He who still has his own wife and defiles himself with another, what can anyone say of him? Let no one allow this disease to settle in his soul, but let him tear it out by the roots. For this deed is abominable before God, as the Lord says:
"If anyone dismisses his wife except on account of fornication and marries another, he has committed adultery and has also cast his wife into adultery." For fornication is evil, evil!

It brings undying judgment on the person who does it. Even in this world every adulterer lives an evil life and is a slave of evil. He enters another man's house with fear and great trembling, and he is suspicious of everyone, both slaves and free. So I beg you: put away this evil disease. Those of you who do not put away this evil, do not enter the holy church. No one brings a sheep covered with mange in among the healthy ones. Instead, he keeps it far from them until its disease is cleared away. We are members of Christ, so let us not become members of a harlot. This place is not a brothel; it is a church. If you have the members of a harlot, do not stand in the church, so that this holy place may not be dishonoured,

For how can you bring yourself, after so many vows and so much splendour at your wedding, to commit adultery against your wife like this and defile yourself? Or how can you divorce her for some reason other than fornication and marry another? Are you not ashamed? Do you not fear God?

People who marry a second time after their first spouse dies are looked down on by others, even though the act carries no punishment. But you marry another while your spouse is still alive. How is this not wickedness? It is about such people that the Lord says: "Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be quenched." Fear this word and this wrath! Tremble at that judgment, because the pleasure here is not as great as the torment there. But may no one become liable to those bitter torments. Instead, may all keep purity and attain those eternal good things, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ. To him belong glory and might, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
Chapter 14
This saying: "And Jesus lifted up his eyes to heaven and said:
'Father, I thank you that you have heard me. And I know that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of the people who are standing around me.'"

As I have said many times, I say the same now too: the Lord does not look so much to his own honor as to our salvation, nor is he eager to speak lofty words, but rather such words as we may benefit from,
and for this reason he speaks lofty and great words seldom, and even those in a hidden way, but words of a humble kind very many times.

So at that time Jesus Christ, the King of all, saw that they gained greater benefit from humble words. Yet he did not always speak humbly, so that this would not become a cause of harm to later generations,

Nor did he always speak in keeping with the divine nature, so that he would not cause them to stumble. For the perfect can understand everything from a single lofty word, but the lowly, and those still in a subordinate state, cannot be brought round without hearing such words many times.

For at that time, after so many words and so many deeds, they were still stoning him and persecuting him and calling him a blasphemer. And when he said to the paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven you," they said, "He speaks blasphemy." And again, when he said, "Whoever hears my words will not be given over to death," they called him possessed by a demon. And when he said, "I am in the Father and the Father in me," they left him and took offense. And if they took such offense at these words, had he spoken in this way all the time, when would they ever have listened to him? But when he said, "As the Father commanded me, so I speak," and again, "I say nothing of myself," then they believed in him, as the evangelist says: "Because of these words many believed in him."
But now, if speaking in lowly words drew people to faith, and speaking in lofty ones to unbelief, how is it not complete senselessness not to look for the reason

why he spoke in this lowly way? It was the weakness of his hearers. In another place, for instance, he wanted to say something lofty, but he kept silent and gave Peter the reason: "So that they may not be offended."
cast a hook into the sea," just as he did in this place too,
for when he had said, "You always hear me," he added and said:
"I said it for the sake of the people standing around me, so that they may believe." Do you see these words? For he himself says:

"I speak in a lowly way for this reason, so that they may not stumble." Since he says this, and his deeds also show it to us, how can we fail to understand that those lowly words were spoken not because of his nature but because of the weakness of his hearers? For in another place too a voice came to him, and he himself said:
"This voice was not for my sake, but for yours."
And so for many reasons the Exalted One speaks humbly: because of his goodness and the weakness of his hearers, and again, in order to teach them humility, and further,

so that he might confirm his humanity; and so that they should think him an opponent of God [?]; and so that they would not be unbelieving about his coming from God; and so that they would not regard him as a destroyer of the Law; and again because of their envy; and because it was said many times in the Old [Testament]: "The Lord your God is one Lord."
For he was lofty by nature, and speaking in a lowly way did him no harm.
But one who is lowly by nature ought not to speak loftily at all, for this is arrogance. And now, if anyone should say:

"Why did he speak in such a lowly way, he who was of that lofty and ineffable essence?" Understand that he spoke this way for all the reasons given above, and also for this one: so that no one would think of him that he is unbegotten.
For the apostle Paul was afraid of this. That is why he said:
"Except him who subjected all things to him." But in another place he again points to his equality with the Father, saying:
"If I do not do the works of him who sent me, do not believe me," and again he says:
"I am in the Father and the Father in me," and again:
"He who has seen me has seen my Father," for concerning power he said, "I and the Father are one," and concerning authority he said:
"As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills." It would be impossible to say all this,
if he were of another essence and nature and were not his equal. For the word which says:
"That they may honour the Son as they honour the Father," and, "The works that he does, I also do," and again where he says:

"I am the resurrection and the life of the world." All of this is a sign of his equality. For all these words, which take the form of lowliness, were spoken because of the weakness of the hearers. They could not bear lofty words worthy of his divinity, but would have stumbled. They were also spoken for this reason: so that some would not regard him as unbegotten.

And what is so surprising if the Son, who became man for our sake, does this? Even the Father, who is bodiless and did not become man, often spoke in lowly forms for the sake of his hearers, so that they might benefit. For he says, "Adam, Adam, where are you?" – he who knew all things. And again he says, "so that I may know whether they are doing according to their outcry that has come to me." And again he says to Abraham:
"Now I know that you fear God." And again he says, "If only they would listen." And again he says, "Who will give to the heart of this people to do so?"
And again it is written:

"There is none like you among the gods, O Lord." And thus many words are found among the ancient writings too that are unbefitting the honor and glory of God. And again it is said concerning Ahab, "Who will deceive Ahab for me?"

And he constantly set his own superiority alongside the gods of the pagans, as in "There is none like you among the gods, O Lord," and many such things, all of which are unworthy to be said of God. But he is so loving toward humankind that for the sake of our salvation he takes upon himself those words which do not suit his honor and glory. For the incarnation too, and the putting on of a rational image, and the speaking of such words, and the taking upon himself of such contemptible deeds, all this is unworthy when measured against his dignity. But if one considers that unfathomable depth of his love for humankind, all this appears worthy in view of his love for humankind. There is also another reason for his speaking humbly and saying such words: namely, that they knew and believed in the Father, but did not recognize the Son. And therefore he refers his words to the Father, as to one already acknowledged, for the Son was not yet trusted among them because of their blindness and lack of understanding. For this reason he prays and says:
"Father, I thank you that you have heard me." And if someone says, "If he gives life to whomever he wishes, just as the Father does, why does he pray like this?", then understand well the words of
the Gospel: "When they had taken away the stone, Jesus lifted up his eyes to heaven and said:
"Father, I thank you that you have heard me. And I know that you always hear me, but I said this for the sake of this people standing around, so that they may believe that you sent me."

Commentary: Let us then ask the heretic, "What do you say?" Did he receive power from that prayer and so raise the dead man? And if he did this through prayer, how did he do those other works without prayer, when he said to the demon:

"I tell you, come out of him"; and to the leper he said, "I will it; be cleansed"; and to the paralytic he said, "Take up your bed, and your sins are forgiven you"; and to the sea he said, "Be still"? For the apostles too often did not pray, but only [invoked?] [?] the name of Jesus and worked a miracle. And if his name was able to do such works, would he himself not have been able to do greater ones? Or why would he have needed prayer? And if he had needed prayer, his name would not have been able to do such works. Or when man was being created, what prayer did he use? Do you not see there the oneness of essence, in the words "Let us make man"? For if he had needed prayer, he would have been weak and unable to accomplish all his will. But let us see what his prayer is:
Gospel: "Father, I thank you, for you always hear me."

Commentary: And who has ever prayed in this way anywhere? For before he had yet said anything, he said, "I thank you," to show that he had no need of prayer, as if he were saying, "You do everything that I will." It is not that the Son was unable to do everything and for that reason said to the Father, "You hear me in everything."
Rather, their will and mind are one. Why then did he take on the form of prayer? Do not listen to me on this point, but listen to him himself, when he says:
Gospel: "For the sake of this people standing around me I have said this, so that they may believe that you have sent me."

Commentary: He did not say, "so that they may believe that I am inferior," or "that I need help," or "that without prayer I can do nothing," but: "that they may believe that you sent me." He did not say, "you sent me, a weak one, who can do nothing of myself," but he left all this aside, so that you would not imagine anything unfitting, and he set down the true reason for the prayer, that is: so that no one would think me opposed to you, so that no one would say, "He is not from God," so that I might show that:
"I do every work of mine according to your will."
And this expression, "You have heard me," is used also of friends and of equals.
Gospel: "And I know that you always hear me."
Commentary: That is to say: I do not need prayer in order to do my will, for our will is one, but I pray on account of the weakness of this people standing around.
Gospel: "And when he had said this, he cried out with a loud voice: 'Lazarus, come out!'"
Commentary: Why did he not say, "In the name of my Father, come out"?
Why did he not say, "Father, raise this man," but left all this aside and made the form of a prayer, yet by the deed displayed his own authority?
For this reason, because this too was a work of his wisdom: by his words he showed humility, and by his deeds authority.
For since they could say nothing else about Christ except only this, "He is not from God," and in this way were leading many astray, for this reason he rightly showed them that form too.
which that weakness of theirs indicated.
For it was possible to show his unity with the Father in another way as well, but the people were not able to understand those lofty matters.
Gospel: "And he said: 'Lazarus, come out!'"
Commentary: This is what he was speaking of when he said: "The hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of Man, and those who hear will live."
And so that you might not suppose that he received that power from another, he therefore taught you from the very beginning and demonstrated it through deeds, and he did not say:
"Arise," but: "Come out!" He spoke to the dead man as to one living. What could be equal to this authority?
Now, do you not understand that he had no need of prayer, but was speaking on account of the people? And as he said:
Gospel: "On account of this people standing around me I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me."

Commentary: And it is evident that if they had believed, prayer would have been of no need. For if that prayer had not been unnecessary to him, why did he lay the reason for the prayer on them? Or why did he not say, "so that they may believe that I am not equal to you"? Rather, when they supposed that he was abolishing the law, he said to them, "I did not come to abolish the law"; but for this reason he never said, "I am not equal," but always affirms his equality with the Father. But the heretic says:
"And did he not say, 'I did not come to do my own will'?" But this word too he spoke because of their weakness, and for the same reason for which the prayer also was made.

What is this saying: "You have heard me"? It means this: "There is nothing in me opposed to you." Just as, then, this saying, "You have heard me," does not signify that he himself was able [?] (for if he had not been able, he would not have known that God hears, and if he had not known, how could he have said: "I am going in order to awaken him?" And he announced the miracle beforehand), just as, then, this is a sign not of weakness but of unity, so likewise is this saying: "I know that you always hear me." Since, then, he was neither ignorant nor weak, it is clear that he speaks such words of humility for this reason, that they might benefit them too, and that you might learn from the deeds that those words were spoken by way of dispensation and do not belong to his nature. What, then, is this saying: "You have heard me"? He said this on account of the weakness of the hearers.

But see his deed, how it bears witness to his power, when Lazarus came out bound. And then, so that they might not consider the deed an illusion (for the walking of a bound man was no lesser wonder than rising from the dead), he therefore commanded that he be unbound, so that they might touch him and come near him and know that it was truly he. And the Lord said: "Release him and let him go." But when this wonder had been done, some marveled, and some went and reported it to the Pharisees. And see this deed of theirs: for they ought to have been amazed at that act, but instead they plotted the killing of the one who raised the dead. O great folly! For he who had overcome death after it had entered into other bodies, him they thought to hand over to death, and they said:
Gospel: "What shall we do? For this man performs many signs."
Commentary: They still give the name of man to him, they who had seen so many tokens of his divinity.
Gospel: "What shall we do? If we let him go on like this, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."

Commentary: They wanted to stir up the people, and for this reason they frighten them in this way: that if the Romans see that he is gathering the people, they will accuse us of rebellion and take our nation captive.
Why, O wretched ones? Was he teaching you rebellion? Did he not command you to give tribute to Caesar?
Did you not want to make him king, and he fled? And did he not always seek a lowly life? And he had no house,

nor anything else of the things of this world. But understand, brothers, that it was not that they expected this to happen, or that they feared it from him and therefore said it; rather, they were saying it falsely,

in order to frighten the people, out of the envy they had toward Christ, for in this way they stirred up the people against Christ. But since they killed the Life of all, for this reason both their city and their nation were taken away, and the word they spoke falsely, which they did not expect, came true. Otherwise, whom did Christ teach rebellion?

For he was always putting down rebellion and teaching a godly life and obedience to rulers. For it was those earlier men who were teachers of rebellion, such as Judas and Theudas, whereas Christ taught everything good. Do you see that their word was spoken with guile?
For he did nothing of the sort. Did he not always keep to desert places?
But they did not want to reveal their own passion, and for this reason they made the city and the nation a pretext.
Yet this was not the cause of your being carried off captive, O Jews; rather, for this reason you were continually taken captive, both by the Romans and by the Babylonians and under Antiochus:
because there were among you those who provoked God to anger, and unclean people. This is what delivered you over to evil.
But envy sees nothing; rather, it blinds the soul.
Or did Christ not teach meekness and patience and godliness?
And are these teachings productive of tyranny, or destructive of it?
Teaching 14, on envy and greed: For, as I have said, envy is evil and full of treachery. It has filled the world with countless evils;
through it the law courts have been filled with countless evils;
from it come murders, loves of money, and vain boastings; from it come robberies and thefts;
Through this our race has suffered that great suffering, and whatever evil you may see is its offspring. Behold, it has come upon the churches as well and has done many evils.
This disease gave birth to love of money; this turned everything upside down; this overthrew justice; this made free men slaves.

For this reason we teach you every day, and no profit comes of it: we become worse than beasts, we seize what belongs to orphans, we wrong widows and plunder the poor. Woe upon woe has come upon us. "Woe is me, for the godly man has perished from the earth." It is right to mourn, for we have achieved nothing, either by prayer or by teaching. Now all we need is weeping, as Christ did. When he had taught the people of Jerusalem a great deal and they listened to none of it, he wept for them, as the prophets also did. We too do the same now, for it is a time of lamentation and weeping. It is good to say now as well: "Call the mourning women, and send for the wise women, and let them speak." Perhaps in this way they may be able to heal the disease of those who build splendid mansions and acquire estates by robbery.

Mourning for them is fitting, but help us, you too who have been harmed by them: mourn, shed tears. But when you mourn, mourn for them, for they have harmed not you but their own selves. For if you accept with thanksgiving the affliction they cause you, you will gain the kingdom of heaven, but they will gain the Gehenna of fire. Let us mourn for them from the Scriptures, with the mourning with which the saints mourned. Let us mourn with Isaiah and say: "Woe to those who join house to houses and bring field close to field, so that they may seize something of their neighbor's." Do not settle alone upon the earth: great and beautiful mansions, and there will be no inhabitants in them. Let us mourn with Nahum and say: "Woe to him who builds his house on high," and above all let us say with Christ the King: "Woe to the rich, who have received their reward." Let us mourn for them and not cease. Let us say, as the prophet did: "Do not mourn for the dead, but for the robber and the covetous and the lover of money and the insatiable."
Or why do we mourn for the dead, for whom conversion is not possible?

Rather, let us mourn for these, for whom conversion is possible, although while we mourn they often laugh. And this is what is worthy of mourning: that the one who ought to weep laughs. For if they were mourning, this would be a sign of amendment, but as it is they remain in senselessness. Therefore let us mourn for them, not for all the rich, but for those who were lovers of money, robbers, and covetous.

For it is possible to use wealth well, when we spend it on the poor. But covetousness is destructive and evil. Let us mourn for them, then, in case some benefit may come of it; in case, even if the fallen do not rise, at least others may no longer fall. Rather, may they too be worthy to escape from that disease, and may others not fall into it, so that all of us together may find those eternal good things, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and might, now and ever and to the ages of ages, amen.
Chapter 15
This discourse:
And a certain one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest of that year, said to them:
"You know nothing at all, nor have you considered that it is better for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish."

The heathen have sunk into the destruction that they made; in the snare that they set, their own foot has been caught. This happened to the Jews, for they spoke of killing Jesus so that the Romans would not come and carry them and their city off into captivity. And once they had killed the Lord, the very thing for which they killed him came upon them; and the deed that they did in order to be saved from captivity, because of it they became captives;
and he whom they killed is in the heavens, King of all, while his killers are dead in Gehenna.
And they did not understand this, but wished to kill him, and they said:
Gospel: "The Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
And a certain one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest of that year, said

Commentary: for he was more shameless than all of them: "You know nothing at all." While they were deliberating, debating back and forth and saying, "What shall we do?", he spoke with wickedness and insolence:
Gospel: "You know nothing at all, nor have you considered that it is better for us that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish."
But he did not say this of himself; rather he prophesied, for he was high priest."

Interpretation: Do you see how great the power of the high priesthood is? Since he had received the honor of the high priesthood, he prophesied even though he was unworthy of that office, and he did not know what he was saying. Grace used only his mouth to prophesy,
but it did not come near his defiled heart,
for many other unworthy people also foretold what was to come, such as Nebuchadnezzar and Balaam and Pharaoh, and the reason in each case was evident.
And the saying that he speaks is to this effect: "You are still negligent in this matter and regard him as something worthless, and you do not know that it is necessary for one to die for all."
See how great is the power of the Spirit, for out of a wicked mind it drew words full of marvelous prophecy.
But what does this saying mean: "He was high priest of that year"?

For along with other things the Jews had also abolished that rule, for they no longer served as priests all the days of their lives, but year by year, and for this reason high priesthoods came to be obtained by purchase. Yet in spite of all this, the grace of the Holy Spirit was still upon them to a small degree,
but once they had stretched out their hands against Christ, it then abandoned them completely and went over to the apostles.
and this was shown by the rending of the veil and by the word of Christ, who said: "Behold, your houses are left to you desolate,"
and again Josephus too, who lived a short time after Christ, said of the places that were with them that they abandoned them,

for as long as the vineyard stood, everything was carried out, but when they killed the heir of the vineyard, from then on they perished, and like the splendid garment of a slave who has run away, [?]
Thus Christ stripped his grace from the Jews and clothed with it those faithful servants of his from among the Gentiles, and he left the Jews naked and orphaned.
And this too was no small thing: that an enemy prophesied such prophecies, for in his mind he had another purpose,
and what happened was contrary to his will, for because he died, the believers have therefore been set free from eternal judgment.

And as it is written, he gathered together those far off and those near and made them all one body, and now the one who dwells in Rome regards the believers who are in India as his own member. What is higher than this unity? And the head of all is Christ.
Gospel: And from then on the Jews resolved to kill him.

Commentary: They had been seeking to kill him from the first, as it has been said: "They sought to kill him." But then they were only seeking, whereas now they confirmed their intention and began to set their hand to the deed.
Gospel:
But Jesus no longer went about openly in Judea
Commentary: Again he hides himself in human fashion, and I have often stated the reason why he would go away.
Gospel: and he stayed near the wilderness, in a town whose name was Ephrathah, and there he stayed with his disciples.

Commentary: What do you think, would the minds of the disciples not have been troubled when they saw him hiding in human fashion? And no one followed him, for the feast was near and everyone was going to Judea. And while everyone was rejoicing and celebrating the feast, they were in hiding and in fear. Yet through all this they remained with him, for in Galilee too, when it was Passover and when it was the feast of Tabernacles, they again hid themselves. And again after that, when it was the feast, flight and hiding with their teacher was a joy to them.

And for this reason Luke says: "Jesus said to them: 'You are the ones who have remained with me in my trials, and I have remained with you in trials.'" He said this to show them that they are strengthened by his power.

Gospel: And many went up to Jerusalem from the villages before the Passover to purify themselves, and a command had been given by the chief priests and the Pharisees that if anyone learned where he was, he should inform them, so that they might seize him.
Commentary: Oh, that purification, which they performed with murderous intent and with hands stained with blood!
Gospel: And they said to one another: "What do you think? Will he not come to this feast?"

Commentary: From the Passover they wished to do evil, and they were making the time of the feast the time for killing Christ. O the lawlessness! For when great reverence was due, and forgiveness even for those who had sinned, then they wished to kill the sinless one. At other times too they had hastened to do this deed, and not only were they unable to seize him, but they even became objects of reproach. For this reason he escapes from their hands again and again and makes them unable to touch him, so that by thus showing his power he might soften them, and so that, when they do seize him, they may know that the thing came about not by their power but by his permission. For even then they could not seize him, although Bethany was near, and even then, when they did seize him, he threw them down on their faces.
Gospel:
Then, six days before the Passover, he came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom he had raised from the dead. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those who sat at table with him.
Commentary: And this is a sign of a true resurrection, that after many days he was alive and eating, for that supper took place in his house, for they received Christ as beloved friends.
Gospel: But Mary took a pound of ointment of genuine nard and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped them with her hair.
Commentary: Behold, she fell down before him, not as before a man but as before God, for this is why she poured out the ointment and wiped his feet with her hair,
which is a sign that she did not see him as the others did. But Judas grew angry at her, as if under the guise of piety, and Christ answered:
Gospel: "She has done a good deed for my burial."

Commentary: And why did he not rebuke that disciple before he spoke these words against the woman, the words about which the evangelist says that he spoke them because of his own thievery? The Lord did not speak for this reason: so that by his great long-suffering he might put him to shame. For he knew that he was the betrayer. And he had made this known from the very beginning, when he said, "Not all of you believe this word."
And again he said, "One of you is a devil," and in this way he showed that he knew of his betrayal.

Yet he did not rebuke him openly but let him be, in case he might perhaps turn back. As another evangelist indeed says, "All the disciples said it, and he said it too"; but although the others said it, they did not say it with that intention. But if we should inquire how it was
that he was a thief and yet the Lord entrusted that purse of the poor to him to keep, seeing that he was a lover of money?
To this matter we say this: that God knows its hidden reason.

But if we too should say what we suppose, we say this: that it was in order to cut off his every pretext. For whatever he did, he did out of love of money, and he had from that purse a consolation for that desire of his. And for this reason Christ, who knew everything, did not rebuke his thievery at all,
for he wished that desire not to overpower him, and to cut off his every pretext, but he said only this:
Gospel: "Leave her alone, for she has done this for the day of my burial."

Commentary: Again he reminded the betrayer when he spoke of the burial, but the reproof did not touch him, nor did that word bend his heart, though it was very apt to soften him, as if he were saying:
"I seem burdensome to you, but wait for me a little and I shall go away." For this is why he said, "I am not always with you."

But none of these things bent that merciless and beast-like mind, even though he said and did far more than this to him: he washed his feet that night, and counted him worthy to sit at his table, and gave him bread,

all of which is able to bend even the soul of beasts; and he spoke words to him able to soften even stone. And he did all this not long before, so that it might have been forgotten, but on that very night on which he was betraying him. Yet he despised it all.

Moral teaching 65, on the love of money. For the love of money is evil, evil. It shuts the eyes and the ears and makes a man fiercer than a beast. It lets him consider neither the reproof of conscience, nor friendship,
nor the salvation of his own soul,

but once it has overcome a man, from then on it enslaves him completely, like a wicked tyrant. And what is worse is this: it persuades them even to be grateful to it. The more they serve it, the more their desire grows, and so the disease becomes incurable and the beast cannot be fought.
This made Gehazi a leper, this destroyed Ananias and Sapphira, this made Judas the betrayer of Christ;

this drowned the rulers of the Jews, who took bribes and became partners of thieves; this filled the roads with blood and the lands with mourning and lamentation; this defiled many and spread tables of filth and foods of lawlessness. For this reason Paul called it idolatry. But how is it idolatry? In this way: some have wealth and do not dare touch it, but keep it unapproached from son to son, like some holy thing that a person does not dare approach; and if ever they are forced to approach it, they feel as though they had done something evil. And they guard their wealth as if it were idols, shut up behind doors and bolts, and instead of a temple they have chests, and they keep it in vessels of silver. What do you say, lovers of money? Do you not worship gold as an idol? For even if you do not worship it, you still honor it in every way. And again, the idolater would rather give up his soul than lose his idol, and lovers of money are the same.

But if you say this, man: "I do not worship the gold," neither does that other man worship the idol, but the demon dwelling in it. And likewise you, even if you do not worship the gold, you still worship the demon that enters your soul from the gold and from the desire for it, which is more evil than any demon: the desire of love of money. It teaches you every evil and says to you continually: "Be a fighter against everyone, become a strange enemy to nature, despise God, offer yourself up to me." People offer sheep and calves to idols, but love of money says, "Offer your soul to me," and do you obey it? Do you see what kind of natures they have? What kind of offerings it seeks? The greedy will not inherit the kingdom of heaven, and yet the greedy man is not afraid. And this desire is weaker than all other desires, for it is not implanted by nature; otherwise it would have existed from the beginning.

But now we see that in the beginning there was no gold, and no one loved gold. This evil came in because each person, out of envy of another, began to acquire more, and so this disease spread. For when people see splendid mansions, many estates, silver vessels and every other kind of wealth, they immediately make every effort to outdo them. So the first become the cause of those who come after. Yet even so, lovers of money have no excuse before God, for there are many poor people both in the cities and in the deserts. Even if poverty is too much for you to bear, do not seize the possessions of others. There are many examples of this: people who do not seize anything, but have acquired their property justly and give alms from it. Why, then, do we not emulate and imitate them? Let us remember the men who lived before us. Do their mansions and estates not stand empty, with only their names attached, so that people say, "This is the house of so-and-so" and "This is the village of so-and-so"? Is it not [?]? Let us see how many labours he took on himself and how much he plundered for it, and now it is seen nowhere,
but others whom he never imagined enjoy themselves among his possessions.

And perhaps even his enemies are in it, while he has died a bad death? And this same thing lies before us, for without doubt we are going to die, and without doubt the same end will come upon us. For how many enmities with others did the builders of these mansions incur! How many robberies, how many losses!
And what profit came of all that? Eternal torment and not a single consolation to be found, and here too everyone now speaks evil of them.

Or when we see the portraits of many men, of rulers, painted on their panels, do we not mourn all the more? Truly the prophet spoke well when he said: "Every man toils in vain," for truly zeal for such things is vanity. But it is not so with those dwellings and abodes of heaven, for here one man toils and another takes his rest in what was built, but there each is lord over his own labor and will receive his reward many times over. Let us seek that reward; let us build houses there, so that we may find rest through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever, Amen.
Chapter 66
This saying: "All the people of the Jews learned that he was there, and they came not only for the sake of Jesus,
but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead." Just as wealth becomes harmful to careless men,
The same is true of power: the one leads to greed, and the other to arrogance. See here too how the crowd of the people was better off, while the rulers were utterly lost,
for the unlearned people believed in him many times, as the evangelists say: "Many of the people believed in him."

But the rulers did not believe, and they themselves said: "Has any of the rulers believed in him? Has not this unlearned crowd, who do not know the law, believed in him? They are accursed." So they cursed the believers, while calling themselves, the God-killers, wise.
And here too, then, when they saw the sign that Christ had done, many believed; but for the rulers that other evil was not enough, and they wished to kill Lazarus as well.
O wicked men, you said about Christ: "He breaks the Sabbath and makes himself God,
and the Romans will come because of him and carry us off captive." What will you say about Lazarus? What evil has he done? See how murderous their mind was,

For although the Lord had performed many miracles, they had not hardened themselves this much over any of them, for this one was greater than all the rest and wondrous: a man four days dead walking and speaking,

Yet in the case of the blind man and the paralytic they gave the Sabbath as a pretext and turned the people away, but here they had no pretext, and therefore they fought against the man who had risen from the dead,
for here they could no longer say even this: "He is opposed to the Father," since the prayer had shut their mouths. And since they could find no other pretext,
they then wished to kill him. And they would have done the same to the blind man too,

if they had not had the Sabbath there as a pretext. Moreover, that man was poor and of no account, and they cast him out, but this one was a man of distinction, and for this reason many had come to comfort his sisters, for the Lord raised him in the presence of all, and everyone went to see him. And this is why they were enraged like wild beasts: because during the days of the feast everyone was running to Bethany. And they wished to kill him and counted the deed as nothing,
so murderous were they. And for this reason the prophet says:

"Your hands are full of blood." But how is it that the Lord, who no longer went about boldly and had been in the desert, now again goes there boldly? Because by his departure he had calmed their anger, and now he came again when their wrath had been quieted. And again, that multitude of people who went before him and followed behind him was enough to disturb and distress them, for no other miracle could so sway the people as that of Lazarus. And another evangelist says that "they spread their garments on the roads" and "the whole city was shaken." With such honor he entered. And he did this in order to fulfill one prophecy and to prefigure another, so that his entry became the end of one prophecy and the beginning of another. For it became the fulfillment of that prophecy which says: "Rejoice, daughter of Zion, for behold, your king comes to you, gentle."

But his sitting on a donkey was a sign of something to come, namely, that the unclean race of the Gentiles was going to submit to his commandments. But how is it that the other evangelists say that "he sent disciples to bring the donkey and the colt," whereas this one says nothing of the kind and says only, "He found a donkey and sat on it"? It is because the others told how it happened and how he sent them, and this one did not wish to tell again everything they had said. Instead he says: "He found it and sat on it, and the people spread palm and olive branches and garments before him," in order to show that they regarded him as higher and greater, and not merely as a prophet. And for this reason they said: "Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."
